title: IYT Yachtmaster Coastal
note: Scenario questions written for study, close to the IYT Yachtmaster Coastal syllabus. Not official IYT exam content. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults to verify.

topics.title: Dead reckoning, estimated position & course to steer

questions.q: You draw a straight line on the Mercator chart from your departure to the next waypoint and read its direction off the rose. If you steer that true course, what track do you follow?
options: A rhumb line — one true course all the way
A line whose course changes at each meridian
A curve that bends towards the pole
A great circle — the shortest way on the globe
questions.why: Mercator keeps angles true: a straight line on it is a rhumb line, crossing every meridian at the same angle.

questions.q: You are measuring a leg near the top of this small-scale passage chart. Where do you read the miles?
options: On the longitude scale along the top edge
On the latitude scale level with the leg
On the latitude scale at the bottom edge
On any part of the latitude scale
questions.why: On a Mercator chart the latitude scale stretches towards the pole; read the miles level with the leg's own latitude.

questions.q: You span the leg A–B with the dividers and carry them to the chart's borders. How long is the leg?

figure.title: Leg A–B on the chart
lines: Dividers on the latitude scale beside
Same span on the longitude scale: 11.7'

questions.why: Distance is read on the latitude scale: 1' of latitude = 1 M, so 19.5' − 12.0' = 7.5 M. Longitude minutes shrink with latitude.

questions.q: You are closing an unfamiliar harbour entrance with rocky ledges either side. Which chart do you navigate on now?

figure.title: Charts aboard
lines: Now: closing an entrance between ledges

options: Chart A — it shows the whole picture
Either — both show the same dangers
Chart A — a smaller scale is more exact
Chart B — larger scale, more detail
questions.why: Use the largest-scale chart of the area: 1:25,000 shows dangers, marks and soundings that 1:150,000 leaves out.

questions.q: You plot a fix on this passage chart close to the coast. How much ground does a 1 mm slip of the pencil cover?

figure.title: Plotting a fix
lines: Your pencil point: about 1 mm wide

options: About 200 m
About 20 m
About 2 km
About 2 M
questions.why: 1 mm × 200,000 = 200 m, about a cable — too coarse near a danger. Move to a larger-scale chart.

questions.q: You need this buoy's position for your waypoint list. What do you write down?

figure.note: Parallels and meridians from the border

questions.why: Latitude: 0.9' south of 50°20'N = 50°19.1'N. Longitude: 3.0' east of 004°10'W = 004°07.0'W — west longitude falls eastward.

questions.q: Your crew reads the GPS position aloud: 50°18.5'N 004°06.0'W. Which mark on the chart is the boat?

figure.note: Parallels and meridians from the border

options: B
A
C
D
questions.why: 50°18.5'N is 1.5' south of 50°20'N; 004°06.0'W is 4' east of 004°10'W. The two meet at C.

questions.q: The next waypoint lies on your own parallel. How far away is it, and in which direction?
options: 5.0 M to the east
3.2 M to the east
5.0 M to the west
3.2 M to the west
questions.why: West longitude grows westward. 5' of longitude at 50°20'N = 5 × cos 50.3° ≈ 3.2 M — measure it on the latitude scale.

questions.q: Your crew plots the handheld GPS position on the chart, whose scales are in minutes and decimals. How far out is the plot?
options: About 3 cables, too far south
About 3 M, too far south
About 30 m — it does not matter
About 3 cables, too far north
questions.why: 45" = 0.75', not 0.45': the plot is 0.30' of latitude (0.3 M) too far south; 12" = 0.20' adds only 0.08' of longitude.

questions.q: Your GPS and plotter are set to WGS84. What do you do to a GPS position before plotting it on this paper chart?

figure.title: Chart title panel
lines: Depths in metres below chart datum

options: Convert it to a local datum first
Nothing — plot it as it is
Add the height of tide to it
Apply a datum shift north and east
questions.why: The chart is on WGS84, the same datum as the GPS, so its latitude and longitude plot directly.

questions.q: You are approaching the Galician coast on this older chart. Which position do you plot for the GPS reading?

figure.title: Note on the chart
lines: and 0.09' EAST to agree with this chart

questions.why: Northward adds to N latitude: 27.30' + 0.06' = 27.36'. Eastward takes away from W longitude: 16.40' − 0.09' = 16.31'.

questions.q: The plotter draws the boat on the breakwater while you are clearly in the fairway. What is the most likely cause?

figure.title: Entering the marina at dusk
lines: Plotter: boat drawn on the breakwater
You: mid-fairway, leading lights in line
GPS set-up menu: map datum ED50

options: The GPS antenna is mounted too high
The tidal stream has set you sideways
The compass needs a new deviation card
The GPS datum does not match the chart
questions.why: A GPS set to ED50 feeding a WGS84 chart shifts the boat 100 m or more. Set the GPS to the chart's datum.

questions.q: You are approaching this Aegean islet at night, steering by the plotter. What do you do?

figure.title: Night approach to an islet
lines: Chart from an old survey; its note:
by up to 0.3'; offset not known'
Plotter: reef 0.2 M off your track

options: Pass far wider than the 0.3' offset
Trust the plotter — GPS is good to 10 m
Keep the track — 0.2 M is two cables
Shift every GPS fix 0.3' to the north
questions.why: An unknown offset of up to 0.3' (about 550 m) is bigger than the 0.2 M gap. Pass far wider; check by eye, depth and radar.

questions.q: You plan to enter this harbour tonight. What do you make of the chart?
options: Fine — coastlines and depths seldom change
Out of date — get a current edition
Fine at night — the lights are unchanged
Fine — the edition is only a print date
questions.why: An old edition with no corrections misses the new breakwater and buoys. Navigate on a current, corrected chart.

questions.q: You find this old chart of a Greek bay aboard and plan to anchor on the charted 3. What depth do you expect at chart datum?

figure.note: Depths below chart datum

options: About 0.9 m
About 3.0 m
About 5.5 m
About 1.6 m
questions.why: Read the units in the title: 3 fathoms × 1.83 m = 5.5 m. Fathom and metric charts look alike at a glance.

questions.q: You are passing these three rocks at high water springs. Which one will you still see above the surface?
options: B — it dries 1.2 m above datum
C — it has a depth printed by it
None — every rock covers at HW
A — it stands 2.5 m above MHWS
questions.why: A figure in brackets is a height above MHWS, so A stays dry. B's underlined 1.2 dries only near LW; C has 4.3 m over it.

questions.q: Your passage plan runs straight over this wreck. What do you do?

figure.title: On your planned track
lines: Wreck symbol inside a dotted line

options: Replan to pass outside the dotted line
Keep the track — wrecks are a ship's worry
Keep the track, but only near high water
Keep the track — 18 m all round is ample
questions.why: A wreck inside a dotted danger line with no depth is dangerous to surface navigation: keep outside the line.

questions.q: Your track runs over the obstruction on the chart. What do you do?
options: Carry on — 9 m all round it
Alter round it — too little water
Carry on — obstructions are swept
Carry on — 2.2 m clears a 2.1 m keel
questions.why: Obstn 1.8 is a least depth of 1.8 m. With 0.4 m of tide that is 2.2 m — 0.1 m under a 2.1 m keel. Go round it.

questions.q: You want a quiet night at anchor in this bay. Where do you drop the hook?

figure.note: Chart extract

options: D — by the pipeline, buried in sand
B — on the foul ground, closer in
C — in the charted anchorage
A — beside the cable, in good mud
questions.why: Never anchor over cables, pipelines or foul ground: the anchor snags or does damage. Use the charted anchorage.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — anchorages, cables and pipelines

questions.q: You must anchor here for the night with a blow forecast. Which spot gives your plough anchor the best holding?
options: D — shells: hard, so it bites
B — weed: soft, so it buries
A — rock: it hooks under a ledge
C — sand and mud: it digs in
questions.why: Seabed on the chart: R rock, Wd weed, S sand, M mud, Sh shells. A plough holds best in sand and mud.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — nature of the seabed

questions.q: Your track rounds the headland through the area marked on the chart. What do you expect there now?
options: Steep, breaking seas — pass well outside
Smooth water — the stream flattens it
Shoal water, but only at LW springs
A helpful eddy close under the point
questions.why: Overfalls: the stream runs over an uneven bottom. At springs with wind against tide the seas stand up and break.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — overfalls and tide rips

questions.q: Your planned shortcut crosses this area. What do you do?

figure.title: Chart extract
lines: A magenta pecked line encloses an area

options: Cross it fast, without stopping
Read Note B and keep out if it bans entry
Cross it — such areas are for ships only
Cross it at night, when nobody checks
questions.why: The chart's note says what is prohibited — entry, anchoring or fishing. Obey it, and replan round if entry is banned.

questions.q: Your track crosses the area marked on the chart, where the soundings read 11–12 m. What do you allow for?
options: More water than charted — it is dredged
A ban on all small craft passing
Less water than charted — watch the depth
Strong eddies over the dumped ground
questions.why: A spoil ground is where dredged material is dumped: depths may be less than charted. Watch the sounder and don't anchor.

questions.q: You run the charted measured mile both ways to check your speed under engine. What is your speed through the water at these revs?

figure.title: Measured distance — 1852 m
lines: Run 1, with the stream: 6 min 00 s

options: 6.0 kn
7.5 kn
8.0 kn
questions.why: Average the speeds, not the times: 10.0 and 6.0 kn give 8.0 kn. The mean time, 8 min, would wrongly give 7.5 kn.

questions.q: You plan to cross the shipping lanes ahead. What is the tinted band between them?
options: The separation zone
An inshore traffic zone
A recommended track for yachts
A deep-water route
questions.why: The tinted band between opposing lanes is the separation zone: cross it as part of a right-angle crossing, never linger.

questions.q: What do 21m and 18/15M in this light's description tell you?
options: Tower 21 m tall; 18 M by day, 15 M by night
Light 21 m above MHWS; white 18 M, red 15 M
21 m of water off it; range 18 to 15 M
Light 21 m above LAT; red 18 M, white 15 M
questions.why: Elevation is the light's height above the chart's height datum, here MHWS; nominal ranges are per colour, W then R.

questions.q: You are approaching this sectored light at night. Which sector are you in?
options: Red — sector arcs are from the light
Both — the sector edges overlap
White — sector arcs are from seaward
Neither — the reversed 271° is dark
questions.why: Sector limits are true bearings from seaward towards the light: a bearing of 091°T falls in W 085°–095°.

questions.q: Fog closes in as you near this lighthouse. What do you listen for?
options: Two horn blasts every 3 minutes
One horn blast every 30 seconds
One horn blast every 2 seconds
Two horn blasts every 30 seconds
questions.why: Horn(2) 30s: a group of two blasts, repeated every 30 seconds. Time the cycle to identify the station.

questions.q: The shortcut passes close to the rocky shore, where there are no soundings inside the 10 m contour. What do you read into the blank?

figure.note: Depths in metres

options: Unsurveyed — rocks may be there
A flat bottom of exactly 10 m
Deep water — no soundings needed
Sand — soundings left out on sand
questions.why: A blank inside a contour means no data, not deep water. Near a rocky shore assume dangers and keep to the sounded water.

questions.q: Your crew points at the underlined figure in the middle of the bay and asks if you can sail over it at low water. What does it mean?
options: 21 m — the line marks a decimal
It dries 2.1 m above chart datum
2.1 m more water than charted
2.1 m of water over it at datum
questions.why: An underlined sounding is a drying height: the bottom stands that far above chart datum and is dry at low water springs.

questions.q: To reach the anchorage you must cross the drying bank on the chart. What height of tide do you need to keep your margin under the keel?
questions.why: Height of tide needed = drying height + draft + margin = 2.3 + 1.8 + 0.5 = 4.6 m.

questions.q: You are motoring up the river towards this bridge. What is the least clearance above your masthead you can ever have under it?

figure.note: Vertical clearances above HAT

options: 1.5 m at chart datum — less at HW
18 m — the figure is the gap above you
None yet — add the height of tide first
1.5 m, at HAT — more at any lower tide
questions.why: Charted clearance is above HAT, the highest predicted tide: 18 − 16.5 = 1.5 m is the worst case; a lower tide adds to it.

questions.q: You must pass under this bridge at tonight's high water. What margin will you have above the masthead?

figure.title: Bridge on an older chart
lines: Your air draft with antenna: 16.8 m

questions.why: Above MHWS the gap shrinks: 17.5 − 0.3 = 17.2 m, less 16.8 m = 0.4 m. Too tight for comfort if there is any swell.

questions.q: You are laying off courses on this chart this season. What variation do you use?
questions.why: (9'E) is the annual change: 10 years × 9' = 1°30' eastward, so 4°10'W − 1°30' = 2°40'W.

questions.q: Your crew lays the 245°M bearing straight off the rose's inner magnetic ring. How far out is the position line?

figure.title: Compass rose on an old chart

options: About 5° — the whole old variation
About 1° — variation changes slowly
About 4° — the ring is set for 1998
None — the inner ring is always right
questions.why: 28 years × 8'E = 3°44', so variation is now 1°16'W, not 5°W: the 1998 inner ring is nearly 4° out.

questions.q: You have applied this notice to your paper chart. How and where do you record it?

figure.title: Chart correction
lines: You have just inked it in

options: Beside the edition date in the title
In the logbook only, not on the chart
In pencil by the nearest compass rose
'2026-4512' in the bottom-left margin
questions.why: Small corrections are logged in the chart's bottom-left margin by year and notice number, so the next user knows its state.
questions.ref: Charts — corrections and Notices to Mariners

questions.q: Before the season you check this chart against the Notices to Mariners. Which do you apply?

figure.title: Bringing a chart up to date

options: All three, in number order
2026-0412 only, this year's notice
questions.why: Apply every notice after the last one recorded: 2988 is older than 3120 and already in; apply 3305, then 0412.
questions.ref: Charts — corrections and Notices to Mariners

questions.q: How do you put this temporary notice on your paper chart?

figure.title: Notice to Mariners (T)
lines: East cardinal buoy off the reef

options: In ink, like a permanent correction
In pencil, rubbed out when it is cancelled
Not at all — temporary notices lapse
In the margin only, not on the chart
questions.why: Temporary and Preliminary (T&P) notices go on in pencil and come off when the notice is cancelled or made permanent.
questions.ref: Charts — corrections and Notices to Mariners

questions.q: The leg looks clear on the plotter but not on the paper chart. Why?

figure.title: Plotter, vector chart
lines: Zoomed out to see the whole leg
Paper chart: an isolated rock on the leg

options: A recent update removed the rock
Plotters show only lit dangers
Vector charts drop detail when zoomed out
Raster charts never show single rocks
questions.why: A vector chart shows features by zoom level and display settings. Check every leg zoomed in, or with the route check.

questions.q: Your mate says 15 m is plenty, because the screen shows the rock so clearly. What do you say?

figure.title: Plotter at the harbour approach
lines: Approach chart from an old survey
Route drawn 15 m off a rock

options: Agree — zooming in makes the chart more exact
Agree — as long as GPS has four satellites
Agree — the raster image is the paper chart
Overscale magnifies the errors — give it room
questions.why: Zooming past the chart's scale enlarges its errors, not its accuracy; at ×8 on an old survey, 15 m means nothing.

questions.q: You are checking this route in your passage plan. Is the clearance off the patch enough?

figure.title: Vector chart, data quality
lines: Route: 0.15 M off a 3.0 m patch

options: No — 0.15 M is inside the position error
Yes — 0.15 M is more than a cable
Yes — GPS puts you within 10 m
Yes — the patch is deeper than the keel
questions.why: 0.15 M ≈ 280 m, well inside ZOC C's ±500 m: the patch could be under you. Pass at least 0.3 M off and watch the depth.

questions.q: You are feeling your way into this cove. How far do you trust the charted soundings and rocks?

figure.title: Plotter, vector chart
lines: Soundings 4–6 m, a few rocks shown

options: Fully — the stars mark a recent survey
Little — a poor survey; go slow on the sounder
Fully for depth; positions may be 5 m out
Fully — two stars is a top rating
questions.why: Two stars is ZOC D, worse than C: positions and depths are poor and rocks may be missing. Go slowly, sound and look.

questions.q: Your plotter has died on a night passage. What gives you your position now?

figure.title: 0200, 12 M offshore
lines: Paper chart: last fix plotted at 0100
Log written up hourly: course, log

options: Asking the coastguard for a position
Waiting for the plotter to reboot
A DR from the 0100 fix on the paper chart
Closing the coast to fix on a light
questions.why: This is why you keep a paper plot: the 0100 fix and the log give you a DR or EP at once.

questions.q: Tomorrow you leave a standard port. You need the time and height of HW, the harbour office's VHF channel and the coastguard's weather broadcast times. Which single book do you open?
options: The List of Lights
The chart symbols booklet
The pilot book for the coast
This year's nautical almanac
questions.why: The almanac holds the year's tide tables, tidal stream data, lights, radio data and port information in one book.

questions.q: You are entering this harbour for the first time. How do you use the pilot book's plan?

figure.title: Pilot book, harbour plan
lines: Plan shows the berths and the approach
Printed under it: 'Not to be used

options: With the chart — as a guide to it
Instead of the chart — it is newer
Not at all — it is not allowed
By day only, never at night
questions.why: Pilot book plans are sketches for orientation — berths, facilities, the approach. Navigate on the official chart.

questions.q: You are writing up the lights for a night arrival. Where do you find the full detail of this light?

figure.title: Lighthouse on the chart
lines: You need its sector limits, its fog
signal and how it looks by day

options: The List of Radio Signals
The List of Lights and Fog Signals
The chart symbols booklet
The tidal stream atlas
questions.why: The List of Lights gives each light's full description: sectors, phases, fog signal, structure and elevation.

questions.q: You will arrive at this port tomorrow. Which publication sets all of this out in full?

figure.title: Arriving at a big commercial port
lines: and the times of safety broadcasts

options: The chart symbols booklet
The List of Lights and Fog Signals
The List of Radio Signals
The tidal stream atlas
questions.why: The List of Radio Signals covers coast radio, safety broadcasts, VTS and port operations: channels, times, reporting points.

questions.q: You are planning to round a big headland and want to see the direction and rate of the stream across the whole area, hour by hour. What do you open?
options: The tide tables
The pilot book's harbour plans
The List of Lights
The tidal stream atlas
questions.why: A tidal stream atlas shows the streams over the area for each hour before and after HW at its reference port.

questions.q: On a newly bought chart you meet a symbol and an abbreviation you have never seen, close to your track. Where do you look them up?
options: Chart 5011, Symbols and Abbreviations
The List of Lights
The weekly Notices to Mariners
The pilot book's glossary
questions.why: Admiralty chart 5011 (the INT 1 symbols) explains every symbol and abbreviation used on the charts.

questions.q: Which set of charts and publications do you carry for this passage?

figure.title: Coastal passage, 48 M, overnight
lines: two ports of refuge on the way

options: Plotter charts, a pilot book and the radio list
Passage chart, charts of all four ports, almanac, pilot
Passage chart and almanac; the plotter has the ports
Charts of departure and destination; old almanac
questions.why: Carry paper charts of the route and of every port you may use, this year's almanac and a pilot book; the plotter is extra.

questions.q: You are passing this rock off the Brittany coast near low water. How high above the sea does it stand now?

figure.note: Heights above MHWS, depths below CD

questions.why: (3) is a height above MHWS: 3 + 5.2 = 8.2 m above datum. The sea is 0.8 m above datum, so 8.2 − 0.8 = 7.4 m.

questions.q: Your crew says you will see the rock on the chart and steer round it by eye. When can you expect to see it?
options: Never — it lies 3.1 m below datum
Now — awash means it is at the surface
At HW, when the sea breaks over it
Only near LW — now 3.1 m of water covers it
questions.why: Awash at chart datum: it shows only when the tide is near datum. With 3.1 m of tide it is 3.1 m down — steer by a clearing line.

questions.q: Your track passes over this wreck. How much water will you have under the keel at least?
questions.why: Swept to 4.2 m: nothing on it is shallower. 4.2 + 0.5 m of tide = 4.7 m of water, less the 2.0 m draft = 2.7 m.

questions.q: Your shortcut crosses the shoal patch on the chart, in a long Atlantic swell. What do you do?
options: Cross — swell only matters off a beach
Go round it — the swell may break there
Cross — 1.8 m under the keel is ample
Cross fast, so you are over it briefly
questions.why: 3.4 + 0.6 = 4.0 m, but a trough of a 2.5 m swell leaves about 2.75 m, and seas can break on the patch. Keep off it.

questions.q: Your planned track passes 2 cables south of the rock on the chart. What do you do?
options: Keep the track — 2 cables is ample
Keep the track, but only by day
Give it a much wider berth
Keep the track — PA means it is marked
questions.why: PA — position approximate: the rock was never fixed accurately and may lie some way from its symbol. Allow a wide margin.

questions.q: Your crew suggests sailing straight over the rock, since it may not exist. What do you do?
options: Sail over it slowly, watching the depth
Sail over it, but only at high water
Sail over it — ED means it is gone
Treat it as real and go round
questions.why: ED — existence doubtful: reported but never confirmed. Doubtful is not absent: plan as if the rock is there.

questions.q: The main light is already in sight. Your mate is now looking for this pierhead light, still 12 M off. When do you expect to see it?
options: Within about 3 M of it
Now — clear nights show every light
At about 12 M, with the main light
Within about 6 M — its elevation
questions.why: 3M is the nominal range: in clear weather this light carries only about 3 M. 6m is its height above MHWS, not its range.

questions.q: You are closing the coast at night, expecting to pick up this light. What do you see?
options: A red sector warning you off the land
Nothing — on 230°T it is obscured
Only its loom, as it stands 30 m high
The light — you are within its range
questions.why: Obscd 210°–245°: on those bearings from seaward land hides the light. You will not see it until the bearing leaves that arc.

questions.q: You are 20 M offshore heading in on a clear night. Which light do you see first, and at about what range?
options: A, at about 22 M
B, at about 19 M
B, at about 16 M
A, at about 11 M
questions.why: B clears the horizon at 2.08(√60 + √2) ≈ 19 M but its nominal range is 16 M; A rises only at ≈ 11 M. Take the lesser limit.

questions.q: On a hazy night you watch for this buoy on the radar. What does the chart tell you to look for?
options: A fog signal sounding T in Morse
An AIS target named T on the plotter
A white light flashing T in Morse
A Morse T painted just beyond its echo
questions.why: A racon answers your radar: it paints its Morse letter — here T, one dash — on the screen just beyond the mark's echo.

questions.q: At dawn you reach the position in the notice and see no buoy at all. What do you make of it?

figure.title: Notice to Mariners
lines: Marked by a virtual AIS aid (V-AIS):
east cardinal; no buoy laid yet

options: Normal — the mark exists only on AIS
Your GPS is off — you are lost
The wreck has been cleared away
The buoy has broken adrift — report it
questions.why: A virtual AIS aid is a signal, not a buoy: it shows only on AIS and the plotter. Treat it as an east cardinal and pass east.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — AIS aids to navigation

questions.q: You are approaching this mark on the chart. Which side do you pass it?
options: Either side, keeping close
East of it
North of it
West of it
questions.why: BYB with Q(3) 10s is an east cardinal: the safe water lies to the east of the mark.

questions.q: You arrive late in this crowded bay and want a buoy for the night. Which do you pick up?
options: C — the fish farm's corner buoy
A — any free private buoy
B — a visitors' mooring
D — the big buoy by the fairway
questions.why: The chart marks visitors' moorings for passing yachts. Private buoys have owners, and fairway or fish-farm buoys are not moorings.

questions.q: You need diesel for tomorrow's leg. What is your plan on arrival?

figure.title: Almanac — marina page
lines: Visitors: pontoon C; call Ch 37 first

options: Lie on the fuel berth overnight
Go straight to the fuel berth at 2130
Skip the call and take any free berth
Berth on C tonight, fuel after 0800
questions.why: The page gives the fuel hours: shut at 2130. Call on Ch 37, take a visitors' berth on C and fuel when it opens at 0800.

questions.q: You want to stop in this Croatian cove for the night. What do you do?

figure.note: Note D: no anchoring; visitor buoys

options: Pick up a reserve buoy; do not anchor
Anchor on the sand patch in 10 m
Anchor after dark and leave at dawn
Anchor in the weed — it holds well
questions.why: The chart's note bans anchoring inside the reserve to protect the seagrass. Use its mooring buoys or anchor outside the line.

questions.q: On this chart of the Norwegian coast your GPS reads 60°23.5'N 005°01.0'E. Which mark is the boat?

figure.note: Parallels and meridians from the border

options: B
C
A
D
questions.why: At 60°N a minute of longitude is drawn half as long as a minute of latitude. 1.0' east of 5°00'E and 0.5' south of 60°24'N meet at C.

questions.q: You are motoring east along the Norwegian coast on this leg. When do you reach the waypoint?
You check the plotter's figures for this leg against the chart. What course and distance do you lay off?
Both fixes lie on the same meridian. How far have you made good to the north between them?
questions.why: From 49°58.6' up to 50°00' is 1.4', then 3.1' more: 4.5' of latitude = 4.5 M. Count across the degree line.

questions.q: You have walked the parallel rule from your leg to the rose. What do you write in the passage plan?

figure.title: Laying off the course
lines: Parallel rule walked to the rose

questions.why: The outer ring of a chart rose is true and the inner ring magnetic. A °T column takes the outer reading: 062°T.

questions.q: You check the 0300 EP against the charted rocks. How far apart are they on the paper?

figure.title: Passage chart, 0300
lines: Charted rocks 0.5 M from the EP

options: About 0.2 mm
About 2 cm
About 2 mm
About 9 mm
questions.why: 0.5 M = 926 m; 926 m ÷ 500,000 = 1.9 mm, about a pencil dot. Near danger, plot on a larger-scale chart.

questions.q: What do you make of your mate's 2 cables?

figure.title: Night, passage chart
lines: EP drawn as a dot 1.5 mm across

options: Too coarse — it is nearer 2 M
Right — a dot is plotted to 10 m
Right — the scale does not matter
Too fine — the dot alone is 3 cables
questions.why: 1.5 mm × 350,000 = 525 m, nearly 3 cables: on this scale a 2-cable offset is lost inside the dot itself.

questions.q: The helm loses night vision every time you look at the plotter. What do you change?

figure.title: Night passage, chart table
lines: the white paper glares into the cockpit

options: Switch to the vector chart's night colours
Keep the raster but zoom right out
Turn the raster up bright for contrast
Switch the plotter off for the night
questions.why: A vector chart redraws itself in a dark night palette; a raster is a picture of the paper chart and can only be dimmed or tinted.

questions.q: You need this light's characteristic and sectors from the plotter. How do you get them?

figure.title: Night, vector chart
lines: Light shown only as a magenta flare
You need its character and sectors
No paper chart of this area aboard

options: Rotate the chart to north-up
Tap it to query the object's details
Switch the plotter to night colours
Nothing — vectors hold no light data
questions.why: A vector chart is a database: tap or cursor-pick an object to read its attributes — character, period, sectors, range.

questions.q: Which line does the plotter draw bold as your safety contour?
options: The 10 m contour
A 3 m line of its own
The 5 m contour
The 2 m contour
questions.why: If the chart holds no contour at the value set, the display takes the next deeper one: 3 m becomes the 5 m line.

questions.q: Your mate has just set up the plotter like this. What do you say?

figure.title: Plotter set-up
lines: Chart data ZOC C; seas 1 m

options: Set them shallower to cut false alarms
Fine — it warns you as you touch
Fine — the tide always adds water
Set them deeper: draft plus a margin
questions.why: At 2.1 m the alarm sounds as the keel touches. Add a margin for waves, data error and tide below datum: 3 m or more.

questions.q: The route check flags the bank on this leg. You will cross it near HW. What do you do?

figure.title: Route check on the plotter
lines: Leg crosses a bank charted 1.2 m
Height of tide when you cross: 3.5 m

options: Cross: 4.7 m of water, 2.6 m spare
Cross: 3.5 m of water, 1.4 m spare
Reroute — 1.2 m is less than your draft
Reroute — the plotter knows the depth
questions.why: The plotter judges depths at chart datum and ignores the tide: 1.2 + 3.5 = 4.7 m, less the 2.1 m draft = 2.6 m, over your margin.

questions.q: Before inking in this notice, what do you do?
options: Ink it in — the latest is all you need
Find and apply 2025-4410 first
Ink it in and log 2025-3982 again
Apply it in pencil until next year
questions.why: Each notice names the one before it for that chart. Yours stops at 3982, so 4410 is missing: apply it, then 1120.

questions.q: The new wreck lies near tomorrow's route, but the plotter shows clear water there. What do you do?

figure.title: Notice to Mariners, this week
lines: Marked by an emergency wreck buoy

options: Pass over it — 2.6 m is deep enough
Trust the plotter — it shows clear water
Plot it on chart and route; pass well clear
Ignore it — the buoy will show you
questions.why: Your 2023 cartography predates the wreck. Add it from the notice to the paper chart and the route, and keep well clear.

questions.q: Which of the listed notices do you apply to this chart?
options: Both, in number order
None — a new chart is up to date
questions.why: A new edition includes every notice issued before its date. Only those after 14 May 2026 — here 1544 — still go on.

questions.q: You arrive off the entrance at 2300. Whom do you call first?
options: Harbour Control on Ch 12
Nobody — just go in quietly
The marina on Ch 80
The coastguard on Ch 16
questions.why: The page says call Harbour Control before entering, round the clock. The marina office is shut after 2000.

questions.q: Can you cross the sill now, and with how much under the keel?

figure.title: Almanac — marina sill
lines: Sill dries 1.6 m above chart datum
Gauges at the entrance show the
depth of water over the sill
Gauge now 2.5 m · your draft 1.8 m

options: No — wait for the gauge to show 3.4 m
Yes — 0.7 m under the keel
Yes — 2.3 m under the keel
No — only 0.9 m over the sill
questions.why: The gauge already reads the water over the sill: 2.5 − 1.8 = 0.7 m. Taking the 1.6 m sill off again is the slip.

questions.q: Tomorrow's route takes you a cable north of the beacon. What do you do with this warning?

figure.title: Pilot book, 2024 edition
lines: 'A rock with 1.2 m over it was

options: Keep the track — reports are unconfirmed
Keep the track, but only at high water
Replan to keep clear of the reported rock
Keep the track — the chart is official
questions.why: A newer warning beats an older chart: plan round the reported rock until a notice confirms or cancels it.

questions.q: Your crew trusts the pilot book and wants to go in now. What do you do?
options: Go in now — the pilot is local knowledge
Go in now — silting notes are over-cautious
Go in now, sounding as you go
Wait for the flood — trust the newer chart
questions.why: The corrected 2025 chart is newer than the 2009 pilot: 1.4 m at LW is less than your 2.0 m draft. Go in on the rising tide.

questions.q: Which charts do you use on this leg, and when?

figure.title: Charts for a 50 M coastal leg
lines: B: 1:150,000 — the route on one sheet

options: B on passage, C at the headland, D to enter
D all the way — it has the most detail
C all the way — larger scale is safer
A all the way — one sheet is simplest
questions.why: Plot the passage on the largest scale that holds the route on one sheet (B); move to C and D where detail matters.

questions.q: Your track runs off chart 1 onto chart 2. How do you carry your position across?

figure.title: Moving to the next chart
lines: Chart 2: datum ED50, no shift note
Last fix on chart 1, 3 M off a

options: By latitude and longitude, as read
By bearing and distance from the lighthouse
By lat and long, adding 0.1' north
By the plotter's position, as shown
questions.why: Lat and long differ between datums, and chart 2 gives no shift. A bearing and distance from a feature on both charts carries it true.

questions.q: Your crew wants the GPS fix on this chart before you thread the Cyclades channel at dusk. Where does it go?

figure.title: Note on a Greek chart
lines: and 0.05' WEST to agree with this chart

questions.why: South takes away from N latitude: 05.40' − 0.10' = 05.30'. West takes away from E longitude: 22.80' − 0.05' = 22.75'.

questions.q: You are planning a Croatian passage this way. What is the risk at WP3?

figure.title: Planning in Croatia
lines: Waypoints read off an old ED50 chart
and typed into the WGS84 plotter
Chart note: datums differ by about 0.1'
WP3: in a 2-cable gap between islets

options: None — GPS works on any chart
Only the depths differ, not positions
WP3 is out by 10 m at the most
WP3 may be 200 m out — on the rocks
questions.why: 0.1' is about 185 m — half of a 2-cable gap. Apply the chart's datum shift to every waypoint, or take them off a WGS84 chart.

questions.q: You plan to lie overnight in the charted 2.2 m. What do you make of it?
options: Too tight — the sea may stand below datum
Fine — 0.2 m is a fair margin
Fine — high pressure raises the sea
Fine — Med charts use the lowest water
questions.why: Depths from mean sea level leave nothing in hand: a small tide and high pressure (about 1 cm per hPa) can drop the sea 0.2–0.3 m.

questions.q: You are cruising the Cyclades with this chart. What variation goes into your courses this year?
questions.why: 8 years × 6'E = 48' more east: 4°20'E + 0°48' = 5°08'E. An easterly change adds to an easterly variation.

questions.q: You planned a hand-bearing fix in this area. How do you fix your position here?

figure.title: Note on the chart
lines: of this position the compass may be

options: Hand-bearings, adding 9° to each
The steering compass, swung on the spot
Transits and GPS, not compass bearings
Hand-bearings, as you normally would
questions.why: The anomaly bends every compass by an unknown amount up to 9°. Fix by transits, ranges, depth and GPS until clear of it.

questions.q: Which variation do you apply to this leg?

figure.title: Two compass roses on the chart
lines: Your leg lies close to the east rose

options: 2°10'W, the larger of the two
2°10'W, the first rose printed
1°45'W, the average of both
1°20'W, from the nearer rose
questions.why: Variation changes across a chart: take it from the rose nearest your position.

questions.q: In thick fog and a flat calm you listen for this buoy's fog signal. What do you expect?
options: It may be silent — the waves ring it
A bell louder in a calm than in waves
A bell every 15 seconds, like a clock
A bell only when a ship comes near
questions.why: A bell on a buoy is swung by the sea: in a calm it rings rarely or not at all. Never count on hearing one.

questions.q: Your track crosses the area on Tuesday at 1100. What do you do?
options: Cross it — the line is only a guide
Call range control; keep out while firing
Cross it — yachts are always exempt
Cross it fast, keeping near the edge
questions.why: A danger area is not closed, but live firing makes it deadly. Check with range control and go round while it is active.

questions.q: You are approaching past reporting point 3 in your yacht. What do you do?

figure.title: Port approach, VTS in force
lines: Radio Signals: report at each point
if over 20 m; small craft monitor Ch 14

options: Report at every point, like a ship
Nothing — VTS has no say over yachts
Listen on Ch 14 and keep clear of ships
Call the coastguard on Ch 16 at each
questions.why: The List of Radio Signals sets the reports for vessels over 20 m. A 13 m yacht keeps watch on Ch 14 and out of the way.

questions.q: You need a quick lunch stop with your fluke anchor. Which bottom do you avoid?
options: C — fine sand: it is too loose
D — mud: it is too soft to hold
B — clay: it is too sticky to hold
A — stones: the flukes can't dig in
questions.why: St is stones: a fluke anchor skids over them. Cy clay, fS fine sand and M mud all let the flukes bury.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — nature of the seabed

questions.q: How far do you trust the inshore soundings for the short cut?

figure.title: Source data diagram, paper chart
lines: Inside the 10 m line: lead line, 1902
Your plan: a short cut close inshore

options: Little — rocks may lie between the lines
Fully — the chart is a 2024 edition
Fully — rocky bottoms do not change
As far as the offshore survey
questions.why: A 1902 lead-line survey sounded spots along lines; pinnacles between them were often missed. Keep to well-surveyed water.

questions.q: What does the U tell you about the survey of the cove?

figure.title: Plotter: data quality layer
lines: Soundings and some rocks are shown

options: Unsurveyed — so no rocks exist
Unassessed — its quality is unknown
Uniform — the best quality there is
Updated — surveyed this year
questions.why: ZOC U means the data have not been assessed. Treat the cove as poorly surveyed: go slowly, sound and keep a lookout.

questions.q: You have spanned the breakwater-to-berth distance in the inset. Where do you read it?

figure.title: Chart with a harbour inset
lines: You span a distance in the inset

options: On the nearest compass rose
On the main chart's latitude border
On the inset's own scale bar
On the main chart's longitude border
questions.why: An inset is a separate plan at its own scale: 1 cm is 150 m there but 750 m on the main chart. Use the inset's scale.

questions.q: Can you work the tides for this passage from this almanac?

figure.title: Packing the chart table
lines: The passage depends on two tidal gates

options: Yes, but only at springs
Yes — tides repeat every year
Yes — add 50 minutes to each time
No — tide tables are for one year
questions.why: Tide times and heights are predicted for each year; last year's tables are wrong for this one. Carry the current almanac.

questions.q: You are motoring out of Dartmouth on a calm morning with the log speed steady. How far through the water have you run by now?
You time the boat between two log readings to check her speed under the new sail plan. What is your speed through the water?
options: 5.2 kn
7.8 kn
3.9 kn
questions.why: 2.6 M in 20 min, a third of an hour: 2.6 × 3 = 7.8 kn. 20 min is 0.33 h, not 0.20 h.

questions.q: You are running along the north coast of Brittany at a steady speed over the ground. When do you reach the fairway buoy?
questions.ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

questions.q: You check the log against the plotter at slack water before a long passage. What does the difference tell you?
options: A fair stream of 1.5 kn is running
Leeway is adding 1.5 kn over the ground
The plotter over-reads: trust the log
The log under-reads: clear the paddlewheel
questions.why: At slack water SOG should equal log speed; a log 1.5 kn low with weed about is a fouled paddlewheel.
questions.ref: Navigation — the log and its error

questions.q: Your log over-read on the measured run. Since the 0800 fix it shows this reading. What distance through the water do you lay off?

figure.title: Log calibration
lines: Measured run: true 2.0 M, log 2.2 M

questions.why: The log reads 2.2 for 2.0: divide by 1.1. 16.5 ÷ 1.1 = 15.0 M (not 16.5 less 10%).
questions.ref: Navigation — the log and its error

questions.q: You leave the fix steering a steady course, with no stream and no leeway. Where do you mark the 1412 DR?
options: 5.0 M along 060°T from the fix
6.0 M along 060°T from the fix
6.0 M along 240°T from the fix
5.6 M along 060°T from the fix
questions.why: 1300 to 1412 is 1 h 12 min = 1.2 h; 5.0 × 1.2 = 6.0 M along the course steered.

questions.q: The plotter has failed. From the log entries, where is your 1000 DR from the 0800 fix?
questions.why: 6.0 M on 090°T, then 8.0 M on 160°T, end to end: the DR is 11.5 M on 131°T. Distances don't add.

questions.q: You have laid off the course to the next waypoint on the chart. The boat has no deviation on this heading. What course do you give the helmsman?

figure.note: No deviation

questions.why: True to magnetic: add westerly variation — 247° + 3° = 250°M.

questions.q: You give the helmsman the course for the next leg across Lyme Bay. Which compass course do you write on the board?
Your helmsman has steered a steady compass course all watch. Which true course do you lay off for the DR?
questions.why: Read the card for the ship's head: 312°C − 4°W = 308°M; + 1°E = 309°T.

questions.q: Off Start Point you alter course for the next leg. Which true course do you plot for the new leg?
questions.why: Read the card again for the new heading: 200°C − 3°W = 197°M; + 1°E = 198°T.

questions.q: In the Aegean, you work out the compass course for the night leg from Kos. What do you give the helmsman?

figure.note: Find compass

questions.why: 058°T − 4°E = 054°M; + 2°W deviation = 056°C. East is least, west is best.

questions.q: The plotter is set to show magnetic. You want to draw your ground track on the paper chart. Which line do you draw?
questions.why: Magnetic to true: subtract westerly variation — 085°M − 3°W = 082°T.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port tack with the wind as shown. Which water track do you plot?

figure.note: Heading 085°T · leeway 7°

questions.why: Leeway pushes you away from the wind: wind on the port side, so 085° + 7° = 092°T.

questions.q: You take a bearing of your wake with the hand-bearing compass to measure leeway. What do you plot?
options: 8° leeway: water track 218°M
22° leeway: water track 232°M
8° leeway: water track 202°M
No leeway: water track 210°M
questions.why: Dead astern the wake would bear 030°; it bears 022°, so 8° leeway, to port on starboard tack: 202°M.

questions.q: You plan three legs for tomorrow under sail. Which leeway do you allow for each?
questions.why: Leeway is greatest close-hauled in a breeze, small on a reach and nil running before the wind.

questions.q: A Meltemi leg in the Aegean, with no stream to apply. Where do you plot the 1200 position from the 1000 fix?
options: 12.0 M along 126°T
12.0 M along 120°T
6.0 M along 126°T
12.0 M along 114°T
questions.why: Wind on the port beam pushes you to starboard: 120° + 6° = 126°T; 6.0 kn × 2 h = 12.0 M.

questions.q: You plan a cross-tide leg past a drying ledge. Which line do you check against the ledge?

figure.note: Stream sets towards the ledge

options: The DR line from the course and the log
The ground track, with the stream applied
The heading line given to the helmsman
The water track you will steer along
questions.why: The boat moves over the ground: only the ground track shows where the stream takes you.
questions.ref: Chartwork — ground track and water track

questions.q: You draw the one-hour triangle for an EP and mark each line with its arrowheads. Which line gets three?

figure.note: Heading 090°T, log 6.0 kn · stream 180°T 2.0 kn

options: A: the heading and the log distance
C: the course and speed over ground
B: the stream's set and rate
A: the course steered through the water
questions.why: Convention: water track one arrowhead, ground track two, tidal stream three.

questions.q: You cross with a stream that runs east for the first two hours and west for the last two, equally. What does your ground track look like?
options: A curve ending east of the destination
A straight line along the rhumb line
A straight line east of the rhumb line
A curve bowing east, back on the line at the end
questions.why: Steering one course, you are set east, then set back west by the same amount; you meet the line again at the end.

questions.q: You are crossing the Channel south of the Isle of Wight with no leeway. Where do you plot the 0800 EP?
options: 108°T, 6.3 M from the fix
108°T, 8.0 M from the fix
090°T, 6.0 M from the fix
072°T, 6.3 M from the fix
questions.why: Water track 6.0 M east, then the hour's stream 2.0 M south from its end: 108°T, 6.3 M.

questions.q: You work up the EP from the log book after two hours on the wind. Where do you plot the 1200 EP?
options: 036°T, 8.2 M from the fix
049°T, 8.3 M from the fix
042°T, 13.7 M from the fix
043°T, 8.3 M from the fix
questions.why: Wind on the port side: water track 045°T, 11.0 M; add both hours' streams end to end: 049°T, 8.3 M.

questions.q: The almanac shows this diamond near your track. Where is your EP at the end of the hour, from its start?
You work up an EP for the 40 minutes since the fix. What length of stream do you lay off?
You want to make good the track from A to B. Which course do you steer, and what SOG do you expect?
options: 107°T, SOG 4.8 kn
107°T, SOG 6.5 kn
073°T, SOG 4.8 kn
090°T, SOG 5.2 kn
questions.why: Aim up-tide: sin⁻¹(1.5 ÷ 5.0) = 17°, so 090° + 17° = 107°T; SOG along the track = 5.0 × cos 17° = 4.8 kn.

questions.q: You must make good 180°T to the harbour entrance on a beam reach. What compass course do you give the helmsman?
questions.why: Stream: steer 191.5°T; wind from W, so 5° up into it = 196.5°T; + 2°W = 198.5°M; − 2°E = 197°C.

questions.q: You plan the crossing from A to B as a single two-hour triangle. Which course do you steer?
questions.why: Two hours of stream add to 3.6 M on 146°T; a 12.0 M arc from its end meets the track: steer 028°T.

questions.q: In a cross-stream you keep turning to point the bow straight at the waypoint on the plotter. What happens to your track?
options: It curves up-tide and you arrive early
It stays on the rhumb line as you correct
It is the same as steering one CTS
It curves down-tide and you sail further
questions.why: Chasing the bearing turns you up-tide late: you are set down-tide on a curve and cover more ground. Steer the worked CTS.

questions.q: Your 1400 EP lies 2 M east of the planned track. From where do you work the new course to steer?
options: From the EP, to the next waypoint
From the planned track, abeam the EP
From the departure point, as planned
From the DR, which leaves out the stream
questions.why: Always start a new triangle from your best position, here the EP, not from where you meant to be.

questions.q: You plan this crossing. How do you steer it?
options: Down-tide first, to be up-tide at the end
One course all the way: the streams cancel
The rhumb line, steering to keep XTE at zero
A new course each hour against that hour's stream
questions.why: Sum the hours' streams: they cancel, so one course on the track is the shortest way through the water.

questions.q: You will cross the Channel on one course for the whole four hours. Which course do you steer?
questions.why: Net stream over 4 h: 3.4 M east − 1.8 M west = 1.6 M east; aim off sin⁻¹(1.6 ÷ 22) ≈ 4° up-tide: 356°T.

questions.q: What speed have you made good over the ground on this leg?
options: 5.4 kn
5.6 kn
6.1 kn
5.0 kn
questions.why: Speed made good uses the ground distance: 12.5 M in 2 h 30 min = 5.0 kn. The log's 14.0 M is through the water.
questions.ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

questions.q: You head straight into the stream for the harbour. When do you arrive?
questions.ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

questions.q: Your course-to-steer triangle is drawn. When do you expect to reach the next waypoint?

figure.title: Night leg
lines: Next waypoint 7.0 M along the track

questions.why: Use the SOG from the triangle: 7.0 ÷ 4.6 = 1.52 h = 1 h 31 min; 2215 + 1 h 31 = 2346.
questions.ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

questions.q: You have worked out a course to steer of 095°T for this cross-tide leg. What does the helmsman hold at 095°?
options: COG: it shows where the boat is going
COG: steer until it reads 095°
Heading: COG will differ by the stream
Bearing to waypoint: keep it at 095°
questions.why: A course to steer is a heading through the water; the COG is its result over the ground.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: From these steady readings, what set and rate is the stream giving you?
options: Set 017°T, 1.4 kn
Set 133°T, 2.0 kn
Set 313°T, 1.4 kn
Set 313°T, 2.0 kn
questions.why: Stream = ground vector − water vector: 078°T 4.2 kn minus 095°T 5.6 kn leaves 2.0 kn setting 313°T.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: It is two hours before HW at the reference port. What stream do you use at this diamond for the hour?
questions.why: Range 4.0 m is 2/3 of the way from neaps (2.0 m) to springs (5.0 m): 1.2 + 2/3 × 1.2 = 2.0 kn; set as given.

questions.q: You are planning a leg in the Solent. Which atlas page gives the stream for it?

figure.title: Tidal stream atlas
lines: One page per hour, HW−6 to HW+6

options: HW+1
HW+3
HW+4
HW+2
questions.why: Each page covers half an hour either side of its time: 1400–1500 is centred on 1430, HW + 3 h.

questions.q: The atlas page shows this arrow off the headland. What rate do you apply there this hour?

figure.title: Atlas page HW+1
lines: Mean ranges: springs 4.8 m, neaps 2.2 m

options: 1.4 kn
3.0 kn
2.3 kn
1.6 kn
questions.why: 16,30 means neaps 1.6, springs 3.0 kn. 3.5 m is halfway from 2.2 to 4.8 m: 1.6 + 0.7 = 2.3 kn.

questions.q: Your two-hour leg runs from 1000 to 1200. Which streams do you apply?

figure.title: Tidal stream atlas
lines: Pages centred on each whole hour

options: HW+2 only, taken for two hours
All of HW+3 and all of HW+4
All of HW+2 and all of HW+3
Half of HW+2, all of HW+3, half of HW+4
questions.why: HW 0800: the HW+2 page covers 0930–1030, HW+3 1030–1130, HW+4 1130–1230. Take each for the time it applies.

questions.q: Looking at tomorrow's legs, on which one is a plain DR, without an EP, good enough?

figure.title: Tomorrow's legs
lines: A  Ionian, motoring in a calm, 2 h
B  across the Channel, 2 kn stream, 6 h
C  past the Alderney Race at night, 3 h
D  up the Solent against the spring ebb

options: A: no stream and no leeway to apply
B: the streams cancel over six hours
D: the ebb is along the track
C: the race runs too fast to plot
questions.why: DR leaves out stream and leeway. Only where both are nil, as motoring in a calm with no stream, is it enough.
questions.ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

questions.q: It is 0600 on a night passage. How far from the 0600 EP could you really be?

figure.title: 0600, night passage
lines: Last fix 0200; EP worked hourly since
Log and leeway good to ±0.3 kn
Shoal 2 M to leeward of the EP track

options: Up to about 1.2 M
Up to about 2.4 M
No more than 0.3 M
Up to about 0.6 M
questions.why: Errors grow with time: up to 0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6 M each hour, four hours since the fix = 2.4 M. The shoal is inside it.
questions.ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

questions.q: At night you close this headland. Your EP comes from a fix four hours old. What do you do?

figure.note: Plotter out since 2300 · last fix 2300

options: Close the headland to pick up its light sooner
Turn when the log shows the planned distance
Open the distance off and get a fix before turning
Turn at the EP time: the plot allows for the stream
questions.why: An old EP is an area, not a point. Keep sea room until a fix (a light, the depth) shows where you are.
questions.ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

questions.q: Your fix does not match your EP. What do you allow for on the next leg?

figure.title: Noon check
lines: 1200 fix lies 1.5 M NE of the 1200 EP

options: No change: one fix proves nothing
About 0.5 kn more stream setting SW
About 1.5 kn more stream setting NE
About 0.5 kn more stream setting NE
questions.why: 1.5 M of unexplained set in 3 h is about 0.5 kn towards the NE: add it to the next EP and check it at the next fix.
questions.ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

questions.q: On your night watch the plotter dies. Which entries in the log let you carry on the plot?

figure.title: Night watch, 0300
lines: Paper chart on the chart table

options: Time, log reading and heading steered
Barometer, wind and sea state
Engine hours and fuel used
Time, SOG and COG from the plotter
questions.why: DR is rebuilt from time, distance run by the log and the heading; plotter COG/SOG are gone with it.

questions.q: Between the hourly entries you bear away to clear a fishing fleet. What do you write in the log?

figure.title: 0240, night
lines: Bear away to clear a fishing fleet

options: Nothing until the next hourly entry
The time, log reading and new heading, now
The new heading only, at the next hour
The plotter position, at the next hour
questions.why: Every change of course is a new DR leg: it needs the time and log at the moment of the change.

questions.q: On a night passage the plotter works well. How do you keep the paper plot?
options: Plot only at the change of watch
Plot only if the plotter shows a fault
Mark a position each hour, with time and log
Leave it until dawn: the plotter logs the track
questions.why: An hourly position on paper means a failure at 0300 costs one hour of DR, not the whole night.
questions.ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

questions.q: At 0200 the plotter freezes on a night passage. Which DR do you plot for 0200?
options: 256°T, 4.8 M from the 0100 position
258°T, 4.8 M from the 0100 position
254°T, 4.8 M from the 0100 position
252°T, 4.8 M from the 0100 position
questions.ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

questions.q: You are motor-sailing along the coast to the next harbour. When do you arrive?
questions.ref: Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

questions.q: You are motor-sailing into a foul stream. What does running at 2600 rpm buy you on this leg?
options: 27 min sooner for 3.8 l more fuel
48 min sooner for 4.4 l more fuel
48 min sooner for 2.0 l more fuel
48 min sooner for the same fuel
questions.why: SOG 4.0 vs 5.0 kn: 4 h 00 × 2.5 = 10.0 l against 3 h 12 × 4.5 = 14.4 l — 48 min sooner, 4.4 l more.
questions.ref: Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

questions.q: You time the boat between two transits on the chart, motoring in flat water. What is your speed?
options: 1.3 kn
8.0 kn
0.8 kn
questions.why: 4 cables = 0.4 M; 3 min is 1/20 of an hour: 0.4 × 20 = 8.0 kn. A cable is a tenth of a mile.

questions.q: At night you close a rocky shore and plot a position every six minutes. How far do you lay off between plots?
options: 6.0 cables
3.3 cables
9.2 cables
5.5 cables
questions.why: Six minutes is a tenth of an hour: a tenth of 5.5 M is 0.55 M, 5.5 cables. Not 0.06 h.
questions.ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

questions.q: Fog closes in and you slow right down for the fairway buoy. When do you expect to reach it?

figure.title: Fog, visibility 200 m
lines: Fairway buoy 9.5 M ahead on the DR

questions.why: 9.5 ÷ 3.8 = 2.5 h = 2 h 30 min; 0610 + 2 h 30 = 0840. Half an hour, not 50 minutes.

questions.q: You run a measured distance both ways at the same revs to check the log in a steady stream. What is your real speed through the water at these revs?

figure.title: Log check, 2200 rpm
lines: Run 1, with the stream: 2.0 M in 15 min
Run 2, against it: 2.0 M in 24 min
Log showed 7.0 kn on both runs

options: 7.0 kn
6.5 kn
6.2 kn
8.0 kn
questions.why: Run speeds 8.0 and 5.0 kn: the stream adds to one and takes from the other, so their mean, 6.5 kn, is the speed through the water.
questions.ref: Navigation — the log and its error

questions.q: The paddlewheel jams at 1400 in a tidal stream and the log reads zero. How do you carry on the EP until it is cleared?
options: 7.1 kn from the plotter, then add the stream
Stop the EP until the log is working
5.5 kn from the rpm, then add the stream
5.5 kn from the rpm, with no stream added
questions.why: SOG already holds the stream: use it as the log speed and the stream counts twice. Take the speed through the water from the rpm.
questions.ref: Navigation — the log and its error

questions.q: The log has failed and fog makes you slow down. How far north of the 0700 fix is your 0830 DR?
The electrics fail at 0300. The log book has a gap: the 0130 alteration has no log reading. Where is your 0300 DR from the 0100 fix?

figure.title: Log book, night
lines: Speed steady all night · no stream

questions.why: 12.0 M in 2 h is 6.0 kn: 3.0 M on 020°T to 0130, then 9.0 M on 110°T. End to end the DR is 9.5 M on 092°T.

questions.q: After 30 M you find you applied the deviation for 045° to this whole leg. With no stream, where is the boat against the planned track?
options: 5.2 M NE of the track
2.6 M NE of the track
0.5 M NE of the track
2.6 M SW of the track
questions.why: 3°E used where 2°W applies: you headed 5° to port. 30 × sin 5° = 2.6 M, to the left of a SE track: NE.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port tack, steering this compass course. Which water track do you plot?

figure.note: Port tack · leeway 6°

questions.why: 040°C + 4°E = 044°M; − 2°W = 042°T. Port tack: leeway takes you to starboard, 042° + 6° = 048°T.

questions.q: Handing over, your helmsman admits holding 3° to port of the course all leg. Roughly how far off the track are you?

figure.title: End of the leg
lines: Steered 3° to port of the course

questions.why: 1 in 60 rule: 1° off puts you 1 M off in 60 M. 3° over 20 M: 20 × 3 ÷ 60 = 1.0 M, to port.
questions.ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

questions.q: At the 0300 handover the helmsman tells you what he really steered. Which true heading do you lay off for the last hour's DR?
questions.why: Plot what was steered, not what was ordered: 220°C + 2°E = 222°M; − 3°W = 219°T.
questions.ref: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

questions.q: On a charter catamaran you check the leeway by the wake. Which water track do you plot?
questions.why: Wind on the starboard side pushes you to port: 300° − 11° = 289°T. A cat with stub keels slips far more than 6°.

questions.q: Your catamaran's daggerboards are jammed up as you beat to windward. What leeway do you expect compared with boards down?
options: Less: the hulls grip better without boards
The same: leeway depends on the wind only
Much more: allow extra and check it by the wake
None: a catamaran makes no leeway
questions.why: The boards are the cat's grip on the water: raised, she slides sideways far more. Measure it, don't guess.

questions.q: At slack water, close-hauled on starboard tack, you read the plotter. What leeway is she making, and which water track do you plot?
options: None: water track 250°T
14°: water track 236°T
7°: water track 257°T
7°: water track 243°T
questions.why: With no stream, heading and COG differ by leeway alone: 250° − 243° = 7°, to port on starboard tack.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: Off the Brittany coast you work up the EP for 1130 from the 1000 fix. Where do you plot it?
options: 295°T, 6.4 M from the fix
301°T, 6.7 M from the fix
307°T, 6.0 M from the fix
320°T, 9.0 M from the fix
questions.why: Wind on the starboard beam: water track 310°T, 7.5 M in 1 h 30; then 1.5 h of stream, 2.1 M south: 295°T, 6.4 M.

questions.q: You steer north for an hour and leave the stream out of the plot. Where are you really at the end of the hour?
options: 5.0 M west of the DR
1.8 M west of the DR
1.8 M south of the DR
1.8 M east of the DR
questions.why: A set is the direction the stream flows towards: 270°T carries you west, 1.8 M in the hour.

questions.q: Today's tide is bigger than a mean spring. What rate do you use at this diamond for the hour?

figure.title: Diamond B, HW+1
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.0 m · neaps 2.0 m

options: 1.9 kn
1.3 kn
2.7 kn
2.5 kn
questions.why: 1.3 + (3.6 ÷ 3.0) × 1.2 = 2.7 kn: carry the interpolation on past springs rather than stopping at them.

questions.q: Your last fix was 1 h 30 min ago, and today's tide decides the rate at the diamond. How far has the stream carried you since?

figure.title: Tidal data for today
lines: Tide table: HW 4.6 m, LW 1.2 m
Mean ranges: springs 4.4 m · neaps 2.0 m

questions.why: Range 4.6 − 1.2 = 3.4 m: 1.4 + (1.4 ÷ 2.4) × 1.4 = 2.2 kn; for 1.5 h, 3.3 M. Use the range, not the HW height.

questions.q: The atlas and a diamond disagree for the same hour, at a spot right on your track. Which rate do you plot?

figure.title: HW−2, today's range
lines: Diamond F, on your track: 1.8 kn

options: 1.8 kn, from the diamond on the spot
1.2 kn, from the atlas for the area
1.5 kn, the mean of the two
1.2 kn, the atlas arrow nearest you
questions.why: A diamond is the stream measured at that spot; the atlas draws the general pattern. On your track the diamond wins.

questions.q: Motoring with no leeway, you work up the EP two hours after the 0830 fix. Where do you plot it?

figure.title: Diamond C · HW 1030
lines: Today: halfway between springs and neaps

options: 143°T, 9.9 M from the fix
141°T, 10.5 M from the fix
179°T, 10.7 M from the fix
135°T, 10.9 M from the fix
questions.why: Halfway rates 1.5 then 2.0 kn: 10.0 M on 160°T, then 1.5 M on 060°T and 2.0 M on 075°T: 141°T, 10.5 M.

questions.q: Your crew plotted the 1100 EP this way: an hour of the plotter's COG and SOG from the fix, then the hour's stream from its end. What do you tell them?
options: Correct, but add the leeway on top
Correct: COG and SOG are through the water
The stream is in twice: COG and SOG hold it
Wrong order: lay the stream off first
questions.why: COG and SOG are over the ground, stream included. Plot them alone, or the heading and log plus the stream.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: On the paper chart you mark the 0300 position worked from the log, the heading and the tidal stream. Which symbol do you draw?
options: A circle round the dot, with the time
A square round the dot, with the time
A short line across the track, with the time
A triangle round the dot, with the time
questions.why: By convention a fix is a circled dot, an EP a dot in a triangle, a DR a line across the track; always add the time.

questions.q: You plan two legs at the same speed, with the same strength of stream on each. Which leg needs the bigger aim-off, and which loses more speed?
options: B more aim-off; A loses more speed
A more aim-off; B loses more speed
B more aim-off and more speed lost
The same aim-off and speed on both
questions.why: A: aim 9° but SOG 3.6 kn; B: aim 17° but SOG 4.8 kn. A stream across costs angle; one on the bow costs speed.

questions.q: You must make good 045°T to the next mark against this stream. Which course do you steer, and what SOG do you expect?
options: 045°T, SOG 4.2 kn
038°T, SOG 4.3 kn
038°T, SOG 7.6 kn
052°T, SOG 4.3 kn
questions.why: Its cross part sets you to starboard: aim 7° to port, 038°T. Most of it is on the bow: SOG only 4.3 kn.

questions.q: Running south down the coast with the stream on your quarter, you want to make good 180°T. Which course do you steer, and what SOG?
options: 196°T, SOG 3.4 kn
164°T, SOG 6.2 kn
196°T, SOG 6.2 kn
180°T, SOG 7.0 kn
questions.why: The stream sets you east, so aim 16° west of the track: 196°T. Its along-track part is fair: SOG 6.2 kn.

questions.q: The engine overheats and you throttle back to 3.0 kn on this cross-tide leg. Which course do you now steer, and what SOG?
options: 120°T, SOG 3.0 kn
060°T, SOG 2.6 kn
107°T, SOG 2.6 kn
120°T, SOG 2.6 kn
questions.why: Slower boat, same stream, bigger angle: sin⁻¹(1.5 ÷ 3.0) = 30°, 090° + 30° = 120°T; SOG 3.0 × cos 30° = 2.6 kn.

questions.q: With the engine out and light airs, you try to draw the course to steer across this stream. What do you find?

figure.note: Engine out · light airs

options: The arc can't reach the track: no course works
Steer 053°T: the arc just meets it
Steer 090°T: square into the stream
Steer 000°T: the set evens out
questions.why: Across the track the stream (3.0 kn) is faster than the boat (2.5 kn): the boat-speed arc never reaches the line.

questions.q: You draw two hours of stream and the two-hour boat-speed arc. It cuts the track line 1.4 M beyond B. What does it tell you?
options: Steer it: the extra miles are a margin
You reach B early: rework for the shorter time
Steer it, and stop the clock at B
Add a third hour of stream to fit
questions.why: You will reach B in under 2 h, so two hours of stream is too much. Rework with the time to B and its stream.

questions.q: Three hours of hourly streams lie across this leg. Laying them all off in one triangle, which course do you steer?
questions.why: The three hours add to 4.6 M on 090°T; a 16.5 M arc from its end meets the track: steer 325°T, 15° up-tide.

questions.q: You must make good 270°T to B on a close reach, with the wind as given. Which course do you steer?
questions.why: Stream: water track 256°T. The south wind on your port side pushes you north too, so steer 6° more into it: 250°T.

questions.q: On a catamaran you must make good 090°T on a beam reach in this stream. Which course do you steer?
questions.why: Stream: water track 080°T. The south wind pushes the cat 10° north, so steer 10° to starboard of it: 090°T.

questions.q: Motoring this leg, you lay off both hours' streams in one triangle. Which compass course do you give the helmsman?
questions.why: 2.6 M of stream on 296°T; a 12.0 M arc meets the track: 188°T. + 3°W = 191°M; − 2°E = 189°C.

questions.q: You planned this crossing on one course, but you leave an hour late. Which course do you now steer?

figure.title: Channel crossing, one course
lines: 25.0 M due south at 5.0 kn: 5 h

questions.why: 0900–1400 the streams net 3.0 M E − 5.0 M W = 2.0 M W; aim off sin⁻¹(2 ÷ 25) ≈ 5° east of south: 175°T.

questions.q: Halfway across, the crew want to steer west to get back on the line. What do you tell them?

lines: One CTS 182°T for the 5 h crossing
Stream sets E until 1100, then W

options: Follow the plotter's steer to the waypoint
Steer west of 182°T until the XTE is zero
Add the XTE to the course, in degrees
Hold 182°T: the west-going stream brings you back
questions.why: One CTS is meant to drift off and come back. Steering for zero XTE fights the stream both ways and costs miles.

questions.q: Your single course to steer for this crossing gives a ground track bowing east, over a drying bank halfway. What do you do?
options: Work a CTS each hour to keep the track off the bank
Steer the rhumb line and correct at the end
Steer the one CTS: it ends on the line anyway
Steer the one CTS and watch the depth
questions.why: One CTS is shortest only if the whole curve is safe. Where it crosses a hazard, plan each hour's course to keep clear.

questions.q: Two hours after the last fix, your new fix lies on the track line but 1.0 M short of the EP. What do you suspect first?
options: Direction: leeway on the wrong side
Distance: the log or the stream's rate
Direction: the stream's set
Direction: the compass deviation
questions.why: An error along the track is one of distance: a log over-reading, or a foul stream stronger than plotted.

questions.q: At the end of the leg your fix lies off the DR as shown. What heading error explains it?

figure.title: Motoring at slack water
lines: Fix lies 1.5 M east of the DR

options: 5° to port of the course set
8° to starboard of the course set
5° to starboard of the course set
1.5° to starboard of the course set
questions.why: 1 in 60: 1.5 M off in 18 M is 1.5 × 60 ÷ 18 = 5°. East of a northerly track means you headed to starboard.

questions.q: You kept a plain DR from the 1000 fix. The 1200 fix lies as shown. What mean stream did you have?
options: Set 020°T, 1.2 kn
Set 020°T, 2.4 kn
Set 200°T, 2.4 kn
Set 200°T, 1.2 kn
questions.why: DR to fix is the stream's work over 2 h: 2.4 M towards 200°T, so 1.2 kn setting 200°T.

questions.q: Motoring along the coast, you compare the plotter with the log. What is the stream doing?

lines: Steady for the last half hour

options: 1.3 kn fair, along your track
1.3 kn across, from port
6.8 kn fair, along your track
1.3 kn foul, against your track
questions.why: Heading and COG agree, so there is no cross set; SOG 6.8 against log 5.5 kn: a fair stream of 1.3 kn.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: Motoring slowly in a swell, you watch the plotter's COG and SOG jump about. What do you use for the DR?

lines: Motoring slowly in a big swell

options: The last steady COG and SOG you saw
The compass heading and the log
The mean of the plotter's COG and SOG
The bearing and distance to the waypoint
questions.why: At low speed in a seaway COG and SOG swing with every wave; the heading and the log give a steady DR.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: You join a cross-tide leg and the plotter shows this. What does its CTS figure give you?

lines: No tidal data in the plotter

options: The compass course, deviation applied
The heading that allows for the stream
A steer back to the line, with no stream in it
The COG you will make good over the ground
questions.why: With no tidal data the plotter's CTS is only the steer back to the route line. Work the stream yourself.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: Your heading points well clear of the rocks, but the plotter's COG line runs onto them. Where is the boat going?

figure.note: Heading 030°T · stream sets east

options: Between the two: they average out
Along the heading, once the stream eases
Along the heading: the COG line lags
Along the COG line: alter up-tide now
questions.why: COG is the track over the ground, stream included; the heading only shows where the bow points.
questions.ref: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG

questions.q: The plotter gives this ETA at the next harbour. When do you really expect to arrive?

lines: 1200 now · log 5.0 kn, stream fair 1.5 kn
From 1300 the stream runs foul at 1.0 kn

questions.why: To 1300 at 6.5 kn: 6.5 M. The last 6.5 M at 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 kn take 1 h 38: 1438. The plotter assumes today's SOG.
questions.ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

questions.q: In thick fog the plotter screen goes blank. Where do you start the DR from?
options: The last plotter position you recall
The 0700 fix written in the log
The next waypoint on the route
The spot where the depth fits best
questions.why: Restart from the last position you wrote down with its time and log: here 1.7 M on 270°M from the 0700 fix.

questions.q: Your next fix is hours away. Which possible error moves your EP furthest from the truth?

figure.title: 4 h at 6 kn since the fix
lines: Stream rate: could be 1 kn out

options: The leeway, 3° out
The log, 3% out
The stream rate, 1 kn out
The heading, 5° out
questions.why: Over 4 h: stream 1 kn × 4 = 4.0 M; heading 24 M × sin 5° = 2.1 M; leeway 1.3 M; log 3% of 24 M = 0.7 M.
questions.ref: Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

questions.q: In fog with no radar you close this coast to find the harbour, your EP good to about a mile. Where do you aim?

figure.note: EP good to ±1 M · fog, no radar

options: 2 M west of it, then follow the coast west
Straight at it, then search either side
0.5 M east of it, then follow the coast west
2 M east of it, then follow the coast west
questions.why: Aim off by more than the EP error: when you meet the coast or the depth line, you know which way to turn.

questions.q: You have beaten towards the windward mark for two hours. What speed have you made good towards it?

figure.title: Beating to the mark, no stream

options: 4.2 kn
6.0 kn
8.5 kn
3.0 kn
questions.why: Each 6.0 M tack runs 45° off the bearing: 6.0 × cos 45° = 4.24 M towards the mark, twice: 8.5 M in 2 h = 4.2 kn.
questions.ref: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA

questions.q: Against a foul stream, how much time does hoisting the main save you on this leg?

figure.title: Motor-sailing leg
lines: Same fuel per hour either way

options: 20 min
36 min
60 min
13 min
questions.why: SOG 4.0 vs 5.0 kn: 12.0 ÷ 4.0 = 3 h 00, 12.0 ÷ 5.0 = 2 h 24 — 36 min. Against the stream each knot counts for more.
questions.ref: Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

questions.q: You can leave now into the foul stream or wait for the fair one. What does leaving at 1000 buy you?
options: 3 h 00 sooner for 3.6 l more fuel
1 h 30 sooner for 7.2 l more fuel
1 h 30 sooner for 3.6 l more fuel
1 h 30 sooner for the same fuel
questions.why: Leave 1000: 10.5 M by 1300, 9.5 M more at 7.0 kn, in at 1421. Wait: 20 ÷ 7.0, in at 1551. 1 h 30 longer running: 3.6 l.
questions.ref: Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

questions.q: You are motoring the catamaran across to the next harbour. What does running both engines buy you?

figure.title: Catamaran, flat calm
lines: Leg 24.0 M · foul 1.5 kn for 3 h, then slack

options: 56 min sooner for 7.5 l more fuel
1 h 38 sooner for 8.6 l more fuel
1 h 07 sooner for 20.4 l more fuel
1 h 07 sooner for 9.0 l more fuel
questions.why: Both: 16.5 M in 3 h, 7.5 M more in 1 h 04, 20.4 l. One: 12.0 M, then 12.0 M in 2 h 11, 11.4 l. 1 h 07 sooner, 9.0 l more.
questions.ref: Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

questions.q: You are motoring east along this coast and want a three-point fix with the hand-bearing compass. Which mark do you take last?
options: B — abeam, its bearing changes fastest
C — on the quarter, soon out of sight
The nearest mark, whatever its bearing
A — fine on the bow, the easiest to see
questions.why: Take marks ahead or astern first — their bearings change slowly — and the one abeam last; then note the time and log.

questions.q: You can see these three marks but have time for only two bearings. Which pair gives the most reliable fix?
options: A and C
A and B
B and C
Whichever two are nearest
questions.why: Two position lines cut best near 90°: A and B are about 90° apart, the other pairs cut at shallow angles.

questions.q: You come on deck at night and find this. What do you do first?

figure.title: Night watch, 0230
lines: Crew's phone left beside the compass

options: Swing the compass at first light
Steer by the GPS COG for the night
Move the phone well away from the compass
Apply 15° of deviation from the card
questions.why: A phone (its speaker magnet) next to the compass deflects it; remove it before you trust any heading.

questions.q: Your three bearings give this cocked hat, with a reef to the south. Which point do you take as your position?
options: Any corner — the triangle is small
The centre of the triangle
A — the corner furthest from the reef
C — the corner nearest the reef
questions.why: Assume the worst: use the corner of the cocked hat nearest the danger and plan your next course from it.

questions.q: You want a fix from these two radar targets. Which position lines do you plot?
options: The two range arcs
The two radar bearings
One bearing with the other's range
The bearings, averaged with the compass
questions.why: Radar ranges are accurate; radar bearings suffer from beam width and yaw — cross two ranges.

questions.q: Your house batteries die on a night passage. What do you steer by now?

figure.title: 0400, house batteries flat
lines: Handheld GPS in the grab bag

options: The radar's heading line
The steering compass — it needs no power
The autopilot's last heading
The handheld GPS and its COG
questions.why: A fluxgate needs power; the magnetic steering compass does not — it is the backup for every electronic heading.

questions.q: This alarm sounds on a night passage. What do you do?

figure.title: Plotter alarm
lines: Lights of the coast in sight

options: Reset the plotter and trust its next fix
Heave to until the GPS comes back
Run a DR from the 0255 fix and fix by the lights
Keep steering on the plotter's boat icon
questions.why: With no satellites the icon is frozen or guessing: work by DR from the last fix and fix visually.

questions.q: This is the state of your boat in spring. What do you do before the first passage?

figure.title: After the winter refit
lines: Plotter moved next to the binnacle

options: Keep the old card — it will be close
Use only the hand-bearing compass
Add 2° to the old card on every heading
Swing the compass and make a new card
questions.why: New magnets and electronics near the compass change its deviation: swing it and draw up a new card.

questions.q: Two lighthouses on this coast could be this light. How do you tell which one it is?

figure.note: Unidentified light ahead, 2200

options: Time its period with a stopwatch and count flashes
Note its colour and compare it with the chart
Wait until it is abeam, then take a bearing
Judge its brightness against the charted range
questions.why: Identify a light by its characteristic: count the flashes, time the full period, match the chart or List of Lights.

questions.q: This is your plan for the day. How do you change the fixing routine at 1100?
options: Fix only at each waypoint on the plotter
Fix far more often — every 10 to 15 minutes
Fix less often — you need eyes on deck
Keep the hourly fix — the plan is unchanged
questions.why: The closer the danger, the more often you fix: hourly in open water, every few minutes among rocks.

questions.q: You take this bearing of a headland light with the hand-bearing compass, well clear of any steel. Which bearing do you plot?

figure.note: Hand-bearing compass

questions.why: Magnetic to true: subtract westerly variation — 312°M − 3°W = 309°T. Clear of steel there is no deviation.

questions.q: You take these three bearings for a fix. Which true bearings do you plot?
