questions.why: Easterly variation is added going from magnetic to true: +4° on each bearing.

questions.q: You steer straight down this charted transit and read the steering compass. What deviation does it have on this heading?
questions.why: 125°T + 3°W = 128°M; the compass reads 131°C, 3° high, so deviation is 3°W (C + dev = M).
questions.ref: Compass — checking deviation on a transit

questions.q: You sight along this charted transit with the hand-bearing compass and read this. What does it tell you?

figure.note: Transit 058°T

options: It reads 2° low — apply 2°E to bearings
No error — 058°T is 060°M here
It reads 2° high — apply 2°W to bearings
Variation here must be 4°W, not 2°W
questions.why: 058°T + 2°W = 060°M, exactly what the compass reads: from that spot it has no deviation.

questions.q: The rose on your chart was printed some years ago. Which true bearing of the lighthouse goes on the chart?
You take this bearing over the steering compass. Which true bearing do you plot?
questions.why: Deviation goes with the ship's head, not the bearing: 075°C + 4°E = 079°M; − 2°W = 077°T.

questions.q: Your three bearings give this cocked hat, about a mile across. What do you do?
options: Check each mark's identity and retake the bearings
Use its centre — the errors average out
Accept it — any fix beats a DR
Plot the corner nearest your DR and go on
questions.why: A big cocked hat means an error — a wrong mark, a misread, a slow round of bearings: check and fix again.

questions.q: You plan a three-point fix from these marks. Which one do you leave out?
options: A — a lighthouse is too close to plot
B — a buoy can drag or be off station
None — any charted object will do
C — a church spire is not a sea mark
questions.why: Use fixed, well-charted objects; a floating mark may be out of position, so it makes a poor fix mark.

questions.q: You work up this running fix. How do you transfer the 1015 position line?
options: 5.2 M along 320°T
5.2 M along 270°T
5.2 M along 090°T
5.2 M along 030°T
questions.why: Move the first line by the run between bearings: log 19.4 − 14.2 = 5.2 M along the course, 090°T.

questions.q: You allow for the tide in this running fix. By what do you move the first position line?
options: 6.1 M along 281°T
6.0 M along 270°T
7.2 M along 270°T
6.1 M along 259°T
questions.why: Water track 270°T 6.0 M plus tide 180°T 1.2 M gives the ground track: 6.1 M along 259°T.

questions.q: You note the log at these two bearings of the light. How far off it are you when it comes abeam?

figure.title: Bow and beam bearings
lines: Light 45° on the starboard bow, log 22.6

questions.why: 45° on the bow, then abeam: a right isosceles triangle, so distance off abeam = run = 25.9 − 22.6 = 3.3 M.

questions.q: The angle of the light on your bow has doubled. What is your distance off it now?

figure.title: Doubling the angle on the bow
lines: Light 30° on the port bow, log 8.4
Light 60° on the port bow, log 11.2

questions.why: Doubling the angle on the bow makes an isosceles triangle: distance off at the second bearing = run, 11.2 − 8.4 = 2.8 M.

questions.q: You want a position line from the depth. Which charted depth are you over, and so which contour are you on?
options: 18.0 m — between 15 and 20 m
21.0 m — beyond the 20 m contour
15.0 m — the 15 m contour
14.4 m — inside the 15 m contour
questions.why: Water depth 17.4 + 0.6 = 18.0 m; minus 3.0 m of tide = 15.0 m below chart datum: the 15 m contour.

questions.q: You plot this fix and check the sounder, which reads from the waterline. What do you make of the fix?
options: It stands — the chart is simply out of date
It stands — the sounder must be faulty
It stands — the tide explains the gap
It is suspect — fix again and check the marks
questions.why: 12.0 m − 1.5 m of tide = 10.5 m below datum, not the 27–31 m charted round the fix: the depth says the fix is wrong.

questions.q: You are closing the coast at night. At what distance do you expect this light to rise above the horizon?
questions.why: Geographical range 2.08 × (√36 + √2.5), heights in metres = 15.8 M; inside the 18 M nominal range, so it rises there.
questions.ref: Position lines — rising and dipping lights

questions.q: You hope to get a distance off as this light rises above the horizon. Will it work?
options: Yes — it rises at about 17.5 M
No — you first see it at about 12 M
Yes — it rises at about 14.6 M
Yes — it rises at about 18.7 M
questions.why: 2.08 × (√49 + √2) = 17.5 M geographical, heights in metres, but the light carries only 12 M: it appears at 12 M, not on the horizon.
questions.ref: Position lines — rising and dipping lights

questions.q: You stand on the coachroof and watch the lighthouse dip below the horizon. How far off is it?

figure.title: Dipping distances (M)
lines: Light 30 m: eye 2 m 14.3 · eye 3 m 15.0
Light 40 m: eye 2 m 16.1 · eye 3 m 16.8
Light 50 m: eye 2 m 17.6 · eye 3 m 18.3
You: eye 3 m, the 40 m light dips

questions.why: The table is 2.08 × (√H + √h) with heights in metres: a 40 m light seen from 3 m dips at 16.8 M.

questions.q: You take a bearing at the moment the light rises. Where are you?
options: 20.0 M from the light, on 218°T from it
13.3 M from the light, on 038°T from it
13.3 M from the light, on 222°T from it
13.3 M from the light, on 218°T from it
questions.why: 2.08 × (√25 + √2), metres = 13.3 M; 040°M − 2°W = 038°T, so you lie on the reciprocal, 218°T from the light.
questions.ref: Position fixing — rising light and bearing

questions.q: You read the radar like this for a fix. Which true bearing of the headland do you plot?
questions.why: A head-up EBL is relative to the bow: 250°M + 040° = 290°M; − 2°W = 288°T.

questions.q: You want a radar range for a fix off this coast. Which target do you use?
options: The nearest echo, whatever it is
B — the steep cliffs
C — the hills inland
A — the low sandy beach
questions.why: Steep cliffs give a hard echo at the water's edge; a low beach may not show, and hills lie well behind the coastline.

questions.q: You expect this buoy on the radar screen but cannot find it. What do you do?

figure.title: Radar, 0500
lines: Sea moderate · range 1.5 M, rings 0.5 M
Red can buoy 0.4 M ahead not showing

options: Switch to the 12 M range for a wider view
Turn the gain up to maximum as well
Turn sea clutter down until speckle just shows
Trust the screen — the buoy has gone
questions.why: Too much sea-clutter suppression wipes out weak echoes close in; reduce it until a little sea speckle shows.

questions.q: How do you plot your position from these radar readings?
options: 2.4 M from the headland on 298°T
2.4 M from the headland on 295°T
2.4 M from the headland on 112°T
2.4 M from the headland on 292°T
questions.why: 115°M − 3°W = 112°T to the headland; you lie on the reciprocal, 292°T, 2.4 M out from it.

questions.q: Coasting at night, you open this status page. How do you treat the GPS position?
options: As poor — check it against bearings and depth
As exact — HDOP only affects height
As good once it has settled for a minute
As good — four satellites make a fix
questions.why: A high HDOP means poor satellite geometry and a wide error; cross-check with a visual fix and the sounder.

questions.q: Your only GPS behaves like this. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: Handheld GPS
lines: Kept on the chart table below

options: Deviation — move it from the compass
No sky view — the antenna must be outside
Wrong datum — set it to ED50
Low battery — plug it into 12 V
questions.why: GPS needs a clear view of the sky; below decks or under a sprayhood the signals fade and the fix wanders.

questions.q: The GPS lat/long plots you on these rocks, yet you can see them well clear to the north-east. What is the likely cause?
options: HDOP — wait for more satellites
Lag — the GPS is behind the boat
The datum — apply the chart's shift note
Deviation — the GPS reads magnetic
questions.why: On a chart drawn to an older datum the stated shift must be applied to WGS84 positions, or GPS fixes plot in the wrong place.

questions.q: You use the GPS range and bearing to this charted waypoint for a quick fix. Where do you plot yourself?
options: 3.2 M from the waypoint on 130°T
3.2 M from the waypoint on 310°T
3.2 M from the waypoint on 040°T
3.2 M from the waypoint on 220°T
questions.why: BRG is from you to the waypoint, so you lie on the reciprocal: 040° + 180° = 220°T, 3.2 M from it.
questions.ref: GPS — range and bearing to a waypoint

questions.q: You plot your fix from this waypoint, which is charted on the rock itself. Where are you?
options: 4.6 M from it on 283°T
4.6 M from it on 103°T
4.6 M from it on 287°T
4.6 M from it on 291°T
questions.why: 107°M − 4°W = 103°T from you to the waypoint; you lie on the reciprocal, 283°T, 4.6 M from it.

questions.q: You are on this bearing of the light, and the sounder reads from the waterline. Where on the line are you?
options: C — where it crosses the 5 m depth
B — where it crosses the 10 m depth
Anywhere — one bearing gives no fix
A — where it crosses the 20 m depth
questions.why: 13.2 m − 3.2 m of tide = 10.0 m below chart datum: the bearing crosses that depth at B.

questions.q: Your fix and your DR disagree like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Log, 1200
lines: Three-bearing fix: 1.8 M SE of the DR

options: Trust the DR — it has three hours of log
Ignore both and wait for the GPS
Trust the fix and restart the plot from it
Split the difference between the two
questions.why: A good fix beats a DR; the gap is the tide you left out — start the DR again from the fix and allow for it.

questions.q: The visual fix and the GPS disagree. Which do you work from?

figure.title: Off the Breton coast, 1530
lines: Visual three-point fix: small cocked hat
GPS position: 0.5 M west of it
Corrected sounding matches the visual fix
Chart: old survey, a datum note

options: A point halfway between, as a compromise
The GPS — but add 0.5 M to all clearances
The GPS — satellites beat a hand compass
The visual fix — the depth agrees with it
questions.why: Two independent checks agree — the bearings and the sounder; the GPS gap is likely the datum, so work from the visual fix.

questions.q: Your crew times the light like this. Which charted light is it?

figure.title: Stopwatch, 2315
lines: White light, groups of three flashes
Dark from end of group to next: 12 s

options: B — its period is 15 s
A — the dark gap is 12 s
Neither — the timing fits no light
A or B — the period cannot be timed
questions.why: The period runs from the start of one group to the start of the next: 3 s + 12 s = 15 s, so Fl(3) 15s.
questions.ref: Fixing at night — timing a light

questions.q: You time a light to identify it for a fix. Which charted light are you watching?

figure.title: Timing a light
lines: White light: on 6 s, off 2 s, repeating

options: C — isophase, light equal to dark
D — occulting, light longer than dark
E — long-flashing, a 2 s flash
None — 6 + 2 matches no light
questions.why: Light longer than dark is occulting; on 6 s + off 2 s = an 8 s period: Oc 8s.

questions.q: How often do you need a fix to keep to this plan?

figure.title: Inshore passage at night
lines: Rocks 0.5 M either side of the track
Plan: never run more than 0.5 M unfixed

options: Every 8 minutes
Every 12 minutes
Every 5 minutes
Every 30 minutes
questions.why: 0.5 M at 6 kn takes 0.5 ÷ 6 = 0.083 h = 5 minutes, so fix at least every 5 minutes.

questions.q: Your crew asks why the deviation on this card changes as you change course. What do you tell them?
options: Magnetic north shifts as the course changes
The card is wrong — deviation is fixed
The compass card lags behind in a turn
The boat's iron and wiring turn with her
questions.why: Deviation comes from the boat's own magnetism — engine, keel bolts, wiring — which swings round the compass with each heading.

questions.q: You swing the compass by sighting a transit over it on each heading. Which deviation do you write down for 090°C?
questions.why: On 090°C the transit reads 200°C against 202°M: the compass reads 2° low, so deviation is 2°E.

questions.q: You need a hand-bearing compass fix. Where do you stand to take the bearings?

figure.title: Where to stand
lines: A: beside the steering compass pedestal
B: on the side deck, clear of fittings
C: in the hatch, right over the engine
D: under the sprayhood, by the speakers

options: C — in the hatch
B — on the side deck
A — by the pedestal
D — under the sprayhood
questions.why: A hand-bearing compass picks up deviation near steel, engines and speakers: use it in the open, clear of them.

questions.q: Something is wrong with the heading. What do you suspect first?

figure.title: Day passage, 1100
lines: GPS COG 168°M, no tide, no leeway
Steel kedge stowed under the binnacle at 1000

options: The tide is setting you 12° east
The GPS has lost its datum
The kedge is deflecting the compass
The deviation card is 12° out
questions.why: A steel anchor or tool near the compass adds deviation of its own; move it and check the heading again.

questions.q: You need this fix on the chart quickly and without slips. How do you plot it?

figure.title: Plotting the GPS fix
lines: Boat motion lively at the chart table

options: Lat and long, with dividers on both scales
A photo of the plotter screen instead
Wait to plot it until the sea calms
Range and bearing from the waypoint
questions.why: From a charted waypoint the fix is one line and one distance — quicker, with fewer slips, than lat/long in a seaway.

questions.q: How much do you trust this running fix?

figure.title: Running fix, 2 h between bearings
lines: Tidal stream taken from a diamond
Course held only to ±5° in the swell
Log known to under-read a little

options: Only as far as the run between the bearings
More than two bearings taken at once
Fully — the light is a fixed point
As much as a three-point fix
questions.why: A running fix carries every error of course, log and tide over the run: the longer the run, the poorer the fix.

questions.q: You altered course between the two bearings. How do you transfer the 2200 position line?

figure.title: Running fix with a course change

options: 2.0 M along 060°T
3.0 M along 035°T
3.5 M along 060°T
3.5 M along 030°T
questions.why: Add the legs as vectors: 1.5 M on 000°T then 2.0 M on 060°T give a resultant of 3.0 M along 035°T.

questions.q: You take these bearings with the hand-bearing compass from the foredeck, clear of all steel. Which true bearings do you plot?

figure.title: Three-point fix, 1615
lines: Steering compass card: 3°E on this heading

questions.why: The deviation card belongs to the steering compass, not to a hand compass used clear of steel: apply only the 2°W variation.

questions.q: You check the hand-bearing compass on a transit from the cockpit, then take a fix from the same spot without altering course. Which true bearings do you plot?

figure.title: Hand compass check, cockpit
lines: Hand compass on the transit reads 151°

questions.why: 145°T + 3°W = 148°M, the compass reads 151°: 3° high. Same spot, same heading: −3° deviation, then −3°W variation.
questions.ref: Hand-bearing compass — deviation found on a transit

questions.q: You hear this foghorn and want a position line from it. Can you use it?

figure.title: Fog, 0700
lines: Foghorn heard, seemingly on the port bow

options: No — sound gives no reliable bearing in fog
Yes — cross its bearing with the sounder
Yes — its loudness gives the distance
Yes — take a hand bearing of the sound
questions.why: Fog bends and blanks sound: the direction and loudness of a fog signal are no guide to its bearing or range.

questions.q: In fog you run a line of soundings east, one every 0.5 M; the sounder reads from the waterline. Which track have you been on?
options: Track B
Track A
Between A and B
Track C
questions.why: Reduce each sounding to chart datum: 21, 17, 12, 9 m − 3.0 m of tide = 18, 14, 9, 6 m — the pattern charted along A.
questions.ref: Fixing in fog — a line of soundings

questions.q: On a night passage you find the plotter like this. Where do you start your DR from?

figure.title: Plotter, 0340
lines: Boat icon still moving on the last COG/SOG

options: The plotter's boat icon where it is now
Your departure harbour at 1800
The 0200 log-book fix, log 41.2
The next waypoint on the route
questions.why: With no fix the plotter only extrapolates its last COG and SOG; the last fix you can trust is the one in the log book.

questions.q: Between these two bearings you sail two legs with the stream setting you SSW. By what do you move the 0900 position line?
options: 5.4 M along 115°T
6.0 M along 140°T
5.4 M along 104°T
5.6 M along 125°T
questions.why: Add both legs and the hour's tide: 3.0 M on 090°T + 3.0 M on 140°T + 1.0 M on 200°T = 5.6 M along 125°T.
questions.ref: Running fix — course change and tide

questions.q: Your bearings are an hour and a half apart, and the stream changes in that time. How do you move the 0800 position line?

figure.title: Running fix, 0800–0930
lines: Bearings of the light at 0800 and 0930

options: 9.2 M along 055°T
6.1 M along 030°T
9.9 M along 057°T
8.4 M along 051°T
questions.why: 7.5 M on 045°T, then the tide hour by hour: 1.2 M + 1.0 M (half an hour at 2.0 kn) on 090°T = 9.2 M along 055°T.
questions.ref: Running fix — tide hour by hour

questions.q: Out of sight of land, you steer straight at the setting sun to check the steering compass. What is its deviation on this heading?

figure.note: Sun bears 292°T

questions.why: Sun 292°T + 2°W = 294°M; the compass reads 297°, 3° high, so deviation is 3°W (C + dev = M).

questions.q: You check the steering compass on a transit on four headings and get this. What does it point to?
options: Steel gear stowed close to the binnacle
A normal deviation curve for a yacht
The compass is mounted out of line with the keel
A compass card that sticks in its bowl
questions.why: Iron gives a deviation that changes with the heading; the same error on every heading is a lubber line set off the fore-and-aft line.

questions.q: Your chart has two compass roses, both corrected to this year. You take a hand bearing of the light. Which true bearing do you plot?
questions.why: Variation changes across a chart: use the rose nearest you, 2°W here — 060°M − 2° = 058°T.

questions.q: Your chart has two roses printed some years ago. You are close to the east one. Which true bearing of the light do you plot?
questions.ref: Variation — annual change and the nearest rose

questions.q: You close the coast at low water, waiting for this light to rise. At what distance do you expect it?

figure.title: Light list and tide
lines: Light Fl 10s, 30 m above MHWS, 20 M
MHWS 5.0 m · height of tide now 1.0 m

questions.why: At low water the light stands 30 + (5.0 − 1.0) = 34 m above the sea: 2.08 × (√34 + √2.5) = 15.4 M.
questions.ref: Rising lights — height of tide on the light

questions.q: You bob your head to check the light: standing you see it, sitting you do not. How far off is it?

figure.title: Bobbing the light, 2240
lines: Standing, eye 3.0 m: light just in sight
Sitting, eye 1.5 m: light below the horizon

options: Under 14.0 M
Between 17.6 and 20.0 M
Between 16.5 and 17.6 M
Between 14.0 and 16.5 M
questions.why: Just under one horizon, just over the other: 2.08 × (√45 + √1.5) = 16.5 M and 2.08 × (√45 + √3) = 17.6 M.
questions.ref: Rising and dipping lights — bobbing a light

questions.q: You close this low coast at night on radar. How far off the beach are you?
options: About 5.2 M — the echo is the beach
About 3.7 M — halfway, to be safe
About 8.2 M — add the hills' 3.0 M
About 2.2 M — the echo is the hills
questions.why: Low dunes give little echo; the first strong one is the high ground behind: 5.2 − 3.0 = 2.2 M to the beach.

questions.q: You want a radar range on this low island as soon as it appears. At about what range do you expect its first echo?

figure.title: Radar on passage
lines: Low island, 5 m high, no cliffs

options: About 9.3 M
About 24 M
About 4.4 M
About 6.6 M
questions.why: Radar horizon: 2.2 × (√4 + √5) = 2.2 × 4.24 ≈ 9.3 M; a low target shows only when it is above that horizon.
questions.ref: Radar — range of a low target

questions.q: You need the headland on radar for a fix. Which control do you adjust?

figure.title: Radar, 0300
lines: Rain squall between you and the headland
Headland echo lost in a blotch of rain

options: The sea clutter
The rain clutter (FTC)
The range, to a longer scale
The gain, down to minimum
questions.why: Rain clutter (FTC) breaks up the blotch of a shower so the solid echo of the land shows through it.

questions.q: The radar ranges of A and B cross at two points; the sounder reads from the waterline. Which is your position?
options: Y — it is nearer the coast
Either — two ranges can't tell
X — the depth fits it
Midway between X and Y
questions.why: Two range circles cut twice; the depth decides: 31 m − 2.0 m of tide = 29 m below datum, as charted at X.

questions.q: You measure the range of this headland for a fix. Where on its echo do you set the VRM?

figure.title: Radar, 3 M scale, rings 0.5 M
lines: Headland echo: a thick band 0.2 M deep

options: On the nearest range ring
On the echo's far edge
On the middle of the echo
On the echo's near edge
questions.why: The near edge of an echo is the coastline facing you; the echo's depth is the beam and pulse length smearing it outwards.

questions.q: You can just see one headland through the haze. Which pair of position lines gives the best fix on it?

figure.title: Haze, 1500
lines: One headland in sight, about 2.5 M off

options: Radar range and a hand bearing of it
Radar bearings of its two edges
Radar range and a radar bearing of it
Radar bearing and a hand bearing of it
questions.why: Each source at its best: the radar's accurate range crossed with a visual compass bearing, cutting at 90°.
questions.ref: Radar — range with a visual bearing

questions.q: You fix by these three lights at night. In which order do you take the bearings?

figure.title: Night fix, three lights
lines: A: broad on the starboard quarter
B: fine on the port bow

options: A, C, then B
B, A, then C
C, B, then A
C, A, then B
questions.why: Ahead or astern first — their bearings change slowly — and the light nearest the beam last, as its bearing changes fastest.

questions.q: Only these two marks are in sight, one ahead and one astern. How good is a fix from their bearings?
options: Good — the marks lie on opposite sides
Good — if both are taken quickly
Poor — the lines cut at a fine angle
Good — both marks are well charted
questions.why: Bearings ahead and astern are nearly one line: they hold you on track but say little about how far along it you are.

questions.q: As the front and rear beacons come in line, you take one compass bearing for a fix. Which mark do you choose?
options: D — it lies closest to the transit
E — it lies on the other side of it
Any — the transit is exact anyway
C — it cuts the transit near 90°
questions.why: A transit is a perfect position line without a compass; cross it with the bearing that cuts it nearest 90°.
questions.ref: Position fixing — a transit and a bearing

questions.q: Your new fix disagrees with both the EP and the sounder. What do you make of it?

figure.title: Log, 1940
lines: EP with tide: 1.5 M north of the fix
Chart: 25 m at the fix, 9 m at the EP

options: Doubt the fix — check each mark's identity
Trust the fix — the cocked hat is tiny
Average the fix and the EP
Trust the fix — the sounder has seen fish
questions.why: A tiny cocked hat only means the bearings agree; when depth and EP both disagree, a misidentified mark is the likely cause.

questions.q: Your 1200 fix lands away from the DR like this. What tidal stream have you had since 1000?

figure.title: Log, 1000–1200
lines: 1200: DR by log and course, no tide
1200: fix lies 2.0 M on 045°T from the DR

options: 225°T at 2.0 kn
045°T at 1.0 kn
225°T at 1.0 kn
045°T at 2.0 kn
questions.why: The DR left the tide out, so the gap from DR to fix is the tide: 2.0 M towards 045°T in 2 hours = 1.0 kn.

questions.q: You have two bearings of the same light, an hour apart. Which line do you move for the running fix, and which way?

figure.title: Running fix
lines: Ground track and run known for the hour

options: The second, back along the course steered
The first, along the bearing of the light
The first, forward along the ground track
The second, forward along the ground track
questions.why: Carry the earlier position line forward by the distance and direction made good over the ground; cross it with the later one.

questions.q: You work a running fix under sail with this leeway. How do you transfer the 1300 position line?
options: 4.0 M along 255°T
4.0 M along 250°T
4.0 M along 065°T
4.0 M along 245°T
questions.why: The wind on the starboard side pushes you to port: water track 250° − 5° = 245°T; run 24.0 − 20.0 = 4.0 M.

questions.q: You use the bow-and-beam bearings of this light with a foul tide. How far off it are you when it is abeam?

figure.title: Bow and beam bearings
lines: Light 45° on the starboard bow, log 10.0
Foul tide dead on the bow, 1.0 kn

questions.why: Distance off abeam equals the run over the ground, not the log: 14.0 − 10.0 = 4.0 M less 1.0 M of foul tide = 3.0 M.
questions.ref: Running fix — bow and beam with tide

questions.q: Your crew puts 28 m into the dipping formula for this light. Which height should go in?
questions.why: Charted light heights are above MHWS; with the tide 5.0 m below it the light stands 28 + 6.0 − 1.0 = 33 m above the sea.

questions.q: This light suddenly appears ahead. Can you take the moment as its rising distance?
options: Yes — every light first shows at its horizon
Yes — it rises at 16.1 M from your height of eye
No — it came out of the haze, not over the horizon
Yes — but take off the 6 M of visibility
questions.why: A rising distance needs a clear night; in 6 M haze the light shows when you close the haze, well inside its 16.1 M horizon.

questions.q: You see this on a clear night. Can you take a rising distance now?

figure.title: Clear night, 0200
lines: A glow sweeps the sky beyond the horizon
Every 10 s, where the Fl 10s light lies
The light itself not yet in sight

options: Yes — the loom marks its geographical range
Yes — the loom's brightness gives the range
Yes — add 2 M to the rising distance
Not yet — wait for the light itself to show
questions.why: The loom is the beam lighting the sky above the horizon; the rising distance applies only when the light itself appears.

questions.q: Two ways of plotting the same GPS reading disagree like this. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: GPS check, 1120
lines: Lat/long fix: at sea, close to your EP
WP 'Bec' typed in by hand last winter

options: The waypoint was mistyped — check it on the chart
The GPS has just lost its fix
The chart is on an older datum
The GPS is set to magnetic bearings
questions.why: A range and bearing is only as good as the waypoint: if lat/long plots fine, check the stored waypoint against the chart.
questions.ref: GPS — range and bearing to a waypoint

questions.q: Your GPS has died on a night passage and only one light is in sight. How do you fix your position?

figure.title: Night passage, 0130
lines: No other lights above the horizon
Steady course, tide from the atlas

options: None — keep the DR until daylight
A running fix: two bearings an hour apart
Its brightness against the nominal range
One bearing of it, plotted as a fix
questions.why: One light gives one position line at a time; transfer the first by the run and tide and cross it with the second.
questions.ref: GPS failure — a running fix at night

questions.q: You read this on a night passage. How do you navigate until 0600?

figure.title: NAVTEX, 2300
lines: GPS track smooth, 3 M off the visual fix
AIS targets jumping about on the plotter

options: On the GPS, shifted 3 M to match the fix
On the GPS — its track is smooth and steady
On visual fixes and DR; the GPS is suspect
On the AIS positions of ships around you
questions.why: Interference can give a smooth but false GPS track; AIS uses the same satellites. Fix by bearings, depth and DR.

questions.q: Your GPS failed an hour ago and you want to identify the first light you see. Which of these should be in sight now?

figure.title: EP 0300, GPS failed
lines: Light A: 60 m, 25 M · 22 M off by EP
Light B: 20 m, 15 M · 12 M off by EP

options: Neither — both are below your horizon
Both — each is inside its nominal range
A — its range is the longer
B — already above your horizon
questions.ref: Rising lights — identifying a landfall light

questions.q: You see this light ahead, and two charted lights share its characteristic. Which one is it?

figure.note: EP: light A 10 M, light B 30 M; both Fl(2) 10s 18 M

options: A — B is far beyond its range
B — it is the brighter of the two
Either — time it again to be sure
Neither — charted lights always differ
questions.why: Use the EP: B lies 30 M off, well beyond its 18 M range, so the Fl(2) 10s in sight must be A at 10 M.
questions.ref: Fixing at night — identifying a light

questions.q: You cross this stream near the rocks. How often do you fix to keep to your rule?

figure.title: Cross-tide passage
lines: Rocks 1.0 M down-tide of your track
Rule: fix before it can set you halfway

options: Only at the waypoints
Every 15 minutes
Every hour
Every 30 minutes
questions.why: Halfway to the rocks is 0.5 M; at 2.0 kn the stream sets you that far in 0.5 ÷ 2.0 = 0.25 h = 15 minutes.

questions.q: You find this when checking the steering compass on a transit. What is the cause?

figure.title: Transit check, same heading
lines: Engine off: compass agrees with the transit
Charging cables run under the binnacle

options: Engine vibration turning the card
Heat from the engine bay below
Current in the cables beside the compass
Variation shifting with boat speed
questions.why: A wire carrying current makes its own magnetic field; run cables in twisted pairs, well clear of the compass.

questions.q: Your crew leaves these by the binnacle on watch. Which one can stay there?
options: The steel rigging knife
The torch with its batteries
The handheld VHF radio
The aluminium winch handle
questions.why: Aluminium is not magnetic; steel, speaker magnets and steel-cased batteries all deflect a compass close by.

questions.q: Your new fluxgate compass shows this message. What do you do?

figure.title: After the refit
lines: New fluxgate compass for the autopilot
Calm sea, open water, no traffic

options: Motor slow full circles, as the manual says
Nothing — a fluxgate needs no calibration
Copy the steering compass deviation card
Enter the chart's variation instead
questions.why: A fluxgate corrects its own deviation once it has been swung: slow, steady turns in calm water while it measures.

questions.q: You take a bearing over the steering compass on a heading between the card's entries. Which true bearing do you plot?
questions.why: Interpolate for the ship's head: 060°C lies a third of the way from 2°E to 4°E ≈ 3°E; 300° + 3° − 1° = 302°T.

questions.q: You leave harbour with these leading marks dead astern and read the steering compass. What is its deviation on this heading?
questions.why: Marks astern on 340°T put your heading on 160°T; + 2°W = 162°M; the compass reads 165°, 3° high, so 3°W.
questions.ref: Compass — checking on a transit astern

questions.q: You doubt the steering compass in mid-Channel, out of sight of land. How can you check it?

figure.title: Mid-Channel, 1840
lines: Steering compass looks a few degrees off

options: Compare it with the GPS COG, tide and all
Compare it with the hand compass at the chart table
Wait for a charted transit tomorrow
Steer at the setting sun and compare its tabled bearing
questions.why: The sun's true bearing at rising or setting comes from tables: point the bow at it and compare with the compass.

questions.q: In fog the plotter and the radar disagree about the headland. What do you do?

figure.title: Fog, visibility 0.1 M
lines: Radar VRM on the headland: 0.6 M
Sounder: the depth charted 0.6 M off

options: Trust the radar and the depth: stand off now
Trust the plotter until the fog lifts
Trust the plotter: radar ranges are poor
Split the difference: call it 0.8 M
questions.why: The radar range and the sounder agree, the plotter stands alone — a chart offset or a bad fix. Open the distance.
questions.ref: Fixing in fog — radar and plotter

questions.q: You take a three-point fix in the usual order. When do you note the time and log?

figure.title: Three-point fix
lines: Time and log go in the log book

options: At the next full hour
As you take the last bearing
Once the fix is on the chart
Before you take the first bearing
questions.why: The abeam bearing, taken last, changes fastest, so the fix belongs to that moment: note time and log as you take it.

questions.q: You check the steering compass on a transit, upright and heeled, on the same heading. What explains these readings?
options: Variation that changes with the tack
Leeway, which differs on each tack
Heeling error — the boat's iron tilts round the compass
A compass card sticking when heeled
questions.why: Heeled, the boat's iron moves relative to the gimballed compass, so deviation changes with the heel and the tack.

questions.q: Your crew took the beam mark first and finished the round of bearings at 1404. How far did you move during the round?
questions.why: 7.5 kn × 4/60 h = 0.5 M; the beam bearing, taken first, is half a mile stale — take the mark nearest the beam last.

questions.q: Light A has dropped out of sight before your second bearing. Can you still get a running fix?

figure.title: Running fix, night
lines: 1100: A out of sight; light B 300°T, log 16.0

options: Yes — A's line moved 6.0 M along 090°T, crossed with B's
Yes — A's line moved 6.0 M along 030°T, crossed with B's
Yes — A's and B's lines crossed as taken
No — both bearings must be of one mark
questions.why: Any position line can be transferred: move A's line by the run, 16.0 − 10.0 = 6.0 M along the track, and cross it with B's.

questions.q: You take one bearing over the steering compass and two with the hand compass on the foredeck. Which true bearings do you plot?
questions.why: Only the steering compass bearing takes the card's 4°E for the ship's head: 020° + 4° − 2° = 022°T; the hand bearings take only −2°W.

questions.q: You pass between rocks at night with these two ways of fixing. Which do you rely on?

figure.title: Inshore at night
lines: Rocks 1 M either side of the track
A: running fix on one light, 2 h run
B: two lights at once, cut at 40°
Tide for A taken from a diamond

options: A and B, averaged together
Neither — wait for a 90° cut
B — no run and no tide to guess
A — one light, so no misidentification
questions.why: A 2-hour running fix carries the errors of course, log and tide; two lights at once at 40° are fresh and need no guesses.

questions.q: You choose a mark for a hand bearing. Which gives the more reliable bearing?

figure.title: Marks for a fix
lines: A: lighthouse on a rock, 4 M off
B: edge of a low, sloping headland, 2 M off

options: Either — both are charted
B — it is bigger and easier to see
B — it is nearer, so less error
A — a sharp point, charted exactly
questions.why: A bearing needs a point you can pin down: the edge of a sloping headland moves with distance and the state of tide.

questions.q: You want to dry out against the harbour wall to scrub the hull, and you need the lowest low waters of the fortnight. Which days do you pick?
options: Monday–Tuesday, a day or two after full moon
Friday–Saturday, just before the full moon
The following Sunday, at the last quarter
Wednesday–Thursday, as the range builds
questions.why: Springs, with the lowest LWs, come a day or two after new and full moon; neaps follow the quarters.

questions.q: This morning's high water was at 0640. You plan to cross the bar on the next high water. About when is it?

figure.title: Tide table
lines: No table aboard for later today

options: About 1255
About 1905
About 1840
About 0730 tomorrow
questions.why: Semi-diurnal tides: two HWs a day about 12 h 25 min apart. 0640 + 12:25 = 1905.

questions.q: Springs are today. You want the weakest streams for a passage through the Chenal du Four with an inexperienced crew. When is the best window in the coming fortnight?
options: In about 14 days, when the cycle repeats
In about 3 days, as the range falls
In about 7 days, at neaps
In about 11 days, before the new moon
questions.why: Springs to neaps is about 7 days, half the ~14.8-day cycle; neap streams run at roughly half the springs rate.

questions.q: You want the lowest low water of the year to scrub on a drying grid. Why does the almanac show bigger spring ranges in March than in June?

figure.title: Almanac — spring ranges
lines: Plan: scrub on a drying grid at LW

options: Low winter pressure deepens every tidal range
The moon is always nearest the earth in March
Winter gales push extra water into the Channel
Equinoctial springs — sun and moon near the equator
questions.why: Near the equinoxes the sun and moon both lie over the equator: equinoctial springs bring the year's largest ranges.

questions.q: The chart shows 1.8 m where you plan to anchor, and the title panel says soundings are reduced to LAT. With ordinary weather, how often will you find less water than that?

figure.note: Soundings in metres below LAT

options: Hardly ever — LAT is the lowest predicted tide
At every spring low water
At every low water, twice a day
At every neap low water
questions.why: Chart datum is about LAT: predicted tides almost never fall below it; only high pressure or offshore winds take it lower.

questions.q: You plan to spend the night over a charted 1.5 m patch with the low water near springs. What depth do you expect at an average spring low water?
options: 0.8 m — you dry out at low water
2.2 m — 0.4 m under the keel
3.4 m — 1.6 m under the keel
1.5 m — you ground by 0.3 m
questions.why: Depth = charted depth + height of tide: 1.5 + MLWS 0.7 = 2.2 m; minus 1.8 m draft leaves 0.4 m.

questions.q: You have today's tide table for the port and the almanac's mean levels. Is today nearer springs or neaps?
options: Springs — HW 4.2 m is close to the spring HW
Springs — 2.4 m is above the 2.2 m neap range
Neaps — 2.4 m range, close to the 2.2 m neap range
Midway — 2.4 m is half the 4.7 m spring range
questions.why: Compare ranges: today 4.2 − 1.8 = 2.4 m; springs 5.4 − 0.7 = 4.7 m; neaps 4.1 − 1.9 = 2.2 m. Near neaps.

questions.q: You are in Saint-Malo, and the almanac gives these times and heights for today. What is the range of this morning's flood?
questions.why: Range = HW − LW of the same tide: 9.8 − 1.1 = 8.7 m.

questions.q: You are at anchor waiting for the flood. What is the height of tide at 0600?
questions.why: Range 4.8 m. After 3 h the tide has risen 1 + 2 + 3 = 6/12: 1.0 + 2.4 = 3.4 m.

questions.q: You leave the marina at 1320 on the ebb. What height of tide do you have at that time?
questions.why: Range 4.8 m. Two hours after HW it has fallen 1 + 2 = 3/12 = 1.2 m: 5.4 − 1.2 = 4.2 m.

questions.q: You are over the charted 1.4 m sounding at 0800. Using the rule of twelfths, what depth of water is there?
You have dried out on a sandbank and want to float off as early as possible. In which hours of the flood does the water rise fastest?

figure.title: Aground on the sand
lines: Keel in soft sand, no swell

options: 0600–0800, the first two hours
Evenly — the same amount each hour
1000–1200, the last two hours
0800–1000, the third and fourth hours
questions.why: Rule of twelfths 1-2-3-3-2-1: the 3rd and 4th hours each bring 3/12 of the range.

questions.q: You are anchoring over the charted 3.2 m sounding. What depth of water do you expect from the surface to the seabed?
questions.why: Depth of water = charted depth + height of tide: 3.2 + 2.5 = 5.7 m.

questions.q: The short cut to the harbour crosses the bank with the underlined 1.8. How much water is over the bank now?
options: 4.8 m — ample for your draft
1.2 m — less than your 1.5 m draft
1.8 m — 0.3 m under the keel
3.0 m — 1.5 m under the keel
questions.why: An underlined figure is a drying height above datum: water over it = 3.0 − 1.8 = 1.2 m, less than 1.5 m.

questions.q: You want to cross the bank with the underlined 1.2 and keep 0.5 m under the keel. By the rule of twelfths, what is the earliest time on the flood?
questions.why: Need 1.2 + 1.2 + 0.5 = 2.9 m of tide. Three hours after LW: 0.5 + 6/12 × 4.8 = 2.9 m — at 1000.

questions.q: You are leaving over the bar, charted 0.8 m, on the ebb and want 0.6 m under the keel. By the rule of twelfths, what is the latest time to cross?
The marina sill dries 2.0 m above chart datum. How much water is over the sill now, and what is left under the keel?
options: 2.1 m over the sill, 0.3 m under the keel
6.1 m over the sill, 4.3 m under the keel
2.3 m over the sill, 0.5 m under the keel
4.1 m over the sill, 2.3 m under the keel
questions.why: Water over the sill = 4.1 − 2.0 = 2.1 m; minus the 1.8 m draft leaves 0.3 m. Tight: most skippers want 0.5 m or more.

questions.q: You want 0.6 m under the keel crossing the marina sill on the flood. Using the port's tidal curve, what is the earliest time?
Using the port's tidal curve, what is the height of tide at 1400?
questions.why: Height = LW + range × factor = 1.0 + 4.0 × 0.70 = 3.8 m.

questions.q: You need the height of tide two hours before LW to enter a shallow creek, and your crew has worked it by the rule of twelfths. What do you do?

figure.title: Almanac — Solent port
lines: Rise about 7 h, fall about 5 h

options: Accept it — the rule works for every port
Use the mean of the HW and LW heights
Add 10% to the answer to be safe
Read it off the port's own tidal curve
questions.why: The rule of twelfths assumes a symmetrical 6-hour tide. With a double HW or a stand, use the port's curve.

questions.q: You are lying to a buoy where the charted depth is 1.8 m. What depth will you have at this morning's low water?

figure.title: Tide table
lines: Charted depth at the buoy 1.8 m

options: 1.6 m — 0.1 m less than your draft
1.4 m — 0.3 m into the mud
2.0 m — 0.3 m under the keel
1.8 m — 0.1 m under the keel
questions.why: A minus height means the tide falls below chart datum: 1.8 + (−0.2) = 1.6 m, under your 1.7 m draft.

questions.q: You are bound for the secondary port. What are the time and height of its high water?
questions.why: Apply the differences with their signs: 0912 − 0035 = 0837; 5.8 − 0.6 = 5.2 m.

questions.q: You will use the rule of twelfths at the secondary port this afternoon. What range do you work with?

figure.title: Secondary port
lines: Standard port: HW 4.9 m · LW 0.9 m
Height diff: HW +0.4 m · LW +0.1 m

questions.why: Correct both heights first: HW 4.9 + 0.4 = 5.3 m, LW 0.9 + 0.1 = 1.0 m; range 4.3 m.

questions.q: Interpolate the height difference for today. What are the time and height of HW at the secondary port?
questions.why: 5.5 m is halfway from MHWN to MHWS, so the difference is +0.6: 6.1 m. Time 1020 − 0030 = 0950.

questions.q: You need the height of tide at the secondary port at 1500. By the rule of twelfths, what is it?

figure.title: Secondary port
lines: Diff: HW and LW heights −0.2 m

questions.why: Secondary HW 1300 4.8 m, LW 1900 0.8 m, range 4.0 m. At HW+2 it has fallen 3/12 = 1.0 m: 3.8 m.

questions.q: It is HW−1 at the reference port and today is a spring tide. What stream do you plot from the diamond's table?
options: Set 225°T, rate 2.4 kn
Set 045°T, rate 2.4 kn
Set 045°T, rate 1.2 kn
Set 060°T, rate 1.8 kn
questions.why: Read the HW−1 row and the springs column: the stream sets towards 045°T at 2.4 kn.

questions.q: You are about to plot the stream for your EP. Which row of the diamond's table covers the time now?
options: HW+2 — round down to the whole hour
HW+3 — 1415 is 2 h 45 min after HW
HW−3 — count to the next high water
questions.why: 1415 is HW+2h45. Each row covers half an hour either side of its hour, so HW+3 (HW+2h30 to HW+3h30).

questions.q: The diamond gives the spring and neap rates for the hour. What rate do you use for today's stream?
options: 3.0 kn
1.4 kn
2.2 kn
2.5 kn

questions.q: You are working up an EP and need the stream at diamond D for the time now. What do you plot?
options: 080°T at 1.7 kn
260°T at 1.7 kn
080°T at 2.4 kn
075°T at 1.3 kn
questions.why: 1140 is HW+2h35, so the HW+3 row. Today is halfway from neaps to springs: 1.0 + 0.5 × 1.4 = 1.7 kn, setting 080°T.

questions.q: You are reading the tidal stream atlas for the next hour and today is a neap tide. What stream do you take from the page?
options: East-going at 1.2 kn
East-going at 0.6 kn
West-going at 0.6 kn
East-going at 6 kn
questions.why: Atlas figures give neaps,springs in tenths of a knot: 06,12 is 0.6 kn at neaps and 1.2 kn at springs.

questions.q: You will reach the headland at 1100 and want the stream there from the atlas. Which page do you open?

figure.title: Atlas and tide times
lines: Atlas pages: hours from HW Dover

options: HW−1 — 1 h 15 min before local HW
HW−2 — rounded down to whole hours
HW−3 — 2 h 40 min before HW Dover
HW+3 — 2 h 40 min after HW Dover
questions.why: Count from the atlas's own reference port: 1100 is 2 h 40 min before HW Dover, so the HW−3 page.

questions.q: You are motoring north through the sound against the foul stream. Where do you expect the weakest stream?

figure.note: Depths in metres

options: In the narrowest part of the sound
In mid-channel, where the water is deepest
Off the points at each end of the sound
Near the edges, out of the mid-channel stream
questions.why: Streams run hardest in the deep middle of a channel, in the narrows and off points; friction slows them at the edges.

questions.q: You are beating west along the coast against a 2 kn foul stream, and the pilot book mentions an eddy in the bay. Where do you sail?
options: Close inshore across the bay, in the eddy
On the rhumb line between the headlands
Well offshore, where the stream is weaker
In mid-bay, clear of both shores
questions.why: Bays often hold an eddy or a counter-current inshore; the main stream runs strongest offshore and off the headlands.

questions.q: You are heading west and plan to round the headland while the spring stream runs west against the westerly F6. What do you do?
options: Motor straight through at full speed
Wait for slack water before rounding
Round close along the edge of the overfalls
Go now, while the stream is fair for you
questions.why: Wind against a spring stream off a headland raises steep, breaking overfalls. Round at slack, or well outside them.

questions.q: You are crossing the channel today. When do you expect the steepest, most uncomfortable sea?
options: At 1700, while the stream is slack
All day the same — only the wind matters
1700–2300, with the stream against the wind
1100–1700, with the stream and wind together
questions.why: A SW wind blows towards the NE; the SW-going stream runs into it. Wind against tide shortens and steepens the waves.

questions.q: You are heading SW through the race with a family crew. The stream is fair for you from 0900. What do you decide?

figure.title: Race passage plan
lines: Pilot book: dangerous in wind v tide

options: Go now and motor-sail hard through it
Go at 0900 to carry the fair stream
Go at 1500, once the stream turns foul
Postpone — wind against a spring stream in the race
questions.why: A SW F6 against the spring SW-going stream makes the race dangerous: here a fair stream means wind against tide.

questions.q: You want to arrive at the headland just as the stream there turns fair. When do you leave?

figure.title: Tidal gate
lines: Fair stream there from HW Dover −1

questions.why: Fair from HW Dover −1 = 0930; 12 M at 6 kn takes 2 h, so leave at 0730.

questions.q: You are waiting to pass under the bridge on the ebb with your margin. By the rule of twelfths, what is the earliest time?
questions.why: Clearance = 11.5 + 4.8 − height; you need 13.6 m, so height ≤ 2.7 m. HW+3: 5.1 − 6/12 × 4.8 = 2.7 m at 1200.

questions.q: You are motoring up the river towards the bridge. Can you pass under it now, and with how much room?

figure.note: Clearances above HAT

options: Yes — 20.8 m clearance, 7.0 m to spare
No — 9.0 m clearance (12.0 − 3.0)
Yes — 14.8 m clearance, 1.0 m to spare
No — 12.0 m is less than your 13.8 m
questions.why: Clearance now = charted 12.0 + (HAT 5.8 − tide 3.0) = 14.8 m: 1.0 m over your 13.8 m air draught.

questions.q: The chart gives 9.5 m under the bridge, and your air draught is 9.0 m. What does the 9.5 m tell you about the room under it?
options: Exactly 9.5 m at every high water
9.5 m only at mean high water springs
9.5 m at chart datum, less at high water
At least 9.5 m at almost any state of tide
questions.why: HAT is the highest predicted tide, so the real clearance is 9.5 m or more, except in a surge.

questions.q: You need to pass under the power cable across the channel. Can you pass under it now?

figure.note: Clearances above HAT

options: Yes — 21.0 m clearance, 2.8 m to spare
Yes — 18 m clears the 17.2 m mast
No — 18.2 m tops the charted 18 m
No — 16.0 m clearance (18 − 2.0)
questions.why: Safe clearance is above HAT: 18 + (5.0 − 2.0) = 21.0 m. Count the aerial: 18.2 m, so 2.8 m to spare.

questions.q: You are about to drop anchor here for the night. Will you stay afloat at low water?
options: No — 1.4 m at LW, under your draft
Yes — 5.0 m now, and it is near HW
questions.why: The tide will drop 4.6 − 1.0 = 3.6 m: 5.0 − 3.6 = 1.4 m at LW, less than the 1.7 m draft.

questions.q: You want 1.0 m under the keel at low water. Using the rule of twelfths, what is the least depth you should anchor in now?
You are off the bar at low water with a swell running. The bar's charted depth is 1.4 m. Do you cross?
options: Yes — the crests add 0.6 m of water
Yes — 3.4 m of water with the swell
Yes — 2.2 m gives 0.4 m under the keel
No — about 1.6 m in the troughs, under your draft
questions.why: Depth 1.4 + 0.8 = 2.2 m, but the boat drops about half the 1.2 m swell in a trough: 1.6 m. Wait for the flood.

questions.q: You are about to cross the bar at low water after a week of settled weather. What depth do you allow for on the bar?

figure.title: Before crossing the bar
lines: Charted depth on the bar 1.6 m
Rule: about 1 cm per hPa from 1013

options: About 1.8 m
About 2.0 m
About 2.2 m
About 1.6 m
questions.why: 20 hPa above 1013 lowers the sea about 0.2 m: 1.6 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 1.8 m.

questions.q: You plan to pass under a bridge near high water tonight, with 0.6 m of margin at the predicted height. What do you expect?

figure.title: Bristol Channel, springs
lines: SW gale F8 for two days
Bridge margin at predicted HW: 0.6 m

options: A lower HW than predicted — more room
A higher HW than predicted — the margin may go
A higher LW only — the HW is unchanged
The predicted HW — the tables allow for weather
questions.why: Onshore gales and low pressure (982 hPa, about +0.3 m) pile water up: a surge lifts HW above the tables.

questions.q: You are lying on a mooring in a shallow harbour, and the wind has blown hard off the land for three days. What do you expect at low water?

figure.title: Before the morning LW
lines: Strong E wind, offshore, for 3 days
Your margin at predicted LW: 0.3 m

options: The predicted depth — the tables include weather
Less water only at neaps, not at springs
Less water than predicted — you may touch
More water than predicted — the wind holds it in
questions.why: Offshore winds and high pressure lower the sea below the prediction; a 0.3 m margin can disappear.

questions.q: You are in the north of the Adriatic, used to tideless Greek harbours, and moor stern-to for the night. Can you ignore the tide at this quay?

figure.title: Northern Adriatic quay
lines: Pilot book: spring range about 1 m

options: Yes — Mediterranean tides are too small
No — about 2.7 m at LW, the tide adds
Yes — charted depths are always at LW
No — about 1.7 m at LW, under your draft
questions.why: Ranges here are near 1 m; with depths from mean sea level, LW is about 0.5 m lower: 2.2 − 0.5 = 1.7 m.

questions.q: You have sailed from the Ionian to the Gulf of Gabès and anchored at high water on a wide shallow bank. What do you expect at low water?

figure.title: Gulf of Gabès, Tunisia
lines: Almanac: spring range here up to 2 m
Anchored at HW in 2.5 m · draft 1.9 m

options: Aground — the depth falls by about 2 m
Afloat — the bank dries only in a gale
Afloat — the drop is only about 0.2 m
Afloat — Mediterranean tides are tiny
questions.why: The Gulf of Gabès has the Mediterranean's largest tides, up to about 2 m at springs: 2.5 − 2.0 = 0.5 m.

questions.q: You are in a shallow Ionian harbour with little water under the keel, and a deep low is coming. What will change the water level most over the next day?
options: The tide — tonight is the full moon
The weather — the pressure and the wind
Nothing — the harbour is enclosed
The tide — its 0.2 m range twice a day
questions.why: Where the range is 0.2 m, a deep low (about +0.2 m) and a gale's surge or set-down move the level more than the tide.

questions.q: The boatyard up the drying creek can only take you on a big spring high water. Today the moon is at first quarter. When do you book the lift?
options: In about 4 days, as the moon waxes
Today, while the moon is at first quarter
In about 8–9 days, just after the full moon
In about 15 days, at the next first quarter
questions.why: First quarter brings neaps; the full moon comes about 7 days later and springs a day or two after it — in about 8–9 days.

questions.q: You went out over the bar on this morning's high water at 1015. You want to come back in on tomorrow morning's high water. About when will it be?
options: About 1040
About 1215
About 1015
About 1105
questions.why: Two tides a day of about 12 h 25 min each: the same HW tomorrow is about 24 h 50 min later — 1015 + 0050 = 1105.

questions.q: You plan to anchor this weekend in a bay with a small margin at low water. The almanac shows the moon at perigee on the day of the full moon. What do you expect of these springs?

figure.title: Almanac — this weekend
lines: Your margin at mean spring LW: 0.3 m

options: A bigger range than usual — lower low waters
A smaller range — perigee damps the tide
Higher low waters — the moon lifts the sea
The usual range — perigee makes no difference
questions.why: At perigee the moon is nearest and pulls hardest: perigean springs have larger ranges, so LW falls below its mean.

questions.q: You want to avoid the day when the streams in the sound run hardest this week. Which day is that, from the port's tide table?
options: Thursday — the first HW over 5 m
Friday — the largest range, 5.0 m
Saturday — the highest HW, 5.6 m
Sunday — the day after the highest HW
questions.why: Stream rates follow the range, not the HW height: Friday 5.5 − 0.5 = 5.0 m beats Saturday 5.6 − 0.8 = 4.8 m.

questions.q: You want to take the boat into the creek behind the drying bank at high water. On which tides can you get in with your margin?

figure.title: The creek over the bank
lines: Draft 1.5 m · want 0.5 m under the keel

options: Neither — the bank dries higher than your draft
Neaps only — the stream over the bank is weaker
Springs only — 2.6 m over the bank, 1.2 m at neaps
Springs and neaps — 4.2 m is plenty for 1.5 m
questions.why: Water over the bank at HW = HW − 3.0: springs 2.6 m (1.1 m under the keel); neaps 1.2 m, less than the 1.5 m draft.

questions.q: At neaps you lie here comfortably, with water under the keel at low water. You plan to stay on into springs. What will you have at a spring low water?
options: 1.5 m of water — the same as at neaps
2.3 m of water — springs bring more water
0.9 m of water — the drying height added
0.1 m of water — the keel is on the bottom
questions.why: Water over a drying height = tide − 0.4: neaps 1.9 − 0.4 = 1.5 m; springs 0.5 − 0.4 = 0.1 m — the 1.2 m keel sits on the sand.

questions.q: You plan to lock out of the marina at high water. What time is high water on the ship's clock?

figure.title: Almanac — Saint-Quay
lines: Ship's clock: French summer time, UT+2

questions.why: The almanac gives UT: add 2 h for French summer time — 1146 + 2 h = 1346.

questions.q: You are at anchor waiting for the flood to carry you over the shallows. Using the rule of twelfths, what is the height of tide at 1100?
You are leaving the marina on the ebb and need 3.0 m of tide for the sill. Until what time is there that much?

figure.title: Tide table
lines: Sill: you need 3.0 m of tide

questions.why: 3.0 m is mid-range, (5.4 + 0.6) ÷ 2, reached at mid-ebb: half of 6 h 30 min after HW — 0800 + 3 h 15 min = 1115.

questions.q: You reach the shallow entrance to the anchorage at 1030 on the ebb. Using the rule of twelfths, what height of tide do you expect?
questions.why: First hour 1/12 × 4.8 = 0.4 m; half the second hour, another 1/12 = 0.4 m: 5.6 − 0.8 = 4.8 m.

questions.q: You are working out heights for a day in this port. When is your crew's rule-of-twelfths answer most likely to be wrong?

figure.title: Almanac — port notes
lines: Stand of the tide at HW: about 2 h

options: Near HW, while the level hardly changes
Evenly, through every hour of the tide
At mid-flood, in the third and fourth hours
At LW, as the flood begins
questions.why: Twelfths assume a smooth, sine-shaped curve; through a long stand the level barely moves, so twelfths overstate the change near HW.

questions.q: You want to leave over the sill at 1400. Your crew's rule of twelfths says there isn't enough water. Can you go?

figure.title: Leaving over the sill
lines: Sill: you need 4.8 m of tide

options: No — the curve gives 4.4 m at 1400
Yes — the curve gives 5.1 m at 1400
Yes — the twelfths give 5.1 m at 1400
No — the twelfths give 4.4 m at 1400
questions.why: Use the curve where there is a stand: 0.8 + 0.90 × 4.8 = 5.1 m, enough for the 4.8 m needed. Twelfths give 5.6 − 1.2 = 4.4 m.

questions.q: Your crew wants a late breakfast before you go. The tide is falling, and you want 0.5 m under the keel over the marina sill. By the rule of twelfths, until when can you still leave?
questions.why: Need 1.8 + 2.1 + 0.5 = 4.4 m of tide. HW+2: 5.6 − 3/12 × 4.8 = 4.4 m — at 1030; then it falls 1.2 m in the next hour.

questions.q: You will cross the bar on the way out at 1600. By the rule of twelfths, what depth will you find over it?
options: 3.8 m — 2.0 m under the keel
1.9 m — 0.1 m under the keel
3.2 m — 1.4 m under the keel
2.9 m — 1.1 m under the keel
questions.why: HW+4: 4.6 − 9/12 × 3.6 = 1.9 m of tide; + 1.0 m charted = 2.9 m, 1.1 m under a 1.8 m keel.

questions.q: Your plan gives 0.3 m under the keel crossing the bar at 2200 on the falling tide, in the dark. What do you do?

figure.title: Bar crossing tonight
lines: Ebb · tide falling about 0.4 m an hour
Dark, slight swell on the bar

options: Cross at 2130 — about 0.5 m under the keel
Cross at 2230 — the ebb will have eased
Cross at 2200 — and slow right down on the bar
Cross at 2200 — 0.3 m is enough at night
questions.why: On a falling tide every minute late costs water: half an hour earlier adds 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 m — 0.5 m under the keel.

questions.q: The crew are taking the tender ashore from the anchorage. They need 0.4 m of water at the foot of the slipway to get back off. By the rule of twelfths, when must they be back?

figure.title: Shore trip
lines: Foot of the slipway dries 2.4 m

questions.q: You are working the height of tide from the port's curve diagram, which has a spring and a neap curve. Which curve do you read today?

figure.title: Tidal curves — standard port
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.9 m · neaps 2.6 m

options: The neap curve — it is the safer, lower one
Halfway between the two, every day
The spring curve — today is close to springs
Either — the two curves give the same
questions.why: Today's 5.8 m range is almost the 5.9 m mean spring range: read the spring curve; interpolate only for ranges in between.

questions.q: You are going up river on the flood and must pass under the bridge before the tide gets too high. From the port's curve, what is the latest time?
questions.why: Room = 10.6 + 5.0 − tide must be at least 13.5 m, so tide ≤ 2.1 m: factor (2.1 − 0.8) ÷ 5.0 = 0.26 — HW−4, 0900.

questions.q: You will cross the drying bar of the secondary port at its high water. When is that, and what will you have under the keel?
options: 1120 — 1.2 m under the keel
1120 — 1.6 m under the keel
1120 — 0.8 m under the keel
1200 — 1.2 m under the keel
questions.why: HW there 1140 − 0020 = 1120, 4.8 − 0.4 = 4.4 m; over the bar 4.4 − 1.5 = 2.9 m: 1.2 m under a 1.7 m keel.

questions.q: You are anchored off the secondary port over a charted 1.2 m. When is low water there, and what depth will you have then?

figure.title: Secondary port — LW
lines: Charted depth where you lie 1.2 m

questions.q: You need the time of high water at the secondary port for an early start. Interpolating the time difference, when is it?
You are anchored for lunch over the underlined 0.4 in the bay and want 0.3 m under the keel when you weigh. By the rule of twelfths, what is the latest time to leave?
questions.why: Need 0.4 + 1.5 + 0.3 = 2.2 m of tide. HW+4: 5.8 − 9/12 × 4.8 = 2.2 m — at 1450; after that the spot dries.

questions.q: You anchored at this evening's low water and are happy with the depth. What will you have under the keel at the next low water?
options: 0.2 m — 0.4 m less than tonight
0.6 m — the same as tonight
1.0 m — 0.4 m more than tonight
0.5 m — the next LW height
questions.why: Springs are building: the next LW is 0.4 m lower (0.5 v 0.9 m), so 2.4 − 0.4 = 2.0 m — 0.2 m under a 1.8 m keel.

questions.q: You must pass under the bridge near tonight's high water, and a surge is forecast. How much room will you have?
options: 14.4 m — 0.8 m to spare
14.1 m — 0.5 m to spare
13.7 m — 0.1 m to spare
14.7 m — 1.1 m to spare
questions.why: Room = 14.0 + (HAT 5.6 − HW 5.2 − surge 0.3) = 14.1 m: the surge eats into the HAT margin, leaving 0.5 m over 13.6 m.

questions.q: Your old chart gives the bridge clearance above MHWS. You plan to pass under it at today's high water. Can you?
options: Yes — 12.0 m is more than your 11.8 m
No — 11.6 m at HW, under your 11.8 m
questions.why: A clearance above MHWS shrinks when HW tops MHWS: 12.0 − (5.0 − 4.6) = 11.6 m, less than the 11.8 m air draught.

questions.q: Your crew wants to go under the bridge at high water, counting on the high pressure to lower the tide. What do you do?

figure.title: Bridge at HW
lines: 0.1 m short at the predicted HW

options: Go — 1038 hPa lowers HW by 0.25 m
Go — the tables already allow for it
Go slowly, watching the masthead
Wait for the ebb to give real room
questions.why: Pressure effects are rough estimates, not predictions: with no margin at the predicted HW, wait for the falling tide.

questions.q: You are working up the EP at the end of a two-hour leg, 1100 to 1300, at springs. What total tide vector do you lay off?
questions.why: Lay off each hour: 1.6 M towards 070° (HW+1), then 2.0 M towards 080° (HW+2) — together about 3.6 M towards 076°T.

questions.q: The next two hours of your leg fall in the HW−2 and HW−1 rows of the diamond. How far does the stream carry you over the two hours?
options: 2.4 M towards 255°T
3.7 M towards 255°T
1.9 M towards 255°T
5.0 M towards 255°T
questions.why: Today is midway between neaps and springs: 1.6 + 2.1 = 3.7 M, both hours setting 255°T.

questions.q: You will cross the bay from 1000 to 1200 and take the streams from the atlas. Which two pages do you use?
options: HW−1, then HW+1
HW−1, then HW
HW, then HW+1
HW+1, then HW+2
questions.why: Each page covers the hour centred on its time: 1030 is 20 min before HW Dover (the HW page), 1130 is 40 min after (HW+1).

questions.q: You are reading the tidal stream atlas for your next hour. What rate do you use today?

figure.title: Tidal stream atlas
lines: Ranges: sp 5.4 m · np 2.4 m · today 4.4 m

options: 1.0 kn
1.6 kn
2.2 kn
1.8 kn
questions.why: 10,22 means 1.0 kn at neaps, 2.2 kn at springs. Today is 2/3 of the way from neaps to springs: 1.0 + 2/3 × 1.2 = 1.8 kn.

questions.q: Today's range is bigger than the mean spring range. What rate do you use for the stream at the diamond?

figure.title: Equinoctial springs
lines: Mean ranges: sp 5.0 m · np 2.0 m

options: 3.3 kn
2.2 kn
3.0 kn
4.6 kn
questions.why: Extend the line past springs: 3.0 + (5.6 − 5.0) ÷ 3.0 × 1.6 = 3.3 kn. Capping it at 3.0 kn underestimates it.

questions.q: You are plotting the stream at the diamond for the time now. Which row of the table do you use?
options: HW+7 — 7 h after the 0410 HW
HW−5 — 5 h 25 min before the 1635 HW
HW−6 — 6 h before the 1635 HW
HW+6 — the last row after the 0410 HW
questions.why: 1110 is 7 h after the 0410 HW, past the last row: count back from the next HW — 5 h 25 min before 1635 is the HW−5 row.

questions.q: You see these two arrows off the harbour entrance on the chart. What does the feathered arrow tell you?

figure.title: Chart — stream arrows
lines: Arrow with a feathered tail: 2.5 kn
Plain arrow, the other way: 2 kn

options: A current of 2.5 kn at all times
The flood stream, 2.5 kn at neaps
The flood stream, 2.5 kn at springs
The ebb stream, 2.5 kn at springs
questions.why: On the chart a feathered arrow is the flood stream and a plain one the ebb; the rate shown is the mean spring rate.

questions.q: You want to cross the race off the point at slack water. From the diamond beside it, about when do you go?
options: About 1340
About 1140
About 0940
About 1240
questions.why: The rate falls to 0.1 kn at HW+3 before the set reverses: HW Dover 0940 + 3 h = about 1240.

questions.q: You want to leave harbour just as the stream outside turns west in your favour. When do you go?

figure.title: Leaving harbour
lines: Stream outside turns W-going: HW Dover +1

options: About 1530
About 1430
About 1230
About 1130
questions.why: Local HW 1130 is HW Dover −3, so HW Dover is 1430; the stream turns at HW Dover +1 — 1530, four hours after local HW.

questions.q: You are beating west along the coast against the last of the foul stream. Where does the stream turn fair first?
options: Offshore, where the stream is strongest
Close inshore, in the shallower water
Everywhere at once, at local HW
Off the headlands, where it runs fastest
questions.why: The stream turns earlier close inshore, where it is weaker and the water shallower, than out in the offing.

questions.q: You are motoring up the winding river against the ebb. Where do you steer through each bend?

figure.note: Draft 1.6 m · mid-tide

options: The outside of the bend, in the deepest water
Wherever the river is narrowest
The inside of the bend, out of the main stream
Mid-river, on the line of the channel
questions.why: The stream runs hardest round the outside of a bend, where the water is deepest; it is weaker on the inside, depth permitting.

questions.q: Your Mediterranean passage plan takes you north through the strait under motor. What do you time the passage by?

figure.title: Strait of Messina
lines: Pilot book: streams up to about 3 kn
Your speed under motor 5 kn, bound N

options: Night — the streams are weakest after dark
Nothing — Mediterranean tides are too small
The wind only — the streams follow the wind
The strait's streams — go with the north-going one
questions.why: The range there is small, but the streams through the narrows run to about 3 kn: time the passage for the north-going stream.

questions.q: You are moored stern-to on a low quay at the north end of the Adriatic, and a two-day Sirocco is forecast. What do you expect of the water level?

figure.title: North Adriatic, Sirocco
lines: Forecast: SE F7 for two days
Moored stern-to on a low quay

options: Higher than predicted — watch the lines
Lower than predicted — the wind blows it out
Lower than predicted — the low pressure
As predicted — the tide here is too small
questions.why: A SE Sirocco piles water into the closed north end of the Adriatic, and the falling barometer adds more: expect well above predictions.

questions.q: Your old boat barely out-motors the foul stream off the point. When do you leave for it?

figure.title: Tidal gate — slow boat
lines: Point 18 M ahead · your speed 4.5 kn
Little stream on the way there
At the point: foul 4 kn until 1430

options: 0930 — reach the point an hour early
1030 — reach the point as it turns fair
1230 — leave two hours before the turn
1430 — leave as the point turns fair
questions.why: 18 M at 4.5 kn = 4 h: leave at 1030 to arrive at 1430. An hour early you would make about 0.5 kn against the 4 kn stream.

questions.q: You are heading up the channel to the harbour, and the crew wants to wait at anchor for the fair stream. What do you decide?

figure.title: Up the channel to harbour
lines: Now: foul stream 2.5 kn for 2 h
Crew: “wait 2 h for the fair tide”

options: Go now — you arrive about 2 h sooner
Wait 2 h — you arrive about 40 min sooner
Go now — you arrive about 40 min sooner
Wait 2 h — the foul stream halves your speed
questions.why: Now: 5 M in 2 h, then 7 M at 7.5 kn = 56 min — 2 h 56. Waiting: 2 h + 12 M at 7.5 kn = 3 h 36.

questions.q: You plan to cross the bar at tomorrow morning's spring low water. What depth do you really expect on it?

figure.title: Spring LW tomorrow
lines: Predicted LW 0.3 m · bar charted 1.6 m
Offshore gale for 2 days: set-down 0.3 m

options: About 2.3 m — the weather adds water
About 1.8 m — only the pressure counts
About 1.9 m — 0.3 m under the keel
About 1.5 m — you would touch
questions.why: 1.6 + 0.3 = 1.9 m predicted; −0.1 m for 1023 hPa, −0.3 m of set-down: about 1.5 m, under the 1.6 m draft.

questions.q: You are drying out your catamaran on the sand over the underlined 1.8 for a scrub. By the rule of twelfths, when do both keels take the ground?
questions.why: She grounds when the tide = 1.8 + 1.1 = 2.9 m. HW+3: 5.3 − 6/12 × 4.8 = 2.9 m — at 1200.

questions.q: You want to dry out your catamaran to scrub both hulls at low water. Where do you put her?

figure.title: Drying out a catamaran
lines: Plan: scrub both hulls at LW
Spots: the harbour wall, sand, soft mud

options: Against the harbour wall, a line from the mast
On level, firm sand — both keels land together
On the sloping beach, bows up the slope
On soft mud, so the keels sink in gently
questions.why: A catamaran stands on her own keels: choose firm, level ground clear of rocks so she settles evenly — no wall or legs needed.

questions.q: You are rounding the headland at 0200 with a fair spring stream, and the pilot book warns that it sets onto the point. How do you pass?
options: On the plotter track, keeping the speed up
Close in to the point, inside the overfalls
Well off, outside the overfalls, fixing often
Straight for the light, then turn away late
questions.why: At night you can't see the race or judge the set: give the point a wide berth and fix often, as the stream speeds up round it.

questions.q: You are approaching the river bar from seaward with an onshore swell running. When do you cross it?

figure.title: River bar, W swell
lines: Onshore swell 1.5 m · wind W F5
Ebb runs out over the bar at 3 kn

options: Early in the ebb, just after HW at 1420
At LW, once the ebb has finished
Any time — the swell decides, not the stream
Late in the flood, before HW at 1420
questions.why: The ebb running out against an onshore swell makes the bar steep and breaking; cross on the last of the flood, with the most water.

questions.q: Your EP is in the bay, close to diamond B; diamond A is out in the main channel. Which stream do you use?

figure.note: Diamonds A and B · depths in metres

options: B — the nearer, in the same water as you
Neither — a bay has no tidal stream
A — the main channel's stream is stronger
The mean of A and B, to be safe
questions.why: Use the diamond nearest you and in the same kind of water; average two only when they are about equally near.

questions.q: In fog you are following the 5 m contour into the bay by echo sounder. What reading keeps you on it?

figure.note: Depths below chart datum

questions.why: Depth over the 5 m contour = 5.0 + 2.3 = 7.3 m; the sounder reads below the keel: 7.3 − 1.8 = 5.5 m.

questions.q: You are alongside a quay wall in a big-tide harbour, with your lines led up to the bollards. How much will the level fall in the next hour?

figure.title: Alongside the wall
lines: Lines led up to bollards on the quay

questions.why: 1100–1200 is the fourth hour of the ebb: 3/12 of the 6.0 m range, 1.5 m — the lines need easing as she drops.

questions.q: You are using an old chart of a quiet anchorage, and tomorrow brings a big spring low water. What may you find there?
options: Never less than the charted depth
Always more water than charted
Exactly the charted depth
Less water than the chart shows
questions.why: MLWS is a mean, not the lowest level: a big spring LW falls below it, so you can find less than charted. Modern charts use LAT.

questions.q: You are checking the pilotage plan your mate wrote for tonight's entry. What is the most useful thing to add to it?

figure.title: Pilotage plan — Porto Vecchio
lines: 3  Pier head → turn to port for the marina

options: What you will see at each turn and the danger past it
The full tidal curve for the whole day
The latitude and longitude of every mark
The opening hours of the marina office
questions.why: A pilotage plan is what you expect to see, when, and what lies beyond if you miss it — not data to look up.

questions.q: You are writing the pilotage plan card for tomorrow's entry. Why do you write every heading and bearing in degrees magnetic?
options: Magnetic bearings are free of variation and deviation
The helm's compass and the hand-bearing compass read magnetic
The compass rose on the chart shows magnetic only
The plotter can display magnetic bearings only
questions.why: In the cockpit you steer and take bearings by magnetic compass — the card must need no arithmetic.

questions.q: You are on leg 2 of your plan. When do you expect the turning mark abeam?

figure.title: Log — night entry
lines: Leg 2: 047°M, 1.3 M to the Fl G 3s

questions.why: Use speed over the ground: 1.3 M ÷ 4.5 kn = 0.29 h = 17 min; 2140 + 17 min = 2157.

questions.q: Your plan says the turning mark should be fine to starboard by now. What do you do?

figure.title: Night entry
lines: 2215  Fairway buoy abeam; leg 2 is 1.0 M
Plan: Fl(2) G 6s fine to stbd by 2228

options: Turn to starboard and search for the green light
Press on along the heading — it will show up soon
Speed up to get in before the night gets darker
Stop, fix your position and go back to the fairway buoy
questions.why: A mark not seen when the plan expects it means you may not be where you think: stop, fix, return to the last safe point.

questions.q: You are entering on the leading lights at night and see them like this. What do you do?

figure.note: Leading lights ahead · rear light open to the left

options: You are to port of the line: come to starboard
You are to starboard of the line: come to port
You are to port of the line: come further to port
You are on the line: hold your heading
questions.why: Rear light open to the left of the front means you are left of the line — steer right until they are one above the other.

questions.q: There are no leading marks into the bay, so you pick a natural transit to hold your line clear of the reef. Which pair do you choose?
options: Two trees on the beach a few metres apart
A chapel high on the hill behind the end of the jetty
A yacht at anchor in line with the beach bar
The end of the jetty in line with a moored boat
questions.why: A good transit uses two fixed, easy-to-see objects far apart: the farther the rear from the front, the sooner it shows you are off.

questions.q: You are entering on the charted leading line with the marks exactly in line, yet the plotter shows you here. What do you trust?
options: Neither — stop until the two agree again
The plotter — GPS is good to a few metres
The transit — the plotter's chart may be offset
The plotter — steer west to put it on the line
questions.why: Marks in line put you on the line whatever the screen says; a plotter chart can be offset from GPS by tens of metres.

questions.q: You are motoring in on the 045°M transit and keep the marks in line, but the compass shows 055°M. What does it mean?
options: The transit is wrong; steer by the compass instead
The compass has 10° of deviation; steer 045°M
A cross-stream sets you to starboard; steer 045°M
A cross-stream sets you to port; holding the transit is right
questions.why: On a transit the heading is whatever keeps the marks in line: bow 10° to starboard of it means the stream sets you to port.

questions.q: What does this line of your pilotage plan tell you?

figure.title: Pilotage plan — leg 2
lines: (shoal lies on the far side of the line)

options: The light must bear 125°T or less to keep clear
Steer 125°T straight for the light on this leg
Pass the light no more than 1.25 M off
The light must bear 125°T or more to keep clear
questions.why: NMT = not more than: the clearing bearing is a limit, and the plan says which side of it is safe.

questions.q: You are coasting east at night past the shoal, using the clearing bearing on the lighthouse. Your hand-bearing compass gives the light 084°M. What do you do?
options: Alter to port until it bears 090°M or more
Alter to starboard until it bears 080°M or less
Hold course — over 080°M is the safe side
Alter to port until it bears 080°M or less
questions.why: The shoal lies where the light bears more than 080°M; heading east, moving south (to starboard) brings the bearing down.

questions.q: You are heading north into the bay between two reefs. Where are you and what do you do?
options: 009°T — east of the safe corridor; come to port
007°T — inside the corridor; hold your course
009°T — west of the safe corridor; come to starboard
005°T — inside the corridor; hold your course
questions.why: 007°M + 2°E = 009°T, over the NMT 008°T limit: the church bears too far right, so you are west — move east.

questions.q: You want a clearing line past a reef that runs parallel to your course. Which object makes the best one?
options: A tower on the beam, whose bearing changes fastest
A ship at anchor ahead, lying on the right line
Any object at all — the plotter checks the line
A fixed light near ahead, whose line clears the reef
questions.why: A clearing line runs from a fixed, charted object past the danger's edge, roughly along your track — ahead or astern.

questions.q: You leave harbour at night along the leading line, steering 040°M with the lights astern. What should they bear by hand-bearing compass?

figure.note: Looking astern · leading lights in line

questions.why: A back bearing is the reciprocal: 040° + 180° = 220°.

questions.q: Leaving the harbour on the planned track, you take a back bearing of the harbour light. Where are you and what do you do?

figure.title: Leaving Ermoupoli
lines: Track 020°M away from the harbour light
Rocks 2 cables either side of the track

options: East of the line: alter to starboard
East of the line: alter to port
West of the line: alter to starboard
On the line: 5° is within the margin
questions.why: Light astern at 205°M puts you on its 025° line, east of the 020° track — to starboard, so come to port.

questions.q: You are following the 10 m contour north at night, the land to starboard. Where are you and what do you do?
options: 8.2 m charted — inshore of it; alter to starboard
9.6 m charted — on it; hold your course
6.8 m charted — inshore of it; alter to port
6.8 m charted — offshore of it; alter to starboard
