questions.why: Charted depth = sounding − height of tide: 8.2 − 1.4 = 6.8 m, shallower than 10 m, so you are inshore — head out.

questions.q: You plan to follow a depth contour along this coast for a night approach. Which do you choose?
options: The 5 m line — closest to the harbour mouth
The 2 m line — the sounder reads it most clearly
Any of them — every contour is equally good
The 20 m line — clean, steep and with margin
questions.why: A good handrail is a steep, even contour well outside the dangers, so the sounder shows at once when you cross it.

questions.q: You are coasting east past an estuary mouth and this red can buoy lies ahead. Which side do you leave it?
options: To starboard — you are going against the buoyage
To port — a red mark is always kept to port
To port — you are going with the buoyage
Either side — it only marks the estuary
questions.why: Lateral marks follow the charted direction of buoyage; heading against it (east, arrow west), red is left to starboard.

questions.q: You are leaving harbour in the Caribbean (IALA region B) and see this buoy ahead. Which side do you leave it?

figure.note: IALA region B · heading out to sea

options: On your starboard side
On your port side
Close on your starboard side
On either side, keeping well off
questions.why: Region B: red marks the starboard side going in ("red right returning"), so going out it stays to port.

questions.q: Heading upstream with the buoyage, you want to stay in the main channel. How do you pass this mark?

figure.title: Mark at the fork
lines: IALA region A, going with the buoyage
Red can, one broad green band

options: Leave it to port; the main channel lies to port
Either side; both channels are the same
Leave it to port; the main channel lies to starboard
Leave it to starboard; the main channel lies to port
questions.why: Region A: red with a green band, Fl(2+1) R, is a port-hand mark with the preferred channel to starboard.

questions.q: The marina you are bound for lies up the minor branch of the river. Which side of the mark at the fork do you leave it?

figure.title: River fork, IALA region A
lines: Green cone, broad red band, Fl(2+1) G

options: Leave it to starboard — green is kept to starboard
Leave it to starboard, then turn right behind it
Either side — it only marks the junction
Leave it to port, then follow the minor channel's marks
questions.why: Fl(2+1) G with a red band: preferred channel to port. The minor branch is on its other side, so the mark goes to port.

questions.q: Coasting by day along a broken Croatian shore, you see this mark fine on the bow, between you and a group of islets. Where is the safe water?

figure.note: Fine on the bow, islets beyond

options: East of the mark
North of the mark
West of the mark
South of the mark
questions.why: East cardinal: black-yellow-black, cones point away from each other; the safe water is to its east.

questions.q: On watch at night you time an unlit mark's light ahead. What is it and how do you pass it?

figure.title: Night watch
lines: White light fine on the starboard bow
Quick flashes: counted nine, then dark

options: A west cardinal: pass east of it
A west cardinal: pass west of it
An east cardinal: pass east of it
A south cardinal: pass south of it
questions.why: Nine quick flashes every 15 s is Q(9) 15s — a west cardinal, like nine o'clock; the safe water is to its west.

questions.q: Your crew has drawn the night route on the plotter past this mark. What do you tell them?
options: Fine — keep the mark close on your starboard side
Re-route north of it — it is a north cardinal
Re-route east of it — it is an east cardinal
Fine — a cardinal may be passed on either side
questions.why: Q(3) is an east cardinal, three o'clock: the danger lies west of it, where the route goes.

questions.q: Your crew asks why this light adds a long flash after its quick flashes. What do you tell them?

figure.note: South cardinal

options: To show that it is the last mark of the channel
To show that the danger lies to the north of it
To show that it marks a new, uncharted danger
So that six can't be miscounted as three or nine
questions.why: South cardinal Q(6)+LFl: the long flash makes the group of six unmistakable next to the E (3) and W (9) marks.

questions.q: At night you identify this mark off a shoal and take its bearing: 200°M. Where are you?

figure.note: Bearing from you 200°M

options: North-north-east of it — on its safe side
South-south-west of it — on its safe side
South-south-west of it — on its danger side
North-north-east of it — on its danger side
questions.why: It bears 200° from you, so you are on its 020° side; a north cardinal has its safe water to the north.

questions.q: On watch you count an unbroken white light ahead. Which mark is it and where is its safe water?

figure.title: Night watch
lines: White light ahead, flashing without a break
Chart nearby: N card VQ · E card VQ(3) 5s

options: The west cardinal: pass west of it
The north cardinal: pass north of it
The east cardinal: pass east of it
The north cardinal: pass south of it
questions.why: Twenty flashes in 10 s is 120 a minute — very quick, unbroken: VQ, the north cardinal.

questions.q: Your route between two Ionian islands passes this mark, alone in open water. How do you pass it?

figure.note: Alone in open water

options: Keep north of it — it is a north cardinal
Close on either side — it marks safe water
Either side, with a good berth — it sits on the danger
Keep it to port — it is a lateral mark
questions.why: Isolated danger mark: black with a red band, two balls, Fl(2) — navigable water all round, the danger under it.

questions.q: Arriving at night off an unfamiliar harbour, your pilotage plan starts from this mark. What does it tell you?

figure.note: Start of the pilotage plan

options: A restricted zone — do not pass inside it
The port side of the channel — keep it to port
A danger under it — pass at least a cable off
Safe water all round — the landfall for the approach
questions.why: Safe water mark: red and white stripes, red ball, Iso, Oc, LFl 10s or Mo(A) — a landfall or fairway mark.

questions.q: Looking for an anchorage off a beach in July, you see a line of small yellow buoys about 150 m off it. What do you do?
options: Anchor outside the line — it marks a bathing zone
Anchor inside the line — it marks a quiet zone
Pass inside the line — yellow marks safe water
Keep north of each buoy — they are cardinals
questions.why: Yellow special marks show a feature the chart or pilot book describes — here a bathing zone where craft may not go.

questions.q: On passage at night you see this light. The mark is on no chart and in no notice you have. What do you do?

figure.note: Not on the chart

options: Keep it to port — it marks a channel
Keep well clear — it marks a new, uncharted wreck
Pass close — it marks the safe water
Ignore it until it appears on the chart
questions.why: Emergency wreck marking buoy: blue and yellow stripes, yellow cross, Al Bu Y — laid on a new danger before notices catch up.

questions.q: Entering at night, you see two red lights on the north side. Which one is the breakwater head?

figure.title: Pilot book — Limenas
lines: Tonight: two red lights on the N side

options: The one that is lit 4 s and dark 4 s
The one that flashes twice, then stays dark
The one lit most of the time, with two short eclipses
The one that alternates red and white
questions.why: Oc(2) = occulting in groups of two: light longer than dark, with two short eclipses in each 8 s.

questions.q: The inner harbour light is shown on the chart like this. What will you see when you time it?

figure.note: Inner harbour light, ahead

options: Steady light, never dark at all
A short flash every 4 s, dark in between
Light for 4 s with a short eclipse
Light for 2 s and dark for 2 s, over and over
questions.why: Iso = isophase: equal periods of light and dark; the period 4 s gives 2 s of each.

questions.q: Your bearing of the light on the islet holds steady, but its colour goes white–red–white–red. What does the change tell you?

figure.title: Night watch
lines: Light on the islet: bearing steady 295°M
Chart: Al WR 6s, no sectors shown

options: Nothing about your position — it is an alternating light
You keep crossing a sector edge — alter away
The red marks a danger sector — turn back
The light is faulty — report it to the coastguard
questions.why: Al WR shows white and red in turn on every bearing; a sector light changes colour only as your bearing changes.

questions.q: You are 9 M off this lighthouse tonight. Do you expect to see it?
options: Yes — lights are seen further at night
Probably not — 16M assumes 10 M visibility
Yes — a light 24 m high is seen from 24 M
Yes — it shows 16 M in any visibility
questions.why: Nominal range is for a meteorological visibility of 10 M; in 2 M visibility the luminous range is far shorter.

questions.q: Heading in on about 000°T towards the directional light, you see it red. What do you do?
options: Red means danger ahead: stop and turn back
You are west of the white sector: come to port
You are west of the white sector: come to starboard
You are east of the white sector: come to port
questions.why: Red shows on bearings 004°–009°: the light bears east of north, so you lie west of the line — turn east.

questions.q: Approaching on the directional light, you take its bearing. Which sector are you in and what do you do?
options: 136°T — in the red sector; come to starboard
130°T — in the green sector; come to port
133°T — in the red sector; come to starboard
130°T — in the white sector; hold your heading
questions.why: Sectors are true bearings from seaward: 133°M − 3°W = 130°T, inside the white 128.5°–131.5°.

questions.q: Coasting west at night, you see the light on the point turn from white to red. What does it mean?
options: You have entered the sector over the shoal: get back into white
It is an alternating light: ignore the colour
You are on the leading line into the harbour
You are past the shoal: you can close the coast
questions.why: A red sector of a coastal light covers a danger; seeing red means you are in it — move until the light is white again.

questions.q: Entering a Greek harbour at night, you see the two breakwater lights. Where do you steer?

figure.note: Harbour entrance ahead · IALA region A

options: Outside the green light, keeping it to port
Between them, the red to port and the green to starboard
Between them, the red to starboard and the green to port
Outside the red light, keeping it to starboard
questions.why: Region A harbour lights follow the lateral rule: red on the port side going in, green on the starboard side.

questions.q: Approaching the road bridge at night, your crew points at the brightest arch, lit by street lamps. Which arch do you take?

figure.title: Pilot book — road bridge
lines: Navigable arch: F G on each side of it
Other arches: F R on the piers

options: Any arch between two red lights
The brightest arch, lit by the street lamps
The arch between the two green lights
The arch with the single white light
questions.why: The pilot book gives the bridge's own lights: the navigable arch is the one between the green pair; red marks the piers.

questions.q: Approaching the harbour entrance, you see this on the signal mast, as the pilot book describes. What do you do?

figure.note: Signal mast at the entrance · steady lights

options: Enter with care — it signals one-way traffic
Enter — the signal is for big ships only
Stop and anchor in the entrance itself
Hold off clear of the entrance and wait
questions.why: IALA port traffic signals: three fixed red lights, vertical — vessels shall not proceed.

questions.q: You are a mile off the port when the signal mast shows this. What does it mean?

figure.note: Signal mast · all three flashing

options: A serious emergency: stop or divert as instructed
The port is closed for the night: anchor off
A ship is leaving: wait to starboard of it
One-way traffic: enter with care
questions.why: IALA port traffic signals: three red lights flashing — serious emergency, all vessels stop or divert as instructed.

questions.q: Arriving at a busy commercial port, you see these lights on the signal mast. What do you do?

figure.note: Signal mast · steady lights

options: Enter — the signal means one-way traffic
Enter only when port control tells you to
Enter — the signal means two-way traffic
Stay out — the port is closed to yachts
questions.why: IALA port traffic signals: green, white, green — a vessel may proceed only when she has specific orders to do so.

questions.q: Arriving at night, you can't pick out the breakwater lights against the town. What do you do?

figure.note: Town ahead · breakwaters: Fl R 5s, Fl G 5s

options: Head for the first red and green pair you see
Go in fast before the confusion gets worse
Stand off and time each light until both heads are certain
Steer for the middle of the town lights
questions.why: Background lights hide harbour lights: stay in safe water, identify each by its characteristic, then commit.

questions.q: You are planning a night entry on the plotter and are about to put the turning waypoint on the buoy itself. Why don't you?
options: A waypoint on a buoy upsets the AIS display
Buoys are charted exactly, so it isn't needed
The plotter can't store a waypoint on a mark
On autopilot it would steer you straight onto the buoy
questions.why: Put waypoints a safe distance off marks and hazards: a route to a buoy leads onto it, as it does for everyone else.

questions.q: Feeling your way into a cove, you zoom right in on the plotter. What do you trust?

figure.title: Entering the cove
lines: Plotter: zoomed ×8, clear to the beach
Pilot book plan: rocks 50 m off the point

options: The pilot book — zooming in adds no detail
The plotter — it is zoomed to the finest detail
Neither — you go by the echo sounder alone
The plotter — electronic charts are always newer
questions.why: Over-zoom only enlarges a small-scale survey; rocks too small for it are simply not there on the screen.

questions.q: You decide to go into harbour rather than wait for the fog to lift. How do you set the boat up?

figure.title: Fog
lines: 1 M from the entrance, radar on
Crew of four, all on deck

options: Slow speed, crew below out of the way, autopilot on
Slow speed, fog signal, lookout forward, radar and sounder watched
Full speed on the plotter route, radar off to save power
Cruising speed, to spend less time in the fog
questions.why: In fog: safe speed, the sound signal, a lookout and every aid — radar, sounder, plotter — cross-checked.

questions.q: Fog closes in 3 M from the harbour. You have no radar. What is the safest way in?
options: Anchor where you are, in 45 m of water
Follow a fishing boat that seems to know the way
Along the 20 m line to the fairway buoy, slow, then its bearing in
A straight line for the entrance at cruising speed
questions.why: Without radar use what you can check: a clean contour as a handrail to a known mark, then a short leg in from it.

questions.q: Arriving at dusk at this harbour for the first time, what do you assume about the breakwater?

figure.title: Arriving at Kamari
lines: Your chart: older edition, no extension
Plotter: the light at the old head

options: The work was never finished — ignore the note
The chart is right — it is the official document
The plotter is right — it shows the light where it is
It may run further out than charted: give it a wide berth
questions.why: When sources disagree, plan for the worse case: the newest note may be right and the old chart out of date.

questions.q: You and one crew bring the boat into a strange harbour at night. How do you split the work?
options: One steers the headings called; the other navigates and calls the marks
Both watch the plotter while the autopilot steers
The skipper steers and navigates; the crew does fenders
The crew navigates from below; the skipper steers by eye
questions.why: In pilotage one person steers and one navigates from the cockpit, calling headings and marks and checking each one.

questions.q: Entering an unfamiliar harbour at night, your navigator stays at the chart table calling "turn now" from the plotter. Why is this a poor set-up?
options: The skipper should be below instead
Nobody on deck checks the marks against the plan
The plotter is less accurate below decks
The helm should be the one at the plotter
questions.why: The navigator belongs in the cockpit with the plan, eyes on the marks; the plotter is a cross-check, not the pilot.

questions.q: You are rounding a headland at night on radar, with a parallel index line set to pass it 0.6 M off. The echo looks like this. What do you do?

figure.note: Radar, north-up · plan: pass the headland 0.6 M off

options: Alter to starboard — you would pass inside 0.6 M
Alter to starboard — you would pass outside 0.6 M
Alter to port — you would pass inside 0.6 M
Hold on — the echo sits on the index line
questions.why: On track the echo slides down the index line; inside the line, your track passes closer than planned — turn away from it.

questions.q: Before you set a parallel index line, you check where your present COG takes you. How far off the headland will you pass?

figure.title: Radar and plotter, 0120
lines: Plan: pass the headland 0.8 M off

questions.why: Passing distance = range × sin(angle off the COG): 2.0 × sin(075° − 045°) = 2.0 × 0.5 = 1.0 M.

questions.q: Rounding a headland at night, you keep the coast outside a VRM ring, as your plan says. The echo now cuts inside the ring on the port bow. What do you do?

figure.note: Plan: keep the coast outside 0.8 M · rocks 0.3 M off

options: Alter to starboard until the echo is outside the ring
Hold on — the ring shows the rocks are past
Alter to port to put the echo back on the ring
Shorten the range scale and hold on
questions.why: The VRM is a clearing range: coast inside the ring means you are closer than the safe distance — open it out.

questions.q: Your radar is head-up and you want it to show the moment of the turn in your plan. Where do you set the EBL?

figure.title: Radar — entering at night
lines: Plan: turn to 300°M for the entrance

options: 300° relative — 60° on the port bow
290° relative — 70° on the port bow
070° relative — 70° on the starboard bow
310° relative — 50° on the port bow
questions.why: A head-up EBL reads relative to the bow: 300° − 010° = 290° relative, i.e. 70° to port.

questions.q: You are writing a pilotage plan for a harbour you may have to enter in fog, using the radar. What do you add for each turn?
options: The colour and rhythm of each buoy's light
The lat/long of each turn for the radar
The range and bearing of a steep echo there
The VHF channel of the harbour office
questions.why: In fog each turn needs a radar check: the range and bearing of a good echo, ready to set on the VRM and EBL.

questions.q: Crossing at night, you see this on the radar. What does it tell you, and what do you do?

figure.title: Radar, crossing at night
lines: Echo 1.5 M ahead with a racon:

options: A ship's radar beacon — ignore it
A fairway buoy's racon — steer for it
Interference — retune the gain and carry on
A new-wreck buoy's racon — keep well clear
questions.why: An emergency wreck marking buoy carries a racon coding Morse D: a new danger, not yet on the chart.

questions.q: You are copying the entry line from the pilot book onto your pilotage card. What do you write?

figure.title: Pilot book — Vathy
lines: in line with the mole head

questions.why: Pilot books give true bearings from seaward: 048°T − 2°E = 046°M (east is least).

questions.q: You are timing your run inside the harbour from the pilot-book plan. How long will it take from the mole head to the fuel berth at the speed limit?

figure.title: Pilot book plan — Kastela
lines: Mole head to the fuel berth: 4.5 cables
Speed limit in the harbour 3 kn

options: 6 min
9 min
1½ min
15 min

questions.q: The pilot book's plan of tonight's harbour looks like this. Which line do you take through the entrance?
options: Midway, then round the W head close in
Close to the W head, rocks to starboard
Favour the east side, clear of the W head's rocks
Hug the W head — the deep water is close in
questions.why: The plan shows rocks running out from the W head: keep to the side of the entrance away from them, in the charted depth.

questions.q: You are 4 M off your planned harbour at dusk and check the pilot book. What do you do?

figure.title: Pilot book — Ag. Nikolaos
lines: S winds over F5: heavy swell breaks
across the entrance — do not enter

options: Anchor off the entrance until it eases
Run in fast on the back of a wave
Go in slowly down the middle of it
Divert to a harbour sheltered from the south
questions.why: The pilot book's warning fits tonight's wind exactly: an entrance with breaking swell is no place to try — go elsewhere.

questions.q: Approaching at night, you point the bow at the directional light and read the steering compass. Which sector are you in?
options: 128°T — the white
132°T — the red
130°T — the red
122°T — the green
questions.why: 127°C − 2°W deviation = 125°M; + 3°E variation = 128°T: inside the white, 124°–129°.

questions.q: Motoring upstream with the buoyage at night, you see these lights on the bridge ahead. Where do you pass under it?

figure.note: Road bridge ahead · heading upstream, region A

options: Close by the green light, leaving it to port
Under the white light, midway between red and green
Under the next span, away from the lights
Close by the red light, leaving it to starboard
questions.why: Bridge marking: red and green lights mark the sides of the navigable span; a white light marks the centre of the channel.

questions.q: You are waiting at a lifting bridge whose signals follow the IALA port traffic signals. As the span lifts, it shows this. What do you do?

figure.note: Lifting bridge · steady lights (IALA port signals)

options: Wait for orders on VHF, then go through
Go through, ready to meet boats coming the other way
Go through — one-way traffic, your way
Hold off — the span is about to come down
questions.why: IALA port traffic signals: three fixed green lights — vessels may proceed, one-way traffic.

questions.q: At 2200 you reach the commercial port where you will spend the night, and its signal mast shows this. What does it allow?

figure.note: Port signal mast · steady lights

options: Entry now — one-way traffic, your way only
No entry — wait outside the port
Entry only once port control orders it
Entry now — with two-way traffic in the entrance
questions.why: IALA port traffic signals: green, green, white — vessels may proceed; two-way traffic.

questions.q: Your 12 m yacht can keep safely outside the dredged channel, as the pilot book allows small craft to. The signal mast shows this. What may you do?

figure.note: Signal mast · steady lights

options: Go in outside the main channel, keeping clear
Go in down the main channel with care
Go in only once port control orders it
Nothing — no vessel may move in the port
questions.why: Three fixed red: do not proceed — but a yellow light beside the top one exempts vessels able to keep outside the main channel.

questions.q: On your first charter in the Caribbean (IALA region B), you meet this mark off a reef. Where is its safe water?

figure.note: IALA region B · Caribbean charter

options: Either side — it stands on the reef itself
East of it — cardinals are the same in A and B
West of it — region B reverses the cardinals
West of it — the topmarks point at the reef
questions.why: Region B changes only the colours of lateral marks; cardinal marks are the same: an east cardinal has safe water to the east.

questions.q: Coming in from sea at night in IALA region B, you see this light ahead marking the channel. Which side do you leave it?

figure.note: Entering from sea · IALA region B (Bahamas)

options: To port — you are going with the buoyage
To port — red is the port side, as in Europe
To starboard — red right returning
Either side — it marks the channel's centre
questions.why: In region B red marks are starboard-hand when entering from sea: 'red right returning'.

questions.q: Your marina lies up the main channel. Which side of this mark at the fork do you leave it?

figure.title: Region B · heading in from sea

options: To starboard — the main channel lies to port
To starboard — green is the starboard-hand colour
Either side — both branches are main channels
To port — the main channel lies to starboard
questions.why: In region B green is port-hand; a green can with a red band, Fl(2+1) G, marks the preferred channel to starboard.

questions.q: Heading west towards your next waypoint, your stopwatch gives this for the light dead ahead. Which mark is it, and how do you pass it?

figure.title: Night watch · heading 270°T
lines: Very quick flashes: six, then a long one
Your plan: pass north of the mark

options: South cardinal — pass south, leaving it to starboard
North cardinal — pass north, leaving it to port
West cardinal — pass west, holding your course
South cardinal — pass north, leaving it to port
questions.why: VQ(6)+LFl 10s is a south cardinal: safe water to the south — heading west, that leaves the mark to starboard.

questions.q: Crossing between two islands at night, you time this light. What mark is it on?

figure.title: Night passage between islands
lines: White light, alone in open water

options: A preferred channel mark
An isolated danger mark
A safe water mark
A south cardinal mark
questions.why: A white Fl(2) is the isolated danger light: the danger is right under the mark — pass with a good berth.

questions.q: Making your landfall at night, you time the light your plan starts from. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Landfall at night
lines: White light fine on the bow
A short flash, then a long one

options: A south cardinal — Q(6)+LFl
An east cardinal — Q(3)
A safe water mark — Morse A
An isolated danger — Fl(2)
questions.why: Mo(A), dot-dash, is a safe water light, like Iso, Oc or LFl 10s: open water all round the mark.

questions.q: Your crew notices on the chart that these two marks flash at different speeds and asks why. What do you tell them?
options: The quick one is a beacon, the other a buoy
The very quick one is to be passed closer
The very quick one marks the worse danger
So the two can be told apart at night
questions.why: Neighbouring cardinals of the same kind use Q and VQ, so you can tell which one you are looking at.

questions.q: Heading downriver to the sea at night, you see this channel light ahead. Which side do you leave it?

figure.note: Leaving the river for the sea · region A

options: To port — you are going against the buoyage
Either side — it marks mid-channel
To starboard — green is starboard-hand
To starboard — you are going with the buoyage
questions.why: Buoyage runs from seaward; heading out to sea, the starboard-hand (green) marks are left to port.

questions.q: Approaching an anchorage at night, you see a row of these lights across the bay. What are they?

figure.note: Across the bay ahead, at night

options: Port-hand marks — leave them to port
Special marks — the chart says what they mark
Fishing nets — pass between them
Cardinal marks — pass to seaward
questions.why: Yellow lights are special marks — a zone, a pipe, a bathing area: find on the chart what they mark.

questions.q: You are shading the red sector of this light onto your chart. Which water does it cover?
options: The sea between 080°T and 245°T from the light
The sea between 260°T and 065°T from the light
The sea between 065°T and 080°T from the light
The sea between 245°T and 260°T from the light
questions.why: Sector limits are bearings of the light from seaward: seen from the light, the red runs out on 065°–080°.

questions.q: You are holding the white sector of the directional light, 4 M out. How far can you stray from its centre line here before the colour changes?

figure.title: Dir Oc WRG 6s — approach
lines: You: in the white, 4.0 M out
Plan: stay well inside the white

options: About 3 cables either side
About ½ cable either side
About 2 cables either side
About 1 cable either side
questions.why: 1 in 60: 1.5° each side at 4 M ≈ 4 × 1.5 ÷ 60 = 0.1 M, one cable; the sector narrows as you close.

questions.q: Approaching the harbour on its sectored light, you see it like this, the colour never settling. What do you do?

figure.note: Sectored light ahead · the colour won't settle

options: Move well into the white — you are on the edge
Hold on — the edge is the leading line
Slow down — the light is faulty
Hold on — it is an alternating light
questions.why: At a sector boundary the colours mix over a degree or two: the edge is uncertain — get into the middle of the white.

questions.q: Entering at night on the directional light, you see it turn green. Where are you, and what do you do?

figure.title: Dir Oc WRG 6s — entering
lines: You were steering 160°T on the white
Stream sets west across the line

options: East of the line: come to starboard, then steer west of 160°
West of the line: come to port, then steer east of 160°
East of the line: come to port, then hold 160° exactly
West of the line: come to starboard, then steer east of 160°
questions.why: Green = bearing under 158.5°T: you are west of the line, to starboard; come back to port and head up into the westerly set.

questions.q: You are about to join this transit with the stream across it. What heading do you give the helm to hold the marks in line?
You are on the transit, crabbing to hold it. How long until you reach the entrance?
options: 21 min
12 min
18 min
13 min
questions.why: Along the transit you make 6.0 × cos 20° = 5.6 kn: 1.2 ÷ 5.64 = 0.21 h = 13 min.

questions.q: A pot line round the prop stops you near a clearing line. If you lie stopped, how long until the stream carries you over it?

figure.title: Pot line round the prop
lines: Engine in neutral to clear it

options: 9 min
6 min
18 min
15 min
questions.why: 0.3 M ÷ 2.0 kn = 0.15 h = 9 min — a clearing line is a limit, not a margin.

questions.q: Leaving the bay northward at night, you check the clearing bearing on the light astern. What do you do?
options: Hold on — under 185°M is the safe side
Alter to starboard until it reads 185°M or more
Alter to starboard until it reads 181°M or less
Alter to port until it reads 185°M or more
questions.why: With the light astern, a westward drift lowers its bearing: 181°M is on the shoal side of 185°M — move east.

questions.q: You are short-tacking north up the channel, with the church ahead as your head mark. At what hand-bearing compass reading do you tack?

figure.title: Beating up the Steno channel
lines: Head mark: church, ahead to the north
Now on starboard tack, heading NW

questions.why: Heading NW the church's bearing rises towards the NMT 010°T limit: 010°T − 3°E = 007°M — tack on it.

questions.q: Leaving harbour at night, you take a back bearing of the harbour light every five minutes. What is happening, and what do you do?
options: Set to port: come to port and aim left of 015°M
Set to starboard: come to port and aim left of 015°M
On track: back bearings always fall as you go
Set to port: come to starboard and aim right of 015°M
questions.why: A falling back bearing puts you west of the 015° line, to port of it: get back, then steer up into the stream.

questions.q: You are following the 5 m contour north at night, the land to port. What should the sounder read while you stay on it?

figure.note: Sounder: no offset, transducer 0.4 m below waterline

questions.why: Depth of water = 5.0 + 2.3 = 7.3 m; the sounder reads below its transducer, 0.4 m down: 7.3 − 0.4 = 6.9 m.

questions.q: Feeling your way towards the harbour in fog, you hear the breakwater's fog signal. How do you use it?

figure.title: Fog, approaching the harbour
lines: Heard faintly, fine on the stbd bow

options: Turn away until you can't hear it
As a sign you're near, not a bearing to steer
Judge your distance by how loud it is
Steer straight for it until it is loud
questions.why: Sound in fog bends and fades: a fog signal says the mark is near, never its exact bearing or range.

questions.q: Fog, no radar, and the stream across your approach is uncertain. How do you plan the landfall on this harbour?
options: Aim west of it, then follow the 10 m line east
Aim straight at it, slowing as you near
Aim well east of it, then follow the 10 m line west
Aim straight at it; turn away if it shoals
questions.why: Aiming off tells you which side you are on when you find the contour: then turn the known way along clean water.

questions.q: Fog closes in halfway through your pilotage between the islets, with two turns still to go. What do you do?
options: Follow the plotter through both turns
Turn back the way you came, at speed
Carry on, timing each leg from the plan
Anchor on the 6 m sand and wait for it to lift
questions.why: With no radar and rocks at each turn, the safe pilotage is to stop: anchor in good holding and wait.

questions.q: The stream has set you east of your planned track, and your crew presses 'go to' on the entrance waypoint again. What is the risk?
options: The new straight line crosses the shoal
The autopilot will steer the old track
None — the waypoint is in deep water
The plotter will now route round the shoal
questions.why: 'Go to' draws a straight line from where you are now; it knows nothing of the dangers your original track avoided.

questions.q: Creeping towards your berth at night, you glance at the plotter. Which do you steer by?
options: The COG — it shows your real track
The compass and the marks — COG is noise here
The average of the COG readings
The plotter's heading line, zoomed in
questions.why: At low speed the GPS COG wanders by tens of degrees: steer by compass and by eye; COG settles only with speed.

questions.q: Approaching at night, you see a mark on the plotter where nothing is in the water. What do you make of it?

figure.title: Plotter at night
lines: Nothing seen in the water there

options: A plotter fault — ignore it
A buoy off station — report it
A virtual AIS mark — obey it as a real one
An unlit buoy — pass close to see it
questions.why: A virtual aid to navigation exists only as an AIS signal; it marks a real danger and is obeyed like a buoy.

questions.q: You are writing leg 2 onto your pilotage card from the chart. What heading do you write?
questions.why: True to magnetic, west is best: 247°T + 3°W = 250°M.

questions.q: Your arrival in the bay has slipped from the afternoon to 0300. What do you change in the pilotage plan?

figure.title: Plan for Ormos Vathy
lines: Day plan: white chapel in line
Lights: Dir WRG 312° on the mole

options: Use the directional light's white sector instead
Keep the transit — it will show by moonlight
Steer 312° on the compass alone
Nothing — the plotter covers the transit
questions.why: A daylight transit vanishes at night: re-plan on lit marks — here the directional light shows the same line.

questions.q: Running west along the coast, you will turn into the bay on a bearing of the church, as your plan says. Do you turn now?
options: Yes — turn now and steer 330°M for it
Not yet — hold on until it rises to 340°M
Not yet — wait until it is abeam to starboard
Yes — 330°M means the turn is past
questions.why: Running west, a mark on the starboard bow draws aft: its bearing rises from 330° towards 340° — turn when it reaches it.

questions.q: You are on the helm for a night entry and the navigator calls "steer 047". What do you do?
options: Steer 047 and stay quiet to keep it calm
Ask why before you turn
Repeat "047" and call when steady on it
Turn and watch the COG reach 047
questions.why: Closed-loop calls: the helm repeats the heading and reports when steady, so a misheard figure is caught at once.

questions.q: Your crew, on the helm, plans to pass this green beacon 5 m off to stay in the deep channel. What do you tell them?
options: Leave it to port — you are heading with the buoyage
Pass close either side — beacons stand in deep water
Pass it close to starboard — it marks the channel edge
Leave it well to starboard — it stands on the rock
questions.why: A beacon is built on the danger itself and the rocks run out round it: give it a berth, green to starboard going in.

questions.q: Closing the coast on a clear night, you are 6 M off the harbour. What do you expect to see of its lights now?

figure.title: Approach to Kissamos
lines: Breakwater heads: Fl R 3s 3M, Fl G 3s 3M

options: Only the main light — the heads show from 3 M
Nothing until you are within 3 M
All three, the heads a little dimmer
The heads first — they're lower and nearer
questions.why: The nominal range is the range in clear weather: 3M head lights won't show at 6 M — find the main light first.

questions.q: You are approaching your planned harbour in the small hours. What do you do?

figure.title: 0140, 3 M off Kaladi
lines: Entrance 50 m wide, rocks each side
Anchorage 2 M back: 8 m sand, sheltered

options: Enter on the plotter at dead slow
Anchor in the bay and enter at first light
Enter on the E light, keeping it close aboard
Enter with the spotlight on the W head
questions.why: A narrow rocky entrance with one head unlit and town lights behind is a daylight job — and a safe anchorage is close.

questions.q: Heading in with the buoyage at night, you reach the fork. Which side of this mark do you leave to stay in the main channel?

figure.title: Night · region A, heading in
lines: Light at the fork: Fl(2+1) G 10s
Your marina: up the main channel

options: Either side — it marks the middle of the fork
To port — the main channel lies to starboard
To starboard — the main channel lies to port
To port — green lights are left to port at night
questions.why: In region A, Fl(2+1) G is a modified starboard-hand mark — preferred channel to port: leave it to starboard.

questions.q: Heading north into the bay, you follow the pilot book's directions. What do you see while you keep to them?

figure.title: Pilot book — Ormos Agrilia
lines: Heading N into the bay: keep the
Ak. Mavro until the chapel is abeam

options: Lighthouse just left of the point — you are east of the transit
Lighthouse hidden behind the point — you are on the transit
Lighthouse just right of the point — you are east of the transit
Lighthouse just left of the point — you are west of the transit
questions.why: 'Open' means not in line: with the far light showing west (left) of the near point, you are a little west of their transit.

questions.q: You are taking a 10 m yacht from Lymington across the Channel to Cherbourg for the weekend. A crew member says a passage plan is only for ships. What is the position?
options: SOLAS V asks every vessel going to sea to plan
Only boats on charter must file a plan
Only vessels over 24 m must plan a passage
Only passages beyond 60 M need a plan
questions.why: SOLAS Chapter V applies to all who go to sea, small craft included: weather, tides, the boat, the crew, dangers.

questions.q: You are about to take a crew of four from Dartmouth to Guernsey, and your plan covers the items on the card. What else does SOLAS V expect you to have thought through?
options: The menu for each meal and who cooks it
Ports of refuge and what you do if it goes wrong
The marina's berth fees on arrival
The crew's passport numbers and nationality
questions.why: SOLAS V: weather, tides, the boat's limits, the crew, the dangers — and a contingency plan with ports of refuge.

questions.q: The purpose of this week is a relaxed family cruise with two young children aboard. Two plans fit tomorrow's weather: a 25 M daylight hop or an 80 M overnight crossing. Which do you choose?
options: The 80 M crossing, as the children will sleep
The 80 M crossing, to gain a day of sailing
The 25 M daylight hop, in by teatime
Either — the plan is the same for any crew
questions.why: The purpose and the crew set the plan: a family cruise wants short, easy legs, not a night crossing.

questions.q: You are setting two watches for an overnight passage with the crew on the card. How do you pair them?

figure.title: Crew for tonight
lines: Ben — a few nights as crew

options: Ben with Chris; Ana with Dana; you on call
Ana with Ben; you alone, the novices asleep
Chris with Dana; Ana with Ben; you on call
Ana with Chris; you with Ben and Dana
questions.why: Each watch needs a leader who can handle the boat and the traffic at night: never two novices alone on deck.

questions.q: You plan to round a headland to the west under engine. Your boat's numbers are on the card. How do you plan the rounding?

figure.title: Your boat's limits
lines: Into a short head sea: about 4 kn

options: Time it for the fair stream — you can barely stem the foul
Go at slack, then motor hard into the foul
Go at the foul stream, close in along the shore
Any time — 4 kn still beats a 3.5 kn stream
questions.why: 4 kn against 3.5 kn leaves 0.5 kn over the ground in a rough sea: plan the rounding for the fair stream.

questions.q: You are planning a day passage along the Brittany coast. What is your ETA?
You are leaving harbour to round a headland at slack water, before the stream there turns foul. When do you slip the lines?

figure.title: Rounding the headland
lines: Boat speed 5 kn through the water
Stream on the leg: 1 kn fair

questions.q: You must pass a tidal race on your way to the next harbour, and two departure times work. Which do you plan?

figure.title: Two departure times
lines: 0500: at the race 0800, wind with tide
1100: at the race 1400, wind against tide

options: 1100 — a stream against the wind flattens the sea
1100 — the later start gives the crew more rest
Either — at force 5 the race makes no difference
0500 — wind and stream go the same way in the race
questions.why: Wind against a spring stream in a race builds steep, breaking seas: time the race for wind with tide.

questions.q: Your crew of four want to sail tomorrow; the GRIB for the route is on the card. Which plan do you make?
options: Leave 0600, in about 1415, before it builds
Leave 1800, in about 0215, ahead of the westerly
Leave 0900, in about 1715, as it reaches 20 kn
Leave 1200, in about 2015, with the fresher wind
questions.why: 45 ÷ 5.5 ≈ 8 h 11 min: from 0600 you are in by mid-afternoon; a GRIB shows no gusts, so keep a margin.

questions.q: You are sailing east along this coast and decide to put in before the wind arrives. Which harbour is your port of refuge?

figure.note: Harbours on your route

options: A or B — whichever you reach first in daylight
C — open at all tides and sheltered from the SW
A — the nearest, and the sill keeps out the sea
B — the biggest, with room to enter at any tide
questions.why: Arriving at HW+4 misses A's sill (HW±2); B is open to the SW 6; C works at any tide and gives shelter.

questions.q: Your track for tomorrow's leg crosses a military firing range. What goes into the plan?

figure.title: Range danger area
lines: Your track crosses it at about 1100

options: The track through it — yachts may pass at any time
A stop at the edge until the safety boat waves you in
A track outside the area, and a watch on the range channel
The track through it at full speed, radar on
questions.why: While firing, keep clear: route round the danger area or pass outside firing hours, and listen to the range.

questions.q: You will round this headland tonight. How do you plan the rounding?
options: Pass 2 M off, on the race's inner edge
Go through the race to keep the track short
Pass 0.5 M off, on the inshore passage
Stand 5 M off, well outside the race
questions.why: Wind against a spring stream at night: the inshore passage is for settled weather, so give the race a wide berth.

questions.q: The pilot book warns of dense pot buoys inside the 20 m line along your route, and you will pass there at night. What does your plan say?
options: Keep the track outside the 20 m line
Follow the 20 m line, as the pots mark it
Motor close inshore, where the pots end
Keep to the route — pot buoys are lit
questions.why: Unlit pot buoys can't be seen at night and foul a propeller: route outside the area where they are laid.

questions.q: Checking the route a crew member built on the plotter, you find WP3 sits exactly on the north cardinal you must round. What do you do?
options: Leave it, but steer by hand on that leg
Move WP3 into safe water a few cables N of the buoy
Leave it — the buoy is the best mark there is
Move WP3 into the gap a few cables S of the buoy
questions.why: A waypoint on a mark invites hitting it at night on autopilot; put it in safe water — north of a north cardinal.

questions.q: Both waypoints of tonight's leg are in deep water. Checking the leg between them on the chart, what do you find?
options: It crosses a 1.8 m patch — fine with 2.1 m at LW
It needs a slower speed over the shallow part
It crosses a 1.8 m patch — add a waypoint to clear it
Nothing — the waypoints are clear, so the leg is
questions.why: Check the whole leg, not only its ends: 1.8 + 0.3 = 2.1 m at LW leaves 0.1 m under a 2.0 m keel.

questions.q: Your plan should say when the light will lift above the horizon. When do you expect to see it?

figure.title: Landfall light
lines: Dipping range at your eye: 16 M
At 2300 the light is 28 M ahead

questions.why: You first see it at its dipping range, 16 M: 28 − 16 = 12 M to run at 6 kn = 2 h; 2300 + 2 h = 0100.

questions.q: At 2310 you see a light fine on the bow and time it as Fl(3) 15s. What do you do first?
options: Time it again and check your position against the plan
Strike it from the plan — lights change
Alter towards it for a closer look
Take it as the 2300 light — close enough
questions.why: A light that doesn't match the plan's characteristic or bearing is a warning: re-time it and fix your position.

questions.q: You are planning a calm-weather passage that may be all under engine. How far can you motor under your reserve rule?
The tank water tastes of the tank, so you carry bottled drinking water for the passage. How much do you take?

figure.title: Drinking water
lines: Allow 2 L per person per day

questions.why: 5 crew × 2 L × 3 days (2 days at sea + 1 spare) = 30 L.

questions.q: Your crew of six keep three watches of two, round the clock. Which watch has 2100–2400 tomorrow evening?
options: Watch A
Whoever is least tired
Watch B
Watch C
questions.why: Eight 3-hour watches a day shared by three: the rota moves on, A B C A B C A B — so C has 2100 tomorrow.

questions.q: Your crew of four stand two watches, 4 on and 4 off. Why does the rota split 1600–2000 into two short watches?
options: So the watches alternate and nobody has 0000–0400 every night
So the watch leaders can both eat with the crew at 1800
So the skipper can stand a two-hour watch on his own
So the change of watch falls at sunset every day
questions.why: Seven watches a day, not six: the odd number moves the rota on, so the 0000–0400 alternates.

questions.q: At 0300 the watch leader sees a ship 5 M off whose bearing has not changed for ten minutes. You are asleep. What should the watch leader do?

figure.title: Skipper's night orders
lines: Call me: any ship with CPA under 1 M
Call me: any doubt at all

options: Wait until she is 1 M off, then call you
Call you now, as the orders say
Call her on VHF and let you sleep on
Alter 90° to port and log it for the morning
questions.why: A steady bearing means risk of collision and a CPA near zero: the night orders say call the skipper.

questions.q: Your crew of five gather in the cockpit before an overnight passage. Besides the safety gear, what does your briefing cover?
options: The menu for each day and who washes up
The marina's rules on arrival and the berth fees
The route, the watches, the weather and plan B
Only the MOB drill — the rest they will pick up
questions.why: A crew briefing gives the plan: route and timings, watch system, forecast, the alternatives and ports of refuge.

questions.q: Tomorrow you sail from Brighton to Fécamp, in France, with the papers on the card. What must you sort out before you leave?
options: A French registration for the boat
A French radio licence for the VHF
Nothing — these papers cover any passage
Extend the insurance to cover French waters
questions.why: Check the policy's cruising limits against the plan: 'UK waters only' does not cover a passage to France.

questions.q: You are leaving for a two-day passage to the Scilly Isles. With whom do you leave the passage plan?
options: Someone ashore, with your ETA and when to call for help
The crew only — the copy lives at the chart table
The fuel berth, who will chase you if you are late
Nobody — the AIS shows the coastguard where you are
questions.why: A float plan ashore — boat, crew, route, ETA, when to raise the alarm — starts a search if you don't arrive.

questions.q: You plan an overnight passage with a force 5 on the beam. What do you plan for the first night's hot meal?
options: Fresh pasta cooked at sea at about midnight
A one-pot stew cooked in harbour, just to reheat
A roast in the oven, ready for the first watch
Nothing hot — cold food until you arrive
questions.why: Cook ahead in harbour: one pot, one burner, a few minutes at sea; hot food keeps the watches going.

questions.q: You have built the route on the plotter zoomed out to show the whole passage. Before you rely on it, what do you check?

figure.title: Route on the plotter
lines: Built zoomed out to show it all
Two legs pass close to headlands

options: Nothing — the plotter warns of every hazard
Only the total distance against the paper plan
Zoom in along every leg, or run the route check
That the route line shows in red on the screen
questions.why: Zoomed out, a plotter hides rocks and shoals: check each leg at large scale or with its hazard check.

questions.q: You are checking the route you typed into the plotter against your paper plan. What do you do?
options: Average the two and log the difference
Trust the paper — plotters round the distance
Trust the plotter — it computes the great circle
Check WP3's lat/long against the chart — one is mistyped
questions.why: A leg that disagrees in distance and bearing means a mistyped waypoint: compare each lat/long with the chart.

questions.q: The forecast is force 7 gusting 8. Your crew vote to sail anyway and say the decision is theirs. Whose decision is it?
options: Yours — the skipper answers for boat and crew
The owner's, if the owner is aboard
The marina's — they close the harbour
The crew's — a majority vote decides it
questions.why: The skipper is responsible for boat and crew; force 7 gusting 8 is beyond the moderate conditions of the ticket.

questions.q: You hold an IYT Yachtmaster Coastal certificate. A friend asks you to skipper this crossing. What do you say?
options: Yes, if you sail it in daylight only
No — it takes you beyond 60 M offshore
Yes — the Coastal covers any Med crossing
Yes — the forecast is moderate, so it is fine
questions.why: Yachtmaster Coastal covers passages up to 60 M offshore in moderate conditions; 95 M off is beyond it.

questions.q: Your night watch's only log entry is on the card. What should each hourly entry hold?
options: The crew on watch and what they have seen
The position from the plotter, nothing else
Time, log, course, position, wind and barometer
Time and a note that all is well on board
questions.why: Hourly: time, log reading, course steered, position, wind, barometer — enough to run a DR if the GPS fails.

questions.q: Overnight, everything runs on the plotter. Why does your watch leader still plot a position on the paper chart every hour?
options: Because a plotter position is not legal at sea
To check that the plotter's clock is right
Only to complete the logbook for the owner
To have a recent position if the electronics fail
questions.why: If the GPS or the power fails, an hourly position on paper lets you run a DR from a known point.

questions.q: At noon you check your progress against the plan. What does it tell you?

figure.title: 1200 — progress check
lines: The stream turns foul there at 1600

options: ETA 1637 — you need 6.0 kn to make it
ETA 1600 — you make it with no change
ETA 1637 — you need 5.5 kn to make it
ETA 1701 — you need 6.0 kn to make it
questions.why: 24 ÷ 5.2 = 4.62 h = 4 h 37 min → 1637, too late; 24 M in the 4 h left needs 24 ÷ 4 = 6.0 kn.

questions.q: It is 1400 and the situation is on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Decision point
lines: If not: plan B, port C

options: Press on — you will be past it by 1436
Turn for port C, as the plan says
Press on and decide again at 1500
Heave to and wait for the next fair stream
questions.why: A decision point is set ashore, rested, with the tide worked out: at 1400 you are not past, so plan B.

questions.q: You are 5 M off the harbour you planned to reach before dark, and the situation is on the card. What do you decide?

figure.title: 0200, approaching
lines: Unknown harbour, rocks at the entry

options: Go straight in — the sooner in, the sooner asleep
Enter now with the plotter zoomed right in
Stand off in open water, rest by turns, enter at dawn
Anchor off the rocks at the entrance until dawn
questions.why: Fatigue breeds mistakes: with sea room and a light offshore wind, waiting for daylight is the safe choice.

questions.q: One of your crew is getting worse, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: 0400, on watch
lines: Crew sick for 6 h, keeps no water down

options: Carry on — the seasickness will pass once ashore
Heave to until they feel better, then carry on
Send them to their bunk below and carry on
Bear away for the port of refuge and get them ashore
questions.why: Six hours unable to keep water down means dehydration: the near, downwind port gets them ashore soonest.

questions.q: You come up to take over the watch at midnight, and this is what you find. What do you do?

figure.title: 0000, change of watch
lines: Ship's lights on the port bow
You haven't seen the plot or the log

options: Call them back for a proper handover first
Wake the skipper to ask about the ship
Take the helm and work it out yourself
Take over and read the log in the morning
questions.why: A handover gives course, position, traffic, sails, weather and orders — before the off-going watch goes below.

questions.q: On a night passage your navigator needs to read the chart below while you keep watch on deck. What light does the chart table use?
options: The bright saloon lights
A dim red light
A white head torch on full
The deck light through the hatch
questions.why: Red light keeps the watch's night vision, which takes 20–30 minutes to come back after white light.

questions.q: It is 0100 and two crew go to the mast to reef. One asks for the spreader lights. What do you tell them?

figure.title: 0100, reefing
lines: Two crew go to the mast

options: Never — reef by feel, with no light at all
Keep them on and switch off the tricolour
On for the job only, then off — it hides your lights
Leave them on all night so ships can see you
questions.why: A deck light dazzles the watch and masks your navigation lights: use it only as long as the job needs.

questions.q: You are writing the harness rule into your night orders. What does it say?
options: Clip on only when the wind is over force 5
Clip on once you are sitting in the cockpit
Clip on only when you go forward of the mast
Clip on before you come up the companionway
questions.why: Clip on from below to a strong point by the hatch and stay clipped on: at night a person overboard is hard to find.

questions.q: You come up at 0300 to check the watch, and this is what you see. What is wrong?

figure.title: 0300, on deck
lines: Second crew asleep in the cockpit
No-one has looked astern for 20 min

options: No lookout is kept — the leader must wake the crew
The second crew should be in a bunk below
Nothing — the leader at the wheel is the lookout
The autopilot should be on so both can rest
questions.why: The watch leader's job: a proper lookout all round, astern included, the log kept, and the skipper called.

questions.q: You must cross this traffic separation scheme to the north. What do you steer?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme

options: Head into the stream to make good 000°T
Heading 000°T, and let the stream carry you west
Steer straight for the waypoint beyond it
Head 045°T to run with the eastbound traffic
questions.why: Rule 10: cross on a heading at right angles to the traffic flow, accepting the set — the quickest, clearest crossing.

questions.q: You cross the scheme on a heading at right angles to the lanes. How long are you in it, and where do you come out?
options: 1 h 55 min, 3.0 M west of where you went in
2 h 00 min, 3.0 M east of where you went in
2 h 00 min, 3.0 M west of where you went in
2 h 06 min, due north of where you went in
questions.why: Across the lanes you make 5 kn: 10 M ÷ 5 = 2 h; the stream sets you 1.5 × 2 = 3.0 M west.

questions.q: Halfway across the scheme, your crew suggest heaving to until there is a gap in the next lane. What do you do?

figure.title: Halfway across
lines: Crew: 'let's wait here for a gap'

options: Turn and follow the zone along to its end
Heave to in the zone until a clear gap opens
Turn into the lane and join the traffic flow
Keep crossing, slowing to pass astern of a ship
questions.why: Rule 10: a separation zone is entered only to cross it; adjust speed to pass astern rather than wait in it.

questions.q: Fog closes in as you approach a shipping lane you must cross. What do you do?

figure.title: Fog
lines: Radar and AIS aboard, crew of four

options: Stay out of the lane, in shallow water, until it lifts
Cross now, slowly, ready to stop for each ship
Run along the lane with the traffic, at speed
Cross now on radar, trusting AIS to show every ship
questions.why: Ships keep up speed in fog and not all show on AIS; shallow water keeps big ships away until you can see.

questions.q: Using the stream for each hour, what is your ETA at the end of the leg?

figure.title: Leg 24 M, depart 0800
lines: Stream along the track, each hour:

questions.q: The wind has died and you are motor-sailing the last leg. Is your fuel enough under your own rule?

figure.title: Motor-sailing leg
lines: Leg 30 M, stream 1.5 kn foul all the way
Rule: arrive with 10 L or more

options: Yes — the leg uses about 17.5 L, leaving 14.5 L
Yes — the leg uses about 14 L, leaving 18 L
No — the leg uses about 23 L, leaving about 9 L
No — the leg uses about 35 L, more than aboard
questions.why: Over the ground 6 − 1.5 = 4.5 kn; 30 ÷ 4.5 = 6 h 40 min × 3.5 L/h ≈ 23 L; 32 − 23 ≈ 9 L, under 10 L.

questions.q: You plan an overnight passage to a harbour you want to enter at 0700. When do you leave?
Your destination marina has a sill. What is the latest time you can leave and still get in?

figure.title: Marina sill
lines: 42 M at 6 kn over the ground

questions.why: The sill shuts at HW+3 = 2020; 42 ÷ 6 = 7 h; 2020 − 7 h = 1320.

questions.q: You will arrive at an unfamiliar harbour at about 0200. When do you prepare the pilotage plan for the entry?
options: On the approach, once the lights are in sight
Before you leave, in daylight, rested
At the entrance, with the plotter zoomed in
Not at all — the leading lights show the way
questions.why: A pilotage plan is made ahead and unhurried: bearings, lights, marks and dangers on a card for the cockpit.

questions.q: You are taking a 12 m catamaran to a harbour dead upwind, with the numbers on the card. Which way gets you there sooner, and how long does it take?

figure.title: Catamaran, harbour 30 M upwind
lines: On the wind under sail: 7 kn

options: Tack under sail — about 7 h 28 min
Tack under sail — about 6 h 04 min
Motor-sail direct — about 6 h 00 min
Tack under sail — about 4 h 17 min
questions.why: Tacking through 110°: 30 ÷ cos 55° = 52.3 M ÷ 7 kn = 7 h 28 min; motor-sailing 30 M at 5 kn = 6 h 00 min.

questions.q: You are loading a 12 m charter catamaran for a week of island passages. The crew want every water tank, jerrycan and locker filled to the top. What do you say?
options: Fill everything — more aboard is always safer
Fill everything — a cat carries weight easily
Fill everything and stow it all in the bows
Load what the plan needs plus a margin — weight slows a cat
questions.why: A catamaran loses speed, windward ability and bridge-deck clearance with weight: load for the plan, heavy items central.

questions.q: You plan a 60 M day passage with the figures on the card. When does your plan say you arrive?

figure.title: 60 M along the coast
lines: Best speed in a breeze: 7 kn
Your average on past passages: 5 kn

options: 2000 — only just before dark
1800 — well before dark
1634 — well before dark
1657 — well before dark
questions.why: Plan on the speed you really average: 60 ÷ 5 = 12 h; 0800 + 12 h = 2000, half an hour before sunset.

questions.q: Two tidal gates fit tomorrow's passage, as on the card. Which do you plan for?

figure.title: Two gates tomorrow
lines: Harbour new to you, rocks at the entry
Crew: you, a watch leader, two novices

options: Either — they are just the two tides of one day
The early gate — in by daylight, after an early night
The late gate — you leave in daylight, so it is safer
The late gate — the crew sleep in and arrive rested
questions.why: A strange, rocky entry at 2330 with novices is the risk to avoid: an early night and a 0300 start bring you in at 1300.

questions.q: Your passage must meet the fair stream at the headland and the marina's sill, as on the card. When do you leave?

figure.title: Gate and sill
lines: Harbour to headland: 12 M at 5 kn
Headland to marina: 18 M at 6 kn

questions.why: Leave 0730: 12 ÷ 5 = 2 h 24 min → headland 0954, stream fair; 18 ÷ 6 = 3 h → marina 1254, sill open.

questions.q: You must be at the gate at slack water, and the stream on the way turns during the leg. Working it hour by hour, when do you leave?

figure.title: To the gate: 25.5 M
lines: Be at the gate at slack: 1300
Boat speed 5 kn through the water

questions.why: From 1000 to 1300 at 6.5 kn: 19.5 M; the other 6 M at 4 kn take 1 h 30 min before 1000 → leave 0830.

questions.q: The tidal gate puts you round the headland at 0200, and the harbour beyond is to be entered in daylight. What is the most you can make over the ground and not arrive too early?
options: 5.4 kn
6.0 kn
4.5 kn
6.8 kn
questions.why: 0200 to 0700 is 5 h: 27 ÷ 5 = 5.4 kn. Any faster and you are off a strange entrance in the dark.

questions.q: Tomorrow's window is on the card. What is the latest time you can leave under your own rule?

figure.title: Tomorrow's window
lines: Your rule: in 2 h before it builds

questions.why: 54 ÷ 6 = 9 h; in by 1600, two hours before the force 7: 1600 − 9 h = 0700.

questions.q: You hold a Yachtmaster Coastal and plan this crossing between two islands. Which route do you plan?

figure.title: Two routes
lines: Route A, direct: 72 M from land midway
Route B, via the island: 38 M off at most

options: Route A, if you cross the middle by day
Route A, as long as the forecast is moderate
Route B — it keeps you within 60 M of land
Route A — 72 M is close enough to 60 M
questions.why: The Coastal covers passages up to 60 M offshore: route B is never more than 38 M off, for 12 M more sailing.

questions.q: The owner of a 13 m yacht asks you, as a Yachtmaster Coastal, to take her on a 50 M coastal passage that runs through the night. Can you?
options: Only with a second skipper aboard at night
Only if no leg is longer than 20 M
No — the Coastal covers daylight passages only
Yes — the Coastal covers day and night passages
questions.why: Yachtmaster Coastal: command up to 24 m, up to 60 M offshore, in moderate conditions, by day and by night.

questions.q: It is 2200 and the wind is rising, so you decide to put in for the night. Which harbour do you plan for?

figure.note: Harbours ahead

options: B — lit entrance, open at all tides
A — the nearest, so the least time out
A, anchoring off the rocks until dawn
A, with the plotter zoomed right in
questions.why: A port of refuge must be safe to enter at the time you get there: at night that means a lit, clear entrance.

questions.q: Fog is forecast for your landfall at dawn. Which harbour does your plan use if it comes?
options: Either — with radar, fog changes nothing
B — in along the 10 m line and the buoyed channel
A — the plotter shows the gap in the rocks
A, slowing to 2 kn as you near the rocks
questions.why: Plan a fog alternative ahead: an approach you can follow by depth and buoys, not a gap between rocks you must see.

questions.q: Tonight's leg can take the short channel inside the banks or go round them outside. Which does your plan take?
options: The inner channel, at full speed to save time
The inner channel, a torch on each buoy
The outer route, round the lit cardinal
The inner channel, on the plotter alone
questions.why: At night unlit buoys can't be seen in time: 3 M more round a lit mark costs half an hour and takes the guesswork out.

questions.q: Tonight's route runs past bays where the pilot book shows fish farms marked by yellow flashing lights. How does your plan treat them?
options: Ignore them — fish farms lie only inside harbours
Pass between the lights — they mark the way in
Pass close by — the cages are only at the lights
Pass well off — moorings reach out beyond the lights
questions.why: Fish-farm cages are held by long moorings and lines: route well clear of the yellow lights, more so at night.

questions.q: Your route crosses the approach to a busy commercial port, as on the card. What goes into the plan for this leg?

figure.title: Port approach
lines: VTS on VHF 12 for the port area
Ships to 300 m, ferries every hour

options: The VTS channel, a watch on it, a quick crossing
A call on 16 for permission to cross
Nothing — VTS is there for the ships only
A track down the channel on the buoys
questions.why: Plan a listening watch on the port's channel and a quick crossing of the deep-water channel at right angles, clear of ships.

questions.q: You can make this overnight passage on either of two nights, as on the card. Which do you choose?

figure.title: Two nights to choose
lines: Tuesday: new moon, dark all night
Friday: full moon, up 2000 to dawn

options: Tuesday — a dark night is a better lesson
Friday — the moon lights the sea, sails and deck
Either — the moon makes no odds at sea
Tuesday — the dark makes ships' lights stand out
questions.why: With novices, a moonlit night shows the sails, the sea and the horizon: plan a night passage by the moon when you can.

questions.q: Your plan lists when each light should come into view. When do you expect to see this one?

figure.title: Light on the next headland
lines: Rising range at your eye: 16 M
6 kn over the ground, good visibility

questions.why: A weak light shows only at its nominal range, not its rising range: 24 − 8 = 16 M at 6 kn = 2 h 40 min → 0040.

questions.q: You are setting the cross-track error alarm for tonight's leg. What limit do you set?
questions.why: The alarm must sound well before you reach danger: with the shoal 0.4 M off the track, set it inside that, about 0.2 M.

questions.q: The plotter's route check reports no hazards on tonight's route. Looking at its settings, what do you do?

figure.title: Route check: no hazards
lines: Leg 3 passes 0.2 M off a reef

options: Widen the corridor past your XTE limit and run it again
Trust it — the check found no hazard
Narrow the corridor to make it stricter
Switch off the XTE alarm for leg 3
questions.why: A check only looks inside its corridor: at 0.03 M it misses a reef 0.2 M off that your 0.25 M XTE limit lets you reach.

questions.q: You let the plotter's auto-route build tomorrow's route, with the settings on the card. Before you trust it, what do you do?

figure.title: Auto-route settings
lines: Draft: 1.5 m (set by the last owner)

options: Add 0.6 m to each depth in your head
Set the true draft and safety depth, then check each leg
Nothing — auto-routing works from the chart
Use it as it is, but by daylight only
questions.why: Auto-routing knows only what it is told: with 1.5 m set for a 2.1 m keel it will route over water too shallow.

questions.q: For the passage home you reverse yesterday's route on the plotter. What do you check before you rely on it?
options: Only the total distance against the outbound
Nothing — the same legs, just sailed the other way
Each leg again — the dangers, marks and tide differ
Only that the waypoints run in the right order
questions.why: A reversed route meets marks from the other side, turns in new places and other streams: plan and check it afresh.

questions.q: At 0200 the plotter dies, as on the card. What lets you carry on safely?

figure.title: 0200 — plotter dark
lines: Power fine, the unit has failed
Next turn in 6 M, rocks to port

options: The plotter's last screen, from memory
The ETA you gave your shore contact
The marina's phone number at the destination
The paper plan: courses, distances, lights for each leg
questions.why: The written plan and the paper chart let you keep a DR and pick up the next light when the electronics fail.

questions.q: Fuel is short for this calm leg in your catamaran. Which way do you motor, and what does the leg take?
options: One engine — about 33 L for the leg
Both engines — about 23 L for the leg
One engine — about 28 L for the leg
Both engines — about 46 L for the leg
questions.why: One engine: 60 ÷ 5.5 = 10.9 h × 3.0 = 33 L; both: 60 ÷ 6.5 = 9.2 h × 5.0 = 46 L. Slower on one saves 13 L.

questions.q: Before a few days among islands with no fuel berth, you check the tank against the plan on the card. Is it enough?

figure.title: Fuel for the trip
lines: Tank 60 L, full; keep 15 L in reserve
Motoring on passage: 10 h at 3 L/h
3 days at anchor: charge 2 h a day

options: No — about 54 L used, 6 L left
Yes — about 39 L used, 21 L left
No — about 48 L used, 12 L left
Yes — about 30 L used, 30 L left
questions.why: Motoring 10 × 3 = 30 L, charging 3 × 2 h × 1.5 = 9 L: 39 L used, 21 L left — above the 15 L reserve.

questions.q: Your crew of six will be away from water for a while, as on the card. What daily allowance per person do you set?

figure.title: Water
lines: Tank 300 L, full; crew of six
Ashore they use about 15 L each a day

questions.why: Keep a day spare: 300 L ÷ (6 crew × 5 days) = 10 L each a day. Their shore habit of 15 L would need 450 L.

questions.q: A lively first night is forecast for your crew of six. What do you stow by the companionway before you leave?
options: Nothing — meals will be cooked to order below
Fresh fruit only, stowed in the forepeak
The week's tins, to help the boat's trim
Snacks, water and a flask, within reach of the watch
questions.why: In a seaway the watch needs food and drink it can reach without cooking: ready snacks and a hot flask by the hatch.

questions.q: You are sailing from Kos across to the Turkish coast, and the pilot book extract is on the card. Where does your plan make the first stop?

figure.title: Pilot book
lines: Harbour A: port of entry — customs, police
Bay B: 5 M closer, anchorage only

options: Harbour A, Q flag up, to clear in first
Bay B, as long as nobody goes ashore
Either — clear in by phone once you arrive
Bay B for the night, clearing in tomorrow
questions.why: Arriving from another country, the first stop is a port of entry to clear customs and immigration, under the Q flag.

questions.q: For the return passage two more crew join you, as on the card. How many hours on deck does each person now stand in 24 h?

figure.title: Watches
lines: Out: crew of 4, two watches, 4 on 4 off
Back: crew of 6, three watches of two
Watches still 4 hours, round the clock

options: 8 h
6 h
questions.why: Three watches of two on 4-hour watches: six watches a day, two each, 2 × 4 = 8 h on deck — down from 12 h.

questions.q: With a crew of four you set the night watches as on the card. Why stagger them like this?

figure.title: Staggered watches
lines: Each stands 4 h; one changes every 2 h

options: So two fresh crew can take over together
So each crew member sleeps eight hours at once
Someone on deck has always seen the last two hours
So the skipper never needs to be called
questions.why: Staggered watches: one person changes every 2 h, so the deck always has someone who knows the traffic and the weather.

questions.q: With a crew of six on a two-night passage, you keep yourself out of the watch rota. Why?
options: So the crew learn without help all night
Because the skipper may not steer at sea
Because a skipper never stands a watch
To be rested for the landfall and on call at any hour
questions.why: A skipper outside the rota sleeps when possible and comes fresh to the decisions, the traffic and the arrival.

questions.q: You and one friend take a 10 m yacht on a 70 M overnight passage. How do you plan the night?
options: Alternate 3-hour watches; the one off sleeps below
Both sleep, with radar and AIS alarms set
Both stay on deck all night together
You stay up all night while your friend sleeps
questions.why: Two-handed, one keeps the watch while the other sleeps from the start: short watches, and never both asleep.

questions.q: At the briefing, a novice asks why she needs to know the ports of refuge and plan B. What do you tell her?
options: The law asks every crew member to sign it
If I am hurt, the crew must get in or call for help
It keeps her busy while she is off watch
She doesn't — only the watch leaders need it
questions.why: The skipper can be the casualty: every crew member should know the route, the refuges and how to call for help.

questions.q: Your navigator prepared tonight's passage plan. At 2300 you find one of its waypoints on a shoal. Who answers for the plan?
options: Whoever is on watch at the time
The navigator who drew it up
You — the skipper checks and owns the plan
The maker of the plotter's charts
questions.why: Planning can be delegated, responsibility cannot: the skipper checks the plan and answers for the boat and crew.

questions.q: At 0300 your watch leader sees the light abeam fade out, as on the card. What should she do?

figure.title: Night orders
lines: Call me if visibility drops below 2 M
It is well inside its nominal range

options: Log it as a failed light and carry on
Carry on — you have left its sector
Swap the lookout — his eyes are tired
Call you — the visibility is closing in
questions.why: A light that fades well inside its range means falling visibility: the night orders say call the skipper.

questions.q: The autopilot is following the route through the night, as on the card. What do your night orders say about WP5?

figure.title: Tonight on autopilot
lines: The route advances at each waypoint
WP5 at about 0330: turn 70° to port
Next leg passes 0.5 M off rocks

options: Call me before WP5; the watch confirms the turn
Let the plotter skip WP5 to save time
Turn at WP5 only if the plotter beeps
Nothing — the autopilot turns there by itself
questions.why: At an auto-advancing waypoint the boat turns on its own: the watch checks the new heading is safe before it does.

questions.q: At 0215 you tack and put in a reef, between the hourly entries on the card. What goes in the log?
options: A note in the morning once all is calm
An entry now: time, log, new course, the reef
The reef only — the course is on the plotter
Nothing until the 0300 hourly entry
questions.why: Log each change as it happens — course, sails, a fix, an event — so a DR can be run from the latest entry.

questions.q: The plotter shows your ETA, as on the card. When do you really expect to arrive?

figure.title: 1000 — 30 M to go
lines: Then foul 1.5 kn to the end

questions.why: To 1200 at 7 kn: 14 M; the last 16 M at 5.5 − 1.5 = 4 kn take 4 h → 1600. The plotter assumes today's SOG holds.

questions.q: You are sailing for a tidal gate and falling behind the plan. What is the latest time you can start the engine and still make it?

figure.title: 1000 — behind the plan
lines: 30 M to the gate; it shuts at 1600

questions.why: Sailing all 6 h makes 27 M, 3 M short; the engine gains 2 kn, so you need 1.5 h of it: 1600 − 1:30 = 1430.

questions.q: You reach the headland three hours late, just as the stream turns against you. If you push on, when are you through?

figure.title: 1500 — at the headland, late
lines: 8 M of strong stream to clear
Foul 4 kn until 2100, then fair 4 kn
Boat 5 kn under engine, calm sea

questions.why: To 2100 at 5 − 4 = 1 kn: 6 M; the last 2 M at 9 kn take 13 min → 2113. Waiting at anchor for 2100 gets you through by 2153.

questions.q: At 0300 your engine fails, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: 0300 — engine dead
lines: It will not restart; no stream to worry
Marina: narrow entry, no room to sail

options: Carry on to the marina and decide at the gap
Sail to the anchorage and anchor under sail
Sail into the marina and drop sails inside
Call MAYDAY for a tow into the marina
questions.why: Plan B must fit the boat you now have: an open anchorage downwind that you can sail into, not a tight entry.

questions.q: A new forecast comes in on passage, as on the card. What do you decide?

figure.title: New forecast
lines: Destination 30 M upwind, 4 kn made good
Port of refuge 12 M on a reach
It is sheltered from the SW

options: Press on and reef when it reaches force 7
Press on — you will be in before it builds
Bear away for the port of refuge now
Heave to until the stronger wind has passed
questions.why: 30 M at 4 kn made good is 7.5 h, and the force 7 arrives in 6 h: a reach to shelter 12 M away is your plan B.

questions.q: On the first night two of your six crew are out of action, as on the card. How do you re-form the watches?

figure.title: Night 1, 2200
lines: Eva: hand injury, can't steer or winch

options: No watches — all four on deck until dawn
Four watches of one, an hour each, Kim too
Keep three watches; Tom and Eva stand theirs
Two watches of two, each led by Ana or Ben
questions.why: Fewer crew, fewer watches — but each still needs an experienced leader: Ana with Kim, Ben with you.

questions.q: You have diverted to your plan B port, as on the card. What do you do as soon as you are in?

figure.title: Plan B port, 1900
lines: Shore contact: alarm if no word by 2000
You planned to be in port A at 1700
Now safe in port C, phone signal good

options: Call your shore contact with the new port
Call the coastguard to close the passage
Call them tomorrow once the plan is final
Nothing — you are safe, so no alarm will come
questions.why: A float plan works only if it is kept up to date: tell your contact where you are before the alarm time.

questions.q: A crew member feeling queasy on passage wants to lie down in the forepeak bunk. Where do you send them instead?
options: The chart table, to keep busy with the plot
On deck in fresh air, or a bunk low and amidships
The forepeak — it is the quietest place aboard
The galley, to cook a big hot meal
questions.why: The motion is worst forward and high: fresh air and the horizon on deck, or a low bunk amidships, ease seasickness.

questions.q: Handing over at 0200, the off-going leader tells you what is on the card. What is missing?

figure.title: 0200 handover
lines: Ship on the port bow, bearing drawing aft
Skipper: call at 0400 or if in doubt

options: The time of breakfast for the morning
The name of the ship on the port bow
Your position and the next waypoint or turn
The engine hours since you left
questions.why: A handover gives the position and the next turn, as well as course, traffic, sails, weather and the skipper's orders.

questions.q: At 0300 the jib sheet fouls on the foredeck. You and one other are on watch. How do you go forward?
