options: Go with no torch so as to keep night vision
Slip forward quietly without telling anyone
Unclip to move fast, clip on again at the bow
Tell your watch mate, clip on, go while they watch you
questions.why: At night nobody goes forward unseen: say so, clip on to the jackstay, and have the helm watch you all the way.

questions.q: You plan to cross a shipping lane at right angles, as on the card. How far does a ship in the lane travel while you cross it?
questions.why: 4 M at 5 kn = 48 min = 0.8 h; 18 kn × 0.8 h = 14.4 M. A ship still out of sight can reach you before you are across.

questions.q: Halfway across a traffic lane, fog shuts in, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Fog in the lane
lines: Radar on; AIS shows two ships 6 M E

options: Stop in the lane until the fog lifts
Hold the heading across, radar watch, fog signals
Turn and run with the traffic flow
Turn back to the side you came from
questions.why: Halfway across, the quickest way out is ahead: keep the right-angle heading at safe speed, plot on radar, sound signals.

questions.q: Your harbour is dead upwind, with the figures on the card. Which makes more progress towards it?

figure.title: Harbour dead upwind
lines: Force 4 and a short, steep chop

options: Motor straight at it — 4.5 kn made good
Motor-sail 30° off — about 6.0 kn made good
Motor-sail 30° off — about 5.2 kn made good
Motor-sail 30° off — about 3.0 kn made good
questions.why: Made good towards the harbour: 6.0 × cos 30° = 5.2 kn, more than the 4.5 kn punching straight into the chop.

questions.q: The wind dies at 2200 with the harbour still ahead, as on the card. At which speed do you motor?

figure.title: 2200 — wind gone
lines: Fuel 30 L; keep 10 L in reserve

options: 6 kn — off the entrance at 0440, 9 L left
5 kn — off the entrance at 0600, 4 L left
6 kn — off the entrance at 0440, 15 L left
5 kn — off the entrance at 0600, 12 L left
questions.why: 6 kn: 6 h 40 min × 3.2 = 21 L, 9 L left, in the dark. 5 kn: 8 h × 2.2 = 18 L, 12 L left, at first light.

questions.q: On a night passage along the Turkish coast you come on deck and find the watch like this. What is missing under Rule 5?
options: A look-out by sight and hearing, all round
A radar guard zone set to 6 miles
An AIS alarm set to a 2-mile CPA
Nothing — radar and AIS are the look-out
questions.why: Rule 5: a proper look-out by sight and hearing as well as by all available means — electronics add to it, never replace it.

questions.q: A charter yacht on port tack is closing with nobody in her cockpit. How does Rule 2 answer your crew?

figure.title: Your crew's view
lines: “She's on port tack, we're on starboard”
“If she hits us, it's all her fault”

options: Right — if you hold course and speed exactly
No rule excuses you from good seamanship
Right — the stand-on yacht is never to blame
Right — until she sounds five short blasts
questions.why: Rule 2(a): nothing in the Rules excuses the neglect of any precaution required by the ordinary practice of seamen.

questions.q: You are the stand-on vessel, but holding your course and speed will put you on the rock in two minutes. What do the rules allow?

figure.title: Standing on, under sail
lines: Motor yacht crossing, slow to give way

options: Turn only after sounding five short blasts
Hold on — the stand-on must keep her course
Turn away from the rock now, clearly
Hold on until she has passed, then turn
questions.why: Rule 2(b): a departure from the Rules is required to avoid immediate danger — here a danger of navigation.

questions.q: Beating into a short sea off Cavtat with the mainsail up, you put the engine in gear to help. Your crew hoists this shape forward. What does it say?

figure.note: Day · hoisted forward

options: You are still a sailing vessel
You are restricted in your ability to manoeuvre
You are a sailing vessel with right of way
You are now a power-driven vessel
questions.why: Rule 3: a sailing vessel using her engine is power-driven; Rule 25(e): she shows a cone, point down, forward.

questions.q: Close-hauled along the Dalmatian coast, you converge with this motor boat trolling two lines astern for tuna. She shows no shape. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Two trolling lines astern · bearing steady

options: She does — trolling lines don't make her fishing
You do — any boat fishing has right of way
Both alter to starboard as if head-on
You do — she is on your starboard bow
questions.why: Rule 3(d): trolling lines do not restrict manoeuvrability, so she is simply power-driven; Rule 18: power keeps clear of sail.

questions.q: Mid-Channel in thick fog you stop the engine and drift to listen for ships. Which fog signal do you sound?

figure.title: Fog, waiting to listen
lines: 13 m yacht, sails down, engine stopped
Drifting — not at anchor, no way on

options: One prolonged blast every two minutes or less
Two prolonged blasts every two minutes or less
One prolonged and two short every two minutes
Rapid ringing of the bell every minute
questions.why: With no sail set you are power-driven; underway with no way on, Rule 35(b): two prolonged blasts, at most 2 minutes apart.

questions.q: On passage through a heavy rainstorm, your crew says the radar screen is clear, so you can keep 7 kn. What does Rule 6 say?

figure.title: Heavy rain, radar on
lines: Moderate sea, clutter out to 1.5 M

options: Safe speed is anything under hull speed
Slow down only once a target appears
Small craft can hide in clutter — slow down
The radar is the look-out — keep 7 kn
questions.why: Rule 6(b): small vessels may not be detected at an adequate range in sea and rain clutter — keep a speed you can stop in.

questions.q: Motoring on a steady course at night, you plot this ship on radar every six minutes. What do you conclude?
options: No risk — the bearing has moved by 1°
No risk yet — check again at 1 mile
Risk only once she is inside 2 miles
Risk of collision — the bearing is not changing
questions.why: Rule 7(d)(i): risk is deemed to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change.

questions.q: Under engine by day, you watch this tug crossing ahead of you with a long tow. Is there a risk of collision?

figure.title: Tug and tow ahead
lines: Range to the tug 1.2 M, closing

options: It may exist — a tow brings risk despite the change
No — a tug with a tow always keeps clear
No — the tug's bearing is clearly changing
No — the bearing draws right, she'll pass ahead
questions.why: Rule 7(d)(ii): risk may exist despite an appreciable bearing change, especially with a large vessel, a tow, or at close range.

questions.q: You are motoring at 6 kn with plenty of sea room. This ship is crossing from your starboard side. What do you do?

figure.note: Bearing steady · 3 M · she makes 18 kn

options: Slow down by 2 knots and hold your course
One bold turn to starboard, early, to pass astern
Three 10° turns to starboard, one by one
A small turn to port to pass ahead of her
questions.why: Rules 15, 16, 8: keep clear and don't cross ahead; one large early turn is seen, small steps or a speed change are not.

questions.q: You want to cross this narrow buoyed channel to reach the marina on the far side. The ferry is 1 M away, coming down the channel. What do you do?

figure.note: Buoyed channel · she can only use the channel

options: Cross now — you are on her starboard bow
Cross now at full speed, at right angles
Wait, and cross astern of her once she is clear
Cross now, sounding one short blast
questions.why: Rule 9(d): do not cross a narrow channel if it impedes a vessel that can safely navigate only within it.

questions.q: You are motoring up a narrow channel, keeping to its starboard side. A ship astern sounds two prolonged blasts and two short. What does she mean, and what do you do?
options: She'll pass on your starboard side — agree, give room
She doubts your intentions — stop at once
She is turning to starboard — hold your course
She'll pass on your port side — agree, give room
questions.why: Rule 34(c): two prolonged + two short = I intend to overtake on your port side; agree with — · — · and make room.

questions.q: Motoring up this river channel, you approach a bend where high wooded banks hide anything coming the other way. Which sound signal do you make?

figure.note: River · the bend is hidden by the banks

options: One prolonged blast
Two prolonged blasts
Five short and rapid blasts
One short blast
questions.why: Rule 34(e): one prolonged blast nearing a bend where other vessels may be hidden; a vessel beyond answers with one prolonged.

questions.q: Motoring from the coast, you want to join the eastbound lane of this scheme from its side, not at its end. How do you enter it?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: Only at the lane's end — never from the side
At as small an angle to the traffic flow as you can
Across the separation zone from the north
At right angles to the flow, to be quick
questions.why: Rule 10(b)(iii): join a lane at its end, or from the side at as small an angle to the general direction of traffic as practicable.

questions.q: You must cross this scheme to the north in a 6-knot boat, with the stream setting east as the panel shows. Which heading do you steer across the lanes?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: 090°T — along the lane to its far end
019°T — the tide angle laid off the other way
000°T — the heading at right angles to the flow
341°T — so the track crosses at right angles
questions.why: Rule 10(c): cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the traffic flow — the heading, not the track.

questions.q: Your crew says that to pass this headland you must go out and use the traffic lanes. What does Rule 10 say?

figure.title: Passing a headland with a TSS
lines: Inshore traffic zone along the coast
Your next port lies beyond the scheme

options: You must use the lane for your direction
You may use it only if bound to a port in it
You may use it only between sunset and sunrise
You may use the inshore traffic zone
questions.why: Rule 10(d): vessels under 20 m, sailing vessels and vessels fishing may use an inshore traffic zone.

questions.q: Under sail, you are crossing the lanes of a traffic separation scheme. This ship is following the lane. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Eastbound lane of a TSS · bearing steady

options: You — you must not impede her in the lane
She does — power keeps clear of sail
Both alter course to starboard
She does — you are on her starboard side
questions.why: Rule 10(j): a sailing vessel or one under 20 m shall not impede a power-driven vessel following a traffic lane.

questions.q: Beating along the coast of Kefalonia, you and this yacht are on the same tack and converging. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Both on starboard tack · converging

options: She does — she is the leeward yacht
You — you are the windward yacht
You both tack away at once
She does — she is on your port side
questions.why: Rule 12(a)(ii): on the same tack, the vessel to windward keeps out of the way of the vessel to leeward.

questions.q: Close-hauled on port tack at dusk, you cannot tell which tack this yacht to windward is on. What does Rule 12 tell you?

figure.title: Port tack, at dusk
lines: A yacht runs down towards you from upwind
Spinnaker set — you can't see her main

options: Stand on — a running yacht keeps clear
Hail her, and stand on until she answers
Keep clear of her — you can't be sure
Stand on — she is to windward of you
questions.why: Rule 12(a)(iii): on port tack, if you can't tell the tack of a vessel to windward, you keep out of her way.

questions.q: Ten minutes ago you came up from astern of this slower motor yacht. Now nearly abeam, the two of you are converging. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: You came up from astern of her · now converging

options: She does — you are on her starboard side
She does — overtaking ends once abeam
Both alter to starboard as if head-on
You — you are still the overtaking vessel
questions.why: Rule 13(d): a later change of bearing does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing one; keep clear until past and clear.

questions.q: Motoring across the Strait of Otranto at 0100, you see these lights fine on your starboard bow. They hold their bearing. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · fine on your starboard bow, steady

options: Alter boldly to starboard — she is head-on
Alter to port — open the gap to starboard
Hold on — she is crossing, you stand on
Slow down and let her pass ahead of you
questions.why: Rule 14: masthead lights nearly in line and both sidelights — head-on; each alters to starboard and passes port to port.

questions.q: On a night passage under engine from Split to Vis, these lights open on your port bow and keep the same compass bearing for ten minutes. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · on your port bow, bearing steady

options: Turn to starboard to pass astern of her
Hold your course and speed, and watch her
Turn to port to pass astern of her
Slow down and let her cross ahead
questions.why: She shows green: you are on her starboard side, so she gives way (Rule 15); you stand on and watch her (Rule 17).

questions.q: Under power south of Mykonos after midnight, you pick up these lights to starboard, closing on a steady bearing. What is she, and who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · on your starboard bow, bearing steady

options: A vessel motor-sailing — she keeps clear
A vessel not under command — you keep clear
A vessel under sail — you keep clear
A power vessel under 12 m — she keeps clear
questions.why: Rule 25(c): all-round red over green at the masthead = sailing; Rule 18: you, under power, keep out of her way.

questions.q: You are the stand-on vessel under power. She has not altered, and your five short blasts got no answer. You decide to act. What do you do?

figure.note: Five short sounded · no response · closing

options: Turn to port to pass astern of her
Speed up to cross ahead of her quickly
Hold course and speed — you must stand on
Turn to starboard or slow down — never to port
questions.why: Rule 17(a)(ii) lets you act; 17(c): a power vessel shall not, if avoidable, alter to port for a vessel on her own port side.

questions.q: You hold your course and speed as this ship closes. At what point does Rule 17 say you MUST act yourself?

figure.title: Stand-on, under power
lines: Ship crossing from your port side
She has made no move to give way

options: When she alone can no longer avoid collision
As soon as risk of collision first exists
As soon as you have sounded five short
Never — the stand-on vessel holds on
questions.why: Rule 17(a)(ii): you may act once she clearly isn't; 17(b): you must, when collision can't be avoided by her action alone.

questions.q: In open water off Kavala, these three vessels are converging. Which of them must keep out of the way of both the others?
options: B — the trawler, trawling
A — you, under sail
C — the dredger, working
None — all turn to starboard
questions.why: Rule 18: sail keeps clear of fishing and of RAM; fishing keeps clear of RAM. The working dredger stands on.

questions.q: In fog, you have this radar target fine on your port bow, closing. You decide to alter course. Which way?

figure.note: Fog · radar only · CPA under 2 cables

options: Either way — fog suspends the steering rules
To port — she will then pass to starboard
To starboard, away from her side
No turn — you are the stand-on vessel
questions.why: Rule 19(d)(i): for a vessel detected forward of the beam, avoid an alteration to port (unless she is being overtaken).

questions.q: Motoring in fog, you hear this signal and can see nothing on the radar. What does Rule 19 require you to do?

figure.title: Fog, motoring at 6 kn
lines: Heard forward of your starboard beam

options: Turn hard to port, away from the sound
Speed up to clear the area quickly
Hold speed and sound five short blasts
Slow to bare steerage way; stop if need be
questions.why: Rule 19(e): on hearing a fog signal forward of the beam, cut to the least speed to keep your course; take all way off if necessary.

questions.q: Your crew says: “We're under sail, so she must keep clear of us.” What do you do?

figure.title: Fog, under sail
lines: Radar: ship 3 M on your port bow

options: Act early yourself — in fog nobody stands on
Stand on — power keeps clear of sail
Stand on — you are on her starboard side
Turn to port to pass ahead of her
questions.why: Rule 19 governs vessels not in sight of one another: no stand-on vessel; each takes avoiding action in ample time.

questions.q: Fitting out for a night passage, you look at the box of the new sidelights. Do they meet the rules for your yacht?

figure.title: Your yacht
lines: New LED sidelights to be fitted

options: Yes — 1 M is enough for a yacht under 20 m
No — 12 to 50 m needs sidelights seen at 2 M
Yes — the rules set no range for sidelights
No — over 12 m they must be seen at 3 M
questions.why: Rule 22: sidelights are seen at 1 M under 12 m, 2 M from 12 to 50 m, and 3 M at 50 m or more.

questions.q: Under engine, you are catching up this yacht from right astern and draw out onto her starboard side. When will her green sidelight come into view?

figure.note: Night · a yacht ahead, you are gaining

options: When you are exactly abeam of her
When you are 45° abaft her beam
When you are 22.5° abaft her beam
When you are ahead of her beam
questions.why: Rule 21: a sidelight shows from right ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam; the sternlight covers the 135° astern.

questions.q: On a night passage you furl the genoa and start the engine, mainsail still up. Which switches do you turn on?
options: Steaming light and the anchor light
Tricolour and the steaming light together
Tricolour only — the main is still up
Steaming light, and the bow and stern lights
questions.why: Under engine you are power-driven (Rule 23): masthead light, sidelights and sternlight. The tricolour is for sail alone.

questions.q: Under sail at night, you see these lights dead ahead, low down and closing fast. What is she?

figure.note: Night · dead ahead, closing fast

options: A motor boat under 12 m, head-on
A sailing yacht under 20 m, head-on
A ship over 50 m, crossing ahead
A vessel at anchor with her deck lit
questions.why: Rule 23(d): a power vessel under 12 m may show one all-round white with sidelights instead of masthead light and sternlight.

questions.q: On a night sail from Zakynthos to Kalamata, these lights sit on your starboard bow and the hand-bearing compass shows no change. Who gives way?

figure.note: Night · on your starboard bow, bearing steady

options: She does — power gives way to sail
You — she is trawling
She does — she is a pilot boat at work
You — she is not under command
questions.why: Rule 26(b): all-round green over white = trawling; Rule 18(b): a sailing vessel keeps out of the way of a vessel fishing.

questions.q: Under sail at night, you want to pass this vessel about a mile ahead. Which side do you pass her?

figure.note: Night · about 1 M ahead, no sidelights

options: To the right, on the lone white light's side
Either side — she is not making way
To the left, away from the lone white light
Between the red-white pair and the lone white
questions.why: Rule 26(c)(ii): an all-round white beside the red over white shows gear out over 150 m that way — pass on the other side.

questions.q: At night off the Peloponnese you see these lights on your starboard bow. What do they tell you?

figure.note: Night · on your starboard bow

options: Constrained by her draught
Aground — keep well clear of her
Not under command, and stopped
Not under command, and making way
questions.why: Rule 27(a): two all-round reds = not under command; she adds sidelights and a sternlight only when making way.

questions.q: Motoring towards Brindisi in the dark, you have these lights on your port bow, the compass bearing unchanged. Who has to keep clear?

figure.note: Night · on your port bow, bearing steady

options: You — she is restricted in ability to manoeuvre
She does — you are on her starboard side
She does — she is a tug with a short tow
You — she is only a pilot vessel on duty
questions.why: Rule 27(b): red-white-red all-round = restricted in ability to manoeuvre; with masthead light and sidelight she is making way.

questions.q: Motoring out along the main channel of a big port at night, you see these lights dead ahead in the channel. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · dead ahead in the channel

options: Hold your course in mid-channel
Keep well to starboard and don't impede her
Stop in mid-channel until she has passed
Alter to port — she will pass to starboard
questions.why: Rule 28: three all-round reds = constrained by her draught; Rules 9 and 18(d): keep to starboard and avoid impeding her.

questions.q: Approaching a busy port at night, you see these lights off the entrance. What is she?

figure.note: Night · off the harbour entrance

options: A vessel fishing, other than trawling
A pilot vessel on duty, at anchor
A pilot vessel on duty, under way
A vessel not under command
questions.why: Rule 29: all-round white over red at the masthead = pilot on duty; with sidelights she is under way.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you are slowly catching up these lights. No other lights are in sight. What should worry you?

figure.note: Night · ahead, on your course, you are gaining

options: She is towing — her tow is ahead of her
She is at anchor — pass her on either side
She is pushing ahead — nothing is astern of her
She is towing — her tow lies between you and her
questions.why: Rule 24: the yellow towing light above the sternlight is shown by the towing vessel — her tow follows astern of her.

questions.q: Under engine at night, you see these lights dead ahead. What do they tell you?

figure.note: Night · dead ahead, bearing steady

options: A tug head-on with a tow over 200 m long
A vessel restricted in her manoeuvring
Three vessels in line, one behind another
A tug head-on with a tow under 200 m long
questions.why: Rule 24(a): three masthead lights in a vertical line = towing, the tow longer than 200 m from her stern to its end.

questions.q: You anchor your 11 m yacht for lunch in a bay off Hvar, among other yachts. The crew asks if you really need this shape. What do the rules say?

figure.note: Hoisted forward, at anchor

options: No — yachts under 12 m are exempt by day
Yes — only boats under 7 m, clear of traffic, are exempt
No — it is needed only in a channel
No — the shape is needed only in fog
questions.why: Rule 30(a),(e): a ball forward at anchor; only vessels under 7 m clear of channels, anchorages and traffic are exempt.

questions.q: Under sail off Rovinj, you approach this vessel working beside a navigation buoy. What does her shape tell you?

figure.note: Day · working beside a buoy

options: She is not under command after a breakdown
She is at anchor and working on deck
She is restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
She is constrained by her draught
questions.why: Rule 27(b): ball-diamond-ball = restricted in ability to manoeuvre, e.g. servicing a mark; Rule 18: keep out of her way.

questions.q: By day you see this coaster with this shape on the edge of a sandbank. If she is still there tonight, what lights will she show?

figure.note: Day · on the edge of a sandbank

options: Three all-round reds, one above another
Two all-round reds and nothing else
Red, white and red, all-round
Anchor lights plus two all-round reds
questions.why: Rule 30(d): aground — three balls by day; at night her anchor lights and two all-round reds in a vertical line.

questions.q: Leaving Rhodes harbour, you watch a ferry back off the quay. As she swings, she sounds two short blasts. What does she mean?
options: I am altering my course to port
I am operating astern propulsion
I intend to overtake you on your port side
I am altering my course to starboard
questions.why: Rule 34(a): one short — altering to starboard; two short — altering to port; three short — operating astern propulsion.

questions.q: You are crossing this narrow channel under engine when the ship sounds five short, rapid blasts. What does she mean, and what do you do?

figure.title: Narrow channel, motoring
lines: You are crossing to the far side
A ship is coming down the channel
She sounds five short, rapid blasts

options: She has stopped her engines — cross ahead
She doubts your intentions — get out of her way
She is in distress — close her to help
She is turning to port — hold your course
questions.why: Rule 34(d): five or more short rapid blasts = I doubt your action; make your intention plain and keep out of her way (Rule 9).

questions.q: You are beating across the Channel in fog, under sail alone. Which fog signal do you sound?
options: Two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes
One short, one prolonged, one short
One prolonged and two short every 2 minutes
One prolonged blast every 2 minutes
questions.why: Rule 35(c): a sailing vessel sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.

questions.q: Besides ringing your bell rapidly every minute, what may you also sound to warn the approaching vessel?
options: One prolonged and two short blasts
Two prolonged blasts every two minutes
Three strokes on the bell before and after
One short, one prolonged and one short blast
questions.why: Rule 35(g): a vessel at anchor may also sound one short, one prolonged and one short blast to warn of her position.

questions.q: Hove-to in fog, you hear these signals, repeated. What is out there?

figure.title: Fog, listening
lines: Then at once: one prolonged + three short

options: A tug and her manned tow — keep well clear
Two sailing yachts close together
A vessel aground and her attending tug
A fishing vessel and her outlying nets
questions.why: Rule 35(c),(e): the tug sounds one prolonged + two short; the manned tow follows at once with one prolonged + three short.

questions.q: Crossing to Kos at dusk, you pass this motor boat a mile off. What is she telling you?

figure.title: A mile off, at dusk
lines: A square flag with a ball below it

options: She is fishing — keep clear of her nets
She is in distress and needs help
She has divers down — keep clear, slow
She wants a pilot to come aboard
questions.why: Annex IV: orange smoke, and a square flag with a ball above or below it, are both signals of distress.

questions.q: Motoring along the coast at midday, you run into this squall. Your crew asks whether the fog rules apply, lights and sound signals included. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Midday, heavy rain squall
lines: Motoring at 6 kn along the coast
Other boats about, out of sight

options: Lights yes, but sound signals only in fog
No — by day you never need navigation lights
Yes — heavy rain is restricted visibility
No — only fog counts as restricted visibility
questions.why: Rule 3(l): heavy rain is restricted visibility; Rule 20(c) wants your lights on in it by day, Rule 35 the sound signals.

questions.q: On a night beat along the Croatian coast, you take over the watch and find the boat set up like this. What does a proper look-out need here?

figure.title: 0100, close-hauled, port tack
lines: Lee bow hidden from the helm

options: Nothing more — boats to leeward keep clear
Nothing more — the radar covers the lee bow
A look round only when the AIS alarm sounds
A regular look under the genoa to leeward
questions.why: Rule 5: a look-out by sight in every direction — the sector hidden by the genoa has to be checked, and often.

questions.q: Approaching Split harbour at night under engine, you see the scene in the card. What does Rule 6 say about your speed?

figure.title: 2300, approaching Split at 7 kn
lines: The city lit up behind the harbour
Their lights hard to pick out

options: Slow down — shore lights can hide boat lights
Keep 7 kn — radar sees through the glare
Speed up — get through the traffic quickly
Keep 7 kn — the harbour is brightly lit
questions.why: Rule 6(a)(iv): background light from the shore is a factor of safe speed — the lights of other vessels get lost in it.

questions.q: Under sail, you are about to cross this channel. When must you act so as not to impede the ship?

figure.title: Crossing a narrow channel
lines: You: 11 m yacht under sail, 5 kn
Ship 5 M off, coming down the channel
She can only navigate within it

options: Once she sounds five short blasts at you
Now, early — before any risk of collision exists
Once she is within about two miles of you
Once a steady bearing shows a risk of collision
questions.why: Rule 8(f): a vessel bound not to impede acts early, leaving room for the other's safe passage — before any risk develops.

questions.q: At night you are the give-way vessel for this ship, which sees your green sidelight. You turn to starboard to pass astern of her. How far must you turn before she sees your red light instead?

figure.note: Night · she bears 045° relative · steady

options: 10° at a time, so that she sees you turn
More than 22.5° — the edge of your sidelight
More than 45° — until she is on your port bow
More than 90° — until she sees your stern
questions.why: She bears 045° relative: past a 45° turn she is on your port bow and sees your red — a bold, obvious alteration (Rules 8, 16).

questions.q: Motoring up this narrow channel at night, you are catching up a ship that can only navigate within it. She must move over for you to pass on her port side. What do you sound?

figure.note: Night · narrow channel · you are gaining on her

options: Two prolonged, two short — then pass at once
Two short blasts — you are altering to port
Two prolonged, one short — then wait for her reply
Two prolonged, two short — then wait for her reply
questions.why: Rule 34(c): 2 prolonged + 2 short = I intend to overtake on your port side; go only after her prolonged-short-prolonged-short.

questions.q: Arriving tired at 0300, your crew suggests anchoring at the edge of this channel, just outside the harbour, until daylight. What does Rule 9 say?

figure.note: Narrow buoyed channel · 0300

options: Avoid anchoring in a narrow channel
Fine — at the starboard edge, out of the way
Fine — as long as your anchor light is on
Fine — boats under 20 m can't impede ships
questions.why: Rule 9(g): every vessel shall, if the circumstances of the case admit, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel.

questions.q: Motoring west along the westbound lane of a scheme at night, you see these lights dead ahead — a vessel coming the wrong way up your lane. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · dead ahead in your lane · steady

options: Alter to port — keep her on your starboard side
Alter to starboard — Rule 14 still applies
Stop in the lane and sound five short blasts
Hold on — she is in the wrong lane, she gives way
questions.why: Rule 10(a): a scheme does not lift any other rule — head-on, both alter to starboard (Rule 14).

questions.q: You cross this scheme to the north at night, on the heading Rule 10 asks for. How long are you in it, and where do you come out?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: 70 min — 2.3 M west of straight across
74 min — straight across, no set
70 min — 2.3 M east of straight across
70 min — straight across, no set
questions.why: Heading 000°T at 6 kn: 7.0 M ÷ 6 kn = 70 min; the stream sets you 2.0 kn × 70/60 h = 2.3 M east.

questions.q: Running dead downwind with your mainsail out to starboard, you converge with this yacht beating to windward. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Mainsail out to starboard · converging

options: She does — you are on starboard tack
She does — she is the windward yacht
She does — a running yacht has right of way
You — main to starboard means port tack
questions.why: Rule 12(b): the windward side is the side opposite the mainsail — main to starboard means port tack, so you keep clear.

questions.q: Under sail on a dark night, you are slowly closing this light. Its bearing hardly changes. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · starboard bow · closing far slower than 6 kn

options: You — you are overtaking her, even under sail
She does — power gives way to sail
Neither — she is at anchor, pass her close
She does — she is on your starboard bow
questions.why: Rule 13: seeing only her sternlight, you come up from over 22.5° abaft her beam — the overtaking vessel keeps clear.

questions.q: Motoring up on this yacht's starboard quarter, you see her sternlight, then her green as she yaws, then the sternlight again. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · on your port bow · she is yawing

options: She does — you are on her starboard side
You — in doubt, you are the overtaking vessel
Neither — hold on and sound five short
She does — her green shows you are crossing
questions.why: Rule 13(c): when in any doubt whether you are overtaking, assume that you are, and keep out of her way.

questions.q: A minute ago this ship, dead ahead, was showing you both sidelights. Now you see this. What is she doing?

figure.note: Night · dead ahead, 1.5 M

options: Turning to port — expect a starboard-to-starboard pass
Going astern — her masthead lights have closed up
Turning to starboard — expect a port-to-port pass
Holding her course — her red says she stands on
questions.why: Her lower, forward masthead light has opened to your left and only her red shows: her bow is swinging to her starboard.

questions.q: You are the stand-on vessel under power. She did not answer your five short blasts and is now 2 cables off on your port beam, showing these lights. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · port beam, 2 cables · both sidelights

options: Turn hard to port, to cross ahead of her
Stop your engine and let her pass ahead
Hold on — keeping clear is still her job
Turn hard to starboard, away from her, now
questions.why: Rule 17(b): she alone can no longer avoid you, so you must act — turn away from her, never to port towards her (17(c)).

questions.q: You were the stand-on vessel; she did not give way, so you turned to avoid her. What does Rule 17 say about your crew's remark?

figure.title: After your alteration
lines: You stood on; she did not give way
You turned to starboard to avoid her

options: Wrong — she still has to keep out of your way
Right — once you have turned, Rule 17 ends
Right — whoever acts first takes on the duty
Wrong — now you both must stop your engines
questions.why: Rule 17(d): action by the stand-on vessel does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way.

questions.q: Beating to windward with the mainsail up and the engine running to help, you converge with this yacht under sail alone. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Mainsail up, engine in gear · bearing steady

options: She does — she's on port tack, you're on starboard
You — with the engine on you are power-driven
She does — you are on her starboard side
Both alter to starboard, as if head-on
questions.why: Rule 3(b): a sailing vessel with her engine in use is power-driven — Rule 18(a): you keep out of the way of a vessel under sail.

questions.q: Under sail off Ithaca, you come up on this coaster lying stopped across your course with this shape hoisted. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Day · stopped across your course

options: She does — she is only at anchor
She does — power gives way to sail
You — she is not under command
You — she is aground on a shoal
questions.why: Rules 27(a) and 18(b): two balls in a vertical line mean not under command; a sailing vessel keeps out of her way.

questions.q: Sailing across the approach to Thessaloniki, you see this tanker coming up the dredged channel with this shape. What does Rule 18 ask of you?

figure.note: Day · a tanker in the dredged channel

options: Nothing until she sounds five short blasts
Keep clear only if she is on your starboard side
Nothing — a power vessel gives way to sail
Avoid impeding her — she is constrained by draught
questions.why: Rules 28 and 18(d): a cylinder means constrained by her draught — every vessel but NUC or RAM avoids impeding her.

questions.q: Under engine off Lefkada, you come up on this small boat with this shape hoisted. What is she telling you?

figure.note: Day · lying stopped

options: She is engaged in fishing — keep clear
She is motor-sailing — she keeps clear
She is aground — keep off the shoal
She is at anchor — pass either side
questions.why: Rule 26: two cones, points together, mean a vessel engaged in fishing; Rule 18(a): power keeps out of her way.

questions.q: Motoring in fog, you have been watching this ship on radar. Now she comes out of the murk, as the card shows. Which rules govern what you do now?

figure.title: Fog, under power
lines: A radar contact for ten minutes
She comes into sight 4 cables off
On your starboard bow, crossing to port

options: Rule 19 — the fog has not lifted yet
The crossing rules — you are now in sight
None — in fog each vessel acts for herself
Rule 19 — she was a radar contact first
questions.why: Rule 19 is for vessels not in sight; once in sight, Rules 11–18 apply — she is on your starboard side, so you give way.

questions.q: In fog you plot this radar target twice. What is the CPA, and what do you do?
options: CPA about 1.5 M — no risk, hold on
CPA about 0.3 M — alter boldly to port
CPA about 0.3 M — alter boldly to starboard
CPA about 0.3 M — hold on, you stand on
questions.why: Plot: closing 7.5 kn, CPA 0.3 M at about 0348 — close quarters; Rule 19(d): she is forward of the beam, so no turn to port.

questions.q: In fog this radar target is coming up on your starboard quarter, CPA 1 cable. You decide to alter course. Which way?

figure.note: Fog · radar only · closing from astern

options: To starboard, to cross ahead of her
Neither — she is overtaking, she keeps clear
To starboard — always starboard in fog
To port, turning away from her side
questions.why: Rule 19(d)(ii): avoid an alteration of course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam — here, no turn to starboard.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you are catching up this tug with a barge lashed alongside her. What lights do you see from astern?

figure.note: Night · you are gaining from astern

options: Two white sternlights side by side, no yellow
Two masthead lights in a vertical line
One white sternlight, a yellow one beside it
A yellow towing light above a white sternlight
questions.why: Rule 24(c),(f): towing alongside, the tug shows a sternlight but no towing light; the barge alongside shows her own sternlight.

questions.q: On a clear night you are motoring towards this ship, head-on. Her masthead light first shows at the range Rule 22 gives it. If neither of you alters, how long before you meet?

figure.title: Head-on, clear night
lines: Her lights seen at their rule ranges

options: About 12 minutes
About 15 minutes
About 20 minutes
About 30 minutes
questions.why: Over 50 m, her masthead light carries 6 M; closing at 18 + 6 = 24 kn, 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 h = 15 min.

questions.q: Radar puts this ship 5 M off on your starboard bow. You see only these two white lights. Which way is she heading, and why no sidelights?

figure.note: Night · starboard bow, 5 M on radar

options: To your left — sidelights carry only 3 M
To your left — her sidelights are off
To your right — sidelights carry only 3 M
To your right — her sidelights are off
questions.why: Her lower, forward masthead light is right of the higher aft one; a ship's masthead light carries 6 M, her sidelights 3 M.

questions.q: After dinner ashore you take this tender back out to the boat. What light does Rule 23 ask her to show?
options: Sidelights and a sternlight, like a yacht
None — tenders under 7 m are exempt from lights
A torch, shown only if a ship comes near
An all-round white; sidelights if practicable
questions.why: Rule 23(d)(ii): a power-driven vessel under 7 m, top speed 7 kn or less, may show an all-round white light instead.

questions.q: These lights cross ahead of you from right to left, the two reds well apart. What is she?

figure.note: Night · crossing ahead, right to left

options: A tug pushing a barge ahead of her
Two power vessels, one overtaking the other
A ship over 50 m, crossing to your left
A tug towing a barge astern of her
questions.why: Rule 24(c),(f): pushing ahead, the tug shows two masthead lights in a line; the barge shows sidelights at her forward end.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you see these lights crossing ahead of you from left to right. What lies between the two green lights?

figure.note: Night · crossing ahead, left to right

options: A fishing net strung between two boats
A towline — never pass between them
A barge pushed ahead of the tug
Open water — they are two separate vessels
questions.why: Rule 24: two masthead lights in a line mean towing; the tow's own green, astern of the tug, marks the end of the towline.

questions.q: Under sail by day, you are about to cross the track of this tug and her tow. What do the shapes tell you?

figure.title: By day, ahead
lines: A tug with a black diamond shape
A barge far astern of her, 400 m

options: She is aground — keep clear of both
She is restricted — pass on either side
A tow over 200 m — pass astern of the barge
A short tow — you may cross between them
questions.why: Rule 24(a)(v),(e)(iii): a diamond on the tug and another on the tow mean a tow longer than 200 m.

questions.q: You take this disabled yacht in tow for the night run to harbour. Your boat has no towing lights. What do you show?
options: The tricolour — you are as slow as a sailboat
Your anchor light too — you are barely moving
Two all-round reds — you can't manoeuvre
Your usual lights, and a light on the towline
questions.why: Rule 24(i): a vessel not normally towing needn't show towing lights, but must show the tow — in particular by lighting the towline.

questions.q: Under sail at night, you see these two tugs, each with a tow, crossing ahead on steady bearings. Who keeps clear of whom?
options: A keeps clear of you; you keep clear of B
You keep clear of A; B keeps clear of you
You keep clear of both — tugs have priority
Both keep clear of you — power gives way to sail
questions.why: Rule 18: towing alone gives no priority; Rule 27(c): red-white-red means B can't deviate, so you keep out of her way.

questions.q: Your new yacht has all these lights on her switch panel. Under sail alone at night, which combination may you show?

figure.title: Switch panel, 14 m yacht
lines: Bow and stern lights · Steaming light

options: Red-over-green together with the tricolour
Red-over-green with the bow and stern lights
Red-over-green on its own, nothing else
The tricolour together with the steaming light
questions.why: Rule 25(c): red-over-green may be added to the sidelights and sternlight, but is never shown with the tricolour.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you see these lights dead ahead, closing. What is she?

figure.note: Night · dead ahead, closing · nothing lower

options: A power boat under 12 m, correctly lit
A yacht under sail, showing red-over-green
A yacht motoring with her tricolour on
A yacht under sail, correctly lit
questions.why: Rule 25(b): the tricolour is for sailing only; a white light on the mast below it is a steaming light — treat her as power.

questions.q: Under sail at night, you see only these two lights on your starboard bow, the bearing drawing slowly aft. What is she doing?

figure.note: Night · starboard bow · nothing else visible

options: Lying at anchor, 50 m or more long
Trawling and making way, end-on to you
Piloting, stopped on her station
Trawling, but stopped — not making way
questions.why: Rule 26(b): green over white means trawling; the sidelights and sternlight are shown only when making way through the water.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you are slowly catching up these lights. What is she, and what do you do?

figure.note: Night · ahead · you are slowly gaining

options: A trawler seen from astern — keep well clear
A trawler at anchor — pass her either side
A trawler seen from ahead — hold your course
A pilot boat seen from astern — keep well clear
questions.why: Rule 26(b): green over white, a sternlight below — a trawler making way, you astern; Rule 13: the overtaking vessel keeps clear.

questions.q: Your crew wants to call MAYDAY RELAY for this ship, which shows only these lights. What do you tell them?

figure.note: Night · 1 M off · no sidelights, not moving

options: Yes — a ship with no way on needs rescue
No — she is not under command, not in distress
No — she is aground and in no danger
Yes — two reds mean a ship in distress
questions.why: Rule 27(a),(h): two all-round reds mean not under command, and are not distress signals; no sidelights, so no way on.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you have this vessel ahead, working and not moving. On which side do you pass her?

figure.note: Night · ahead · working, not moving

options: Neither — keep 1000 m off her all round
On the side of the two reds, to your left
On the side of the two greens, to your right
Either side — she is only at anchor
questions.why: Rule 27(d): red-white-red is RAM; two reds mark the side of the obstruction, two greens the side where you may pass.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you see these lights about 2 M ahead. How close may you pass her?

figure.note: Night · about 2 M ahead

options: Within 200 m, but only astern of her
No closer than 500 m
As close as you like, on her green side
No closer than 1000 m
questions.why: Rule 27(f): three all-round greens mean mine clearance — it is dangerous to come within 1000 m of her.

questions.q: Arriving off the entrance at night, you see these lights. They don't move, and as you pass round her no sidelight ever shows. What is she?

figure.note: Night · off the entrance · not moving

options: A pilot vessel on duty, at anchor
A vessel fishing, at anchor
A pilot vessel on duty, under way
A vessel aground, under 50 m
questions.why: Rule 29: white over red is a pilot vessel on duty; at anchor she adds her anchor light and shows no sidelights.

questions.q: Coming into the anchorage off Piraeus at night, you see these lights on a ship that is not moving. What is she?

figure.note: Night · not moving · decks lit

options: A ship aground, waiting for the tide
A ship at anchor, 50 m or more long
A ship under way, seen from ahead
A ship towing, seen from astern
questions.why: Rule 30(a),(c): two all-round whites, the forward one higher than the after one; a big ship also lights her decks.

questions.q: You anchor your 13 m yacht overnight in a bay off Paxos. Which switch on this panel do you put on?
options: Tricolour — it is seen all round
Steaming — a white light forward is enough
Anchor — the all-round white light
Nav — bow and stern, so you are seen
questions.why: Rule 30(b): a vessel under 50 m at anchor may show one all-round white light where it can best be seen.

questions.q: At 0200 you took this single white light ahead for a sternlight. You have since passed round her and have her abeam, 2 cables off, and it is still all you see. What is she?

figure.note: Night · abeam, 2 cables · a yacht of about 12 m

options: A yacht under sail — it is her tricolour
A yacht under power — it is her steaming light
A yacht under way — it is her sternlight
A yacht at anchor — the light is all-round
questions.why: Rule 21: from abeam an under-way yacht shows a sidelight; one white seen from every side is an anchor light (Rule 30(b)).

questions.q: Leaving harbour at night, you watch this ferry ahead of you at her berth. What is she telling you?

figure.title: Night, at the ferry quay
lines: Ferry ahead, lines just let go

options: I am operating astern propulsion
I am altering my course to port
I am in doubt about your intentions
I am altering my course to starboard
questions.why: Rule 34(a),(b): three short blasts, or three flashes of the all-round white light, mean I am operating astern propulsion.

questions.q: In fog off the Brittany coast, you are under main and engine. Your crew reaches for the horn to sound the sailing-vessel signal. What should you sound?
options: One prolonged and two short every two minutes
One prolonged blast every two minutes or less
Two prolonged blasts every two minutes or less
One short, one prolonged and one short
questions.why: With the engine in use you are power-driven (Rule 3(b)); making way, Rule 35(a): one prolonged blast at most 2 min apart.

questions.q: In fog you hear the signal in the card, repeated, from the same spot for twenty minutes. Which of these could she be?

figure.title: Fog, listening
lines: One prolonged and two short blasts

options: A vessel aground on the bank
A power vessel stopped and drifting
A vessel engaged in fishing, at anchor
A ship over 100 m, at anchor
questions.why: Rule 35(d): a vessel fishing at anchor, or RAM at work at anchor, sounds 1 prolonged + 2 short instead of the bell.

questions.q: Groping towards the harbour in fog, you hear the signal in the card ahead of you, repeated each minute. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Fog, near a shoal
lines: Three separate strokes on a bell

options: A vessel at anchor, over 100 m long
A vessel engaged in fishing, at anchor
A vessel at anchor, under 20 m long
A vessel aground — the shoal is close
questions.why: Rule 35(h): three separate and distinct strokes on the bell before and after the rapid ringing mean a vessel aground.

questions.q: Motoring in fog in your 11 m yacht, your crew says boats this small need no fog signal at all. What does Rule 35 say?

figure.title: Fog, visibility 1 cable
lines: Your 11 m yacht, motoring at 4 kn

options: Some efficient sound signal every 2 minutes
Nothing — boats under 12 m are exempt
Only a bell, rung rapidly every minute
Only once you hear another vessel's signal
questions.why: Rule 35(j): under 12 m you needn't give the full signals, but then you must make some other efficient sound signal at most 2 min apart.

questions.q: In fog off the port entrance, you hear the signal in the card, repeated. What is she?

figure.title: Fog, off the entrance
lines: Then at once: four short blasts

options: A vessel in doubt about your intentions
A pilot vessel on duty, making way
A vessel aground, warning you off
A tug followed by her manned tow
questions.why: Rule 35(k): a pilot vessel on duty may add four short blasts, her identity signal, to her normal fog signal.

questions.q: Dismasted 5 M off the coast, your crew lays out this kit to signal distress. Which of these is not a distress signal?
options: An orange smoke signal
A red handheld flare
A white handheld flare
A red parachute rocket
questions.why: Annex IV lists red rockets, red flares and orange smoke; a white flare only draws attention (Rule 36).

questions.q: By day you see these two yachts a mile off. Which of them is signalling distress?

figure.title: A mile off, by day
lines: Yacht A flies code flags N over C
Yacht B flies code flag V
Both lying still in a calm

options: B — V is the distress flag
Neither — flags are never distress signals
Both — any code flag asks for help
A — N over C is a distress signal
questions.why: Annex IV(f): the code flags N over C mean distress; flag V asks for assistance but is not a distress signal.

questions.q: This is the synoptic picture at noon. Where does the wind come from at your position?

figure.note: You: south of the centre

options: From about WSW
From about S
From about N
From about ENE
questions.why: In the north air circles a low anticlockwise, angled in towards the centre: south of it the wind is about WSW.
questions.ref: Pressure systems — wind round a low

questions.q: You want to know where the low centre lies. Where is it?

figure.title: No forecast for two days
lines: You stand with your back to the wind

options: On your right, a little ahead — E
On your left, a little ahead — NNW
Straight ahead of you — NE
On your left, a little behind — W
questions.why: Buys Ballot: back to the wind, the low is on your left in the north — a little ahead, as the wind angles in.

questions.q: Nothing else changes between the two charts. What mean wind do you plan for at 1200?

figure.title: Two synoptic charts
lines: Isobars every 4 hPa in your area

options: About 12 kn — F4
About 6 kn — F2
About 24 kn — F6
About 48 kn — F10
questions.why: Wind goes inversely with isobar spacing: half the spacing, twice the wind — 12 × 120/60 = 24 kn, force 6.

questions.q: You are where the boat is drawn, on the east side of this high. Where does the wind come from?

figure.note: You: east of the centre

options: From about SSE
From about W
From about E
From about NNW
questions.why: Round a high in the north air turns clockwise and slightly outwards: on its east side the wind is about NNW.
questions.ref: Pressure systems — wind round a high

questions.q: You are planning the week from this chart. Where is this low in its life?

figure.title: Synoptic chart, 1200 UTC
lines: Cold front has caught the warm front

options: Occluded and mature — it will slowly fill
Still deepening — the warm sector widens
Just forming — a new low on the front
A young wave — it will deepen fast now
questions.why: When the cold front catches the warm front the low occludes: its deepening is over and it begins to fill.

questions.q: You are on a day sail along the coast. What is coming, and what follows it?
options: A sea breeze — the wind dies at sunset
A warm front — rain, poorer visibility, then a veer
A cold front — squalls, then clear cold air
A ridge — the cloud will clear by evening
questions.why: Cirrus, a halo, lowering altostratus, a falling glass and a backing wind: the classic approach of a warm front.

questions.q: You kept the log through the afternoon. What happened between 1600 and 1900?
options: An occlusion passed — the wind will now die
The cold front passed — the low is behind you
The warm front passed — you are in the warm sector
The low centre passed overhead — it will clear
questions.why: As a warm front passes the rain eases to drizzle, the wind veers, the glass stops falling and the air turns warm and damp.

questions.q: You will be at sea when the front arrives. What does the front itself bring?
options: Hours of steady rain and a slow back to SE
Thickening fog and a back to the south
A slow clearance and the wind dying to calm
Squalls and heavy rain, a sharp veer, the glass rising
questions.why: A cold front brings a line of squalls and heavy rain, a sudden veer to W or NW and a rising barometer.

questions.q: You need a quiet night at anchor off this island. Where do you go?

figure.note: Forecast: S 5, veering W then NW 6 tonight

options: A — the east side, in the lee of W and NW
Off the south beach, then move at midnight
C — the north side, best shelter from the S
B — the west side, clear of the southerly sea
questions.why: Veering is clockwise: S to W to NW puts B and C on a lee shore tonight, while the east side is sheltered from it.

questions.q: The centre passes south of you during the night. How does the wind shift?
options: It veers to S, then backs to E
It backs through E and NE to N
It stays SE and dies as it passes
It veers through S and SW to W
questions.why: With the low passing to the south of you the wind backs: anticlockwise, from SE through E and NE to N.

questions.q: There is no front on the chart. What do you prepare for at about 1500?
options: A slow fall to calm as the pressure rises
Nothing much — without a front it stays mild
Squalls and a sudden veer as the trough passes
A slow back to S with steady rain
questions.why: A trough is a line of low pressure: like a weak front it brings showers, squalls and a sharp veer as it passes.

questions.q: When do you sail the leg?
options: Tonight, on the easing NW wind
Mid-afternoon, once the ridge settles
Tomorrow evening, on the new S breeze
At first light, to be in by mid-afternoon
questions.why: A ridge between two lows gives a short fair spell: use it early, because the next low's wind follows quickly.

questions.q: Your crew says the main low is too far away to matter. What do you tell them?
options: The secondary may bring the strongest wind of all
A secondary fills before it reaches the Channel
At 1002 hPa the secondary is too high to matter
A secondary is always weaker than the main low
questions.why: A secondary low on the trailing front can deepen fast and bring gales stronger than the primary's.

questions.q: You are 15 M out on a coastal passage. What does the log tell you?
options: A normal swing — nothing to note yet
A fast fall — strong wind or a gale is near
A fall that means the low has passed
A slow fall — a little rain later today
questions.why: 6 hPa in 3 hours is well past the 3 hPa warning sign: expect strong wind or a gale within hours.

questions.q: Your crew wants to leave at 0600 now that the glass is rising. What do you say?

figure.title: Night at anchor, a low passing

options: Wait — the glass will fall again within the hour
Go — a rising glass always means less wind
Wait — a fast rise brings strong wind for hours
Go — the low has passed, the sea drops at once
questions.why: A quick rise behind a low means a steep gradient: strong, gusty NW wind for some hours yet.

questions.q: You write the wind in the log. What force is it?

figure.title: Wind instrument, 10-minute mean
lines: Sea heaps up, foam blown in streaks

options: Force 8 — gale
Force 6 — strong breeze
Force 9 — severe gale
Force 7 — near gale
questions.why: Beaufort goes by the mean wind: 28–33 kn is force 7. Log the gusts beside it.

questions.q: What wave height do you plan for on the open leg?
options: 2.5 to 4 m
4 to 6 m
questions.why: Forecast terms: slight 0.5–1.25 m, moderate 1.25–2.5 m, rough 2.5–4 m, very rough 4–6 m.

questions.q: How will the sea change during your crossing?

figure.title: Crossing the gulf
lines: N 6 set in at 0600 after a calm
Open water to the N: 80 M

options: It stays slight — 80 M is a short fetch
It keeps building — the wind is still young
It peaks at once — the fetch alone sets it
It eases as the wind settles in
questions.why: Waves grow with wind strength, fetch and duration: a new force 6 over 80 M of open water builds the sea for hours.

questions.q: You plan a leg down the open coast tomorrow. What does the swell tell you?

figure.title: Galicia, September, 0800
lines: New long swell from the NW, 14 s

options: A sea breeze is building from the NW
The high is strengthening over you
A deep low far to the NW — get a fresh forecast
Nothing — swell only follows the local wind
questions.why: Long-period swell runs far ahead of a deep low: get the latest forecast before any open-coast leg.

questions.q: When and how do you round the Bill?

figure.title: Bound SW round the Bill
lines: Race off the Bill: 4 kn at springs

options: In the foul stream, close under the cliffs
At the peak of the fair SW-going stream
Any time — a race only runs at neaps
Near slack water, well outside the race
questions.why: The fair stream runs against the wind: SW 6 over 4 kn makes the race dangerous. Round near slack and give it a wide berth.

questions.q: How will the breeze behave through the afternoon?

figure.title: Turkish coast, July, settled
lines: Coast runs E–W, open sea to the S

options: Build to F3–4, veer a little, die at dusk
Swing off the land by 1500 and freshen
Die by 1300 as the land heats up
Back a little and build through the night
questions.why: A sea breeze builds as the land heats, peaks in mid-afternoon, veers through the day in the north and dies at sunset.

questions.q: You are anchored at A in midsummer, in settled weather. How will this breeze change after sunrise?

figure.note: 0500: light breeze off the land

options: It veers to the E and builds all day
It dies, then a sea breeze sets in from the S
It holds all day — it is the gradient wind
It builds to F5 from the N by noon
questions.why: A land breeze blows off the cool land at night and dies as the sun heats it; by late morning the sea breeze takes over.

questions.q: What is this wind, and when will it ease?

figure.title: Gulf of Kotor, April, 0200
lines: Clear, starry sky, no gradient wind
Steep slopes, snow on the peaks
Gusts to F5 pouring off the mountains

options: Anabatic — it builds until sunrise
A sea breeze — it eases at noon
Katabatic — it eases after sunrise
Gradient wind — it lasts until a front
questions.why: On clear nights cold air slides down the slopes: a katabatic wind, strongest before dawn, gone once the sun warms them.

questions.q: Why is it blowing harder than forecast close inshore?

figure.title: Sunny afternoon, south coast of Crete
lines: Steep sun-baked slopes above the shore
Close inshore: S 4–5, towards the hills

options: Funnelling between two islands adds to it
A land breeze off the slopes adds to it
Katabatic flow down the slopes adds to it
Anabatic flow up the hot slopes adds to it
questions.why: On sunny afternoons warm air rises up the slopes — an anabatic wind — and strengthens the onshore sea breeze.

questions.q: You plan to motor-sail through the strait at A. What wind do you expect there?

figure.note: Open sea: NE 5

options: Stronger, blowing along the strait from N
Weaker, sheltered by the islands each side
Stronger, blowing across the strait from E
The same NE 5 as in the open sea
questions.why: A strait between high land squeezes and turns the wind: it blows along the channel, and harder than outside.

questions.q: You are bound east along this coast. Where do you expect the most wind and the worst sea?

figure.note: W 5 along the coast

options: B — in open water, clear of the land
A — off the tip of the headland
C — in the bay past the headland
Equal at A, B and C — same gradient
questions.why: Wind bends and speeds up round a headland, and the stream runs hardest there: expect more wind and a confused sea off the tip.

questions.q: You motor west in calm water at A, close under the cliffs, heading for B. How do you set up?

figure.note: Open sea: N 6

options: Full sail — the lee reaches well past B
Set full sail at A to use the first puffs
Reef before B — the full N 6 returns there
Keep close under the cliffs — no gusts there
questions.why: A high island casts a wind shadow, but its edge is sharp: the full wind returns at once, and gusts fall off the cliffs.

questions.q: You plan the coming days in the Cyclades. What do you expect?

figure.title: Synoptic chart, late July
lines: Isobars run N–S over the Aegean

options: A S gale ahead of a cold front
Light sea breezes only, as under a high
Sirocco — S 5–6 with haze and rain
Meltemi — N 6–7 under clear skies
questions.why: High over the Balkans, low over Turkey: the gradient drives the Meltemi, N in the Cyclades, often force 6–7 for days.

questions.q: Kvarner, January. Where do you spend the night?

figure.note: Forecast: Bora NE 7, gusts 50 kn, tonight

options: B — in the lee of the island, to its SW
A — under the mainland, which is upwind
A — the channel is too narrow for a sea
Either — the Bora always dies at night
questions.why: The Bora falls off the mountains in violent gusts, worst right under them: shelter behind an island, well away from them.

questions.q: Which wind is setting in, and how will it develop?

figure.title: Southern Adriatic, October
lines: Red dust on deck after a shower

options: Bora — sudden NE gusts within the hour
Sirocco — builds over a day or two, big SE seas
Mistral — cold NW wind under clear skies
Meltemi — N 6 by afternoon, then calm
questions.why: Hazy humid air, Saharan dust and a slowly building SE wind: the Sirocco (Jugo), raising long seas up the Adriatic.

questions.q: Your crew says the sky is perfect and the wind is fair. What do you decide?

figure.title: Port-Camargue, April, 0700
lines: Sky clear, air cold and dry, NW 4
Plan: 40 M E across the open gulf

options: Go — the front has passed, it will settle
Go — a NW wind is fair for going east
Stay — a Mistral is building to NW 7–8
Go after the sea breeze sets in at noon
questions.why: High over Biscay and low over Genoa after a cold front: the Mistral, NW 7–8 or more under clear skies, often for days.

questions.q: Which wind is this, and what does the strait do to it?

figure.title: Estepona, bound W for Cádiz
lines: Cloud banner streaming W off the Rock
Málaga: E 3; in the strait: E 6–7

options: Mistral — it pours down from the Pyrenees
Sirocco — it blows across from Africa
Poniente — the strait turns it to the E
Levante — the strait squeezes and speeds it
questions.why: The Levante is the E wind of the Alborán Sea; the strait funnels it, so it blows far harder there than outside.

questions.q: You are choosing a berth for the night. From which direction must it be sheltered?
options: North-east
North-west
South-west
South-east
questions.why: Poyraz is the Turkish name for the NE wind — cold and strong in winter in the Marmara and the north Aegean.

questions.q: Your crew hopes the breeze will blow the fog away. Will it?
options: Yes — any wind over F3 clears fog
No — sea fog lasts until the air mass changes
Yes — the sun will burn it off by noon
No — but it will lift at dusk as it cools
questions.why: Warm moist air over a colder sea makes advection (sea) fog: wind does not clear it — only a change of air mass does.

questions.q: You want to leave for a 20-mile coastal leg. When will the fog clear?

figure.title: River harbour, October, 0700
lines: Thick fog over the river and town
Outside the bar: clear, wind W 2

options: Not until a front brings new air
Only at nightfall, as the air cools
By mid-morning, as the sun warms the land
Not today — it drifts out and thickens
questions.why: Radiation fog forms over land on clear calm nights and burns off as the sun warms the ground, usually by mid-morning.

questions.q: What is cutting the visibility, and when will it improve?

figure.title: Approaching the coast at night
lines: Visibility now under 1000 m in rain

options: Haze from a high — not for several days
Radiation fog — once the sun is up
Sea fog — when the wind drops to calm
Frontal fog in the rain — once the front passes
questions.why: Rain falling into cold air ahead of a warm front saturates it: frontal fog, which lifts once the front has gone through.

questions.q: What is the worst visibility you plan for on the leg?
options: Between 1000 m and 2 M
Less than 1000 m
Between 2 and 5 M
More than 5 M
questions.why: Forecast terms: good is over 5 M, moderate 2–5 M, poor 1000 m to 2 M, fog under 1000 m.

questions.q: How long have you got, and what do you do?

figure.title: Radar, 1510
lines: Squall line on radar 6 M to the W
Your sail: full main and genoa

options: About 24 min — finish the leg first
About 15 min — reef down and secure now
About 4 min — too late to reef now
About 40 min — reef once it is close
questions.why: 6 M at 25 kn is 0.24 h = 14.4 min, about 15 min. A squall line hits hard: reef and secure before it arrives.

questions.q: What reaches you first, and how do you prepare?

figure.title: Afternoon, Ionian
lines: Cumulonimbus 5 M to the W, moving E
Dark curtain of rain under the base

options: A fresher SE breeze into the cell — ease sheets
The rain, then the wind dies — keep full sail
A cold gust from the W, ahead of the rain — reef
Lightning only — the wind stays a light SE
questions.why: Downdraughts spread out ahead of a cumulonimbus as a gust front: a sudden cold squall from the storm's side before the rain.

questions.q: What do you check first?

figure.title: Lightning strike, 1530
lines: Strike at the masthead, crew all well

options: The fridge and the cabin lights
The VHF aerial lead at the masthead
The engine oil and coolant levels
The through-hulls and the hull for leaks
questions.why: A strike can blow out a through-hull or crack the hull as it leaves: look for water first, then check compass and electronics.

questions.q: You plan to sail along the coast under the mountains. What do these clouds warn you of?

figure.title: Corsica, morning
lines: Smooth lens-shaped clouds over the peaks
They stay put while others drift by

options: Strong wind aloft — hard gusts off the high land
A warm front with rain within the hour
Fair weather — light winds all day
Fog forming over the sea by evening
questions.why: Lenticular clouds form in a strong airflow over mountains: expect violent gusts down the lee slopes, even with light wind at sea.

questions.q: You are setting up the NAVTEX receiver before a coastal passage. Which message types can you never switch off?
options: E only — the weather forecasts
A, B and D — nav and met warnings, SAR
A and E — nav warnings and forecasts
B and L — met warnings and extra nav
questions.why: NAVTEX on 518 kHz: types A (navigational warnings), B (met warnings) and D (search and rescue) cannot be rejected.

questions.q: You are the skipper, on watch at the chart table. What do you do?
options: Stay on Ch 16 — the text is repeated there
Note the time and wait for the 0700 forecast
Switch to Ch 23, write it down, then replan
Reply on Ch 16 to say you have received it
questions.why: A SÉCURITÉ on 16 announces safety information on a working channel: go there, copy it word for word, then act on it.

questions.q: Until when, local time, could the gale arrive?

figure.title: Galicia, local time UTC+2
lines: You read it at 1730 local, at sea

options: Any time up to 2100 local
Any time up to 2330 local
Not before 2300 local
Any time up to 2300 local
questions.why: Imminent means within 6 h of issue: 1500 + 6 = 2100 UTC = 2300 local, and it can come at any time before that.

questions.q: What mean wind does the warning give?
options: 41 to 47 kn
28 to 33 kn
48 to 55 kn
34 to 40 kn
questions.why: Severe gale is force 9: a mean of 41–47 kn. Gale 8 is 34–40 kn, storm 10 is 48–55 kn.

questions.q: How do you set the boat up for the leg?

figure.title: GRIB, 0.25°, 3-hourly
lines: Crew: 4, two on their first passage

options: Full sail, and reef if the GRIB tops 22
Reef for gusts of about 25 kn
One reef at 1500, when the GRIB says 18
Full sail — 18 kn is only force 5
questions.why: A GRIB gives a model's mean wind, without gusts or local effects: 18 kn + 40 % = 25 kn in the gusts — reef for that.

questions.q: What do you expect inside the strait?

figure.title: GRIB for the afternoon
lines: Your route: a strait 1 M wide

options: NW 12 kn, but backing W by evening
NW 12 kn — the model covers the strait
More wind, along the strait — the grid misses it
Less wind — the islands shelter the strait
questions.why: A 15-mile grid cannot see a 1-mile strait: funnelling between high islands is smoothed out of the GRIB.

questions.q: When does the front reach you, and what changes then?

figure.title: Synoptic chart, 1200 UTC
lines: Cold front 120 M W of you
You: SW 6 in the warm sector

options: About 1600 — a veer to NW, squalls
About 1800 — a back to SE and fog
About 2400 — a veer to NW, squalls
About 1800 — a veer to NW, squalls
questions.why: 120 M at 20 kn = 6 h: about 1800 UTC. A cold front brings squalls and a sharp veer from SW to NW.

questions.q: You can leave at 0600. Do you go?

figure.title: Forecast issued 0500
lines: Your leg: 50 M at about 6 kn

options: Go — in by about 1420, the refuge as plan B
Go — “later” means not until tomorrow
Stay — “later” means within 6 hours
Go at 1000 — in before the wind rises
questions.why: 50 M at 6 kn = 8 h 20 min: in by 1420. “Later” is over 12 h after issue — after 1700 — and force 6 is within this crew.

questions.q: What do you do?

figure.title: Night passage, 0300
lines: Refuge: 9 M on a reach, lit entrance

options: Press on, logging the barometer hourly
Bear away for the refuge and reef now
Press on — the forecast gave 6 only later
Heave to and wait for the 0600 forecast
questions.why: 5 hPa in 3 hours is ahead of the forecast: the wind is coming sooner and harder. Take the short, lit refuge off the wind.

questions.q: You are in the Cyclades in late July and must make a 30-mile leg due north tomorrow. When do you leave?

figure.title: Cyclades, late July
lines: Builds to N 7 from about noon
Your leg: 30 M due N, 5 kn into it

options: At 1500 — after the midday peak has passed
At 1900 — in by 0100, as it eases off
At 0500 — in by about 1100, ahead of the worst
At 1100 — once it has settled in for the day
questions.why: The Meltemi builds from late morning to an afternoon peak: 30 M at 5 kn = 6 h, so leave at 0500 and be in by 1100.

questions.q: You are in Senj in February, planning to cross 15 miles south-west to Rab today, and your crew points out that a NE wind is fair. What do you decide?

figure.title: Senj, February, 0700
lines: Cloud cap sitting on the Velebit ridge
Plan: 15 M SW across to Rab

options: Go now — get across before it sets in
Go — NE 3 is light and fair for Rab
Go, close under the mainland for shelter
Stay — the Bora can hit within the hour
questions.why: A cap on the Velebit, a rising glass and cold air herald the Bora: its gusts come suddenly and are worst under the mountains.

questions.q: You are in Kvarner, and the coastal forecast gives the Bora gusts in km/h. What do they mean in knots and on the Beaufort scale?

figure.title: Coastal forecast, Kvarner
lines: Gusts up to 100 km/h under Velebit
Your leg: 12 M along the channel

options: About 54 kn — storm force 10
About 45 kn — severe gale 9
About 62 kn — violent storm 11
About 28 kn — near gale 7
questions.why: 100 km/h ÷ 1.852 = 54 kn: force 10 in the gusts. 62 is the figure in mph (÷ 1.609), 28 in m/s (÷ 3.6).

questions.q: You plan a 30-mile leg outside the outer Croatian islands, and either of two forecasts of the same force is possible for the day. Which raises the bigger sea out there?

figure.title: Two forecasts, same force
lines: Bora NE 7: blows off the mainland
Your leg: outside the outer islands

options: The Bora — cold air raises a steeper sea
The Jugo — its fetch runs the length of the sea
The Bora — its gusts are far stronger
Neither — the same force gives the same sea
questions.why: Sea grows with fetch and duration: the Jugo blows over hundreds of miles of open Adriatic, the Bora over a few miles off the coast.
questions.ref: Local winds — the sea they raise

questions.q: You are weatherbound in a northern Adriatic harbour after two days of Jugo. What do you prepare for next?

figure.title: Northern Adriatic, November
lines: Jugo SE 6 for two days, big SE sea
Low over Italy now moving away SE
Cloud cap forming on the mountains

options: A SW wind veering steadily into the NW
A slow fall to calm and a flat sea
A sudden NE Bora on top of the old SE sea
The Jugo building again as the low deepens
questions.why: When the low moves off SE, cold air pours over the mountains: a Jugo often ends in a sudden Bora, with the SE sea still running.

questions.q: You are bound east along this coast in a Mistral, and there are no dangers off it. Where do you meet the easiest sea?

figure.note: Mistral NW 7, off the land

options: The same everywhere — the wind is the same
C — well offshore, where the wind is steady
B — halfway out, clear of the gusts off the land
A — close inshore, where the fetch is short
questions.why: An offshore wind has little fetch near the coast: the sea is slight close in and grows the further out you go.

questions.q: A Mistral has kept you in Marseille since dawn, and your crew is sure it will be gone by tonight. How long do you plan to stay?

figure.title: Marseille, March, 1000
lines: Low deepening over the Gulf of Genoa

options: Days, not hours — until the Genoa low fills
Until tonight — a Mistral dies at sunset
A few hours — it is only a passing squall
Until tomorrow's sea breeze takes over
questions.why: A Mistral lasts as long as the Genoa low and the high behind it hold the gradient — often several days.

questions.q: You are coasting south on the Costa Blanca after two days of Levante and must choose a harbour for tonight. Which do you enter?

figure.title: Costa Blanca, November
lines: Levante E 6 for two days, still blowing
Long E swell, 2.5 m and building
A: 5 M on, entrance faces E over a bar
B: 13 M on, S-facing entrance behind mole

options: A — it is closer, and 2.5 m is only moderate
B — its entrance is sheltered from the swell
Anchor off A and wait for the swell to drop
A — run in fast on the back of a wave
questions.why: A long Levante swell breaks on a shallow, exposed entrance: go on to the harbour whose entrance is shielded from the E.

questions.q: You are at Bozcaada in August, planning to motor 30 miles north-east up the Dardanelles this morning. Do you set off?

figure.title: Bozcaada, August, 0700
lines: Forecast: Poyraz NE 6–7 for two days
Plan: 30 M NE up the Dardanelles
Boat: 6 kn under engine in flat water

options: Yes — the current sets you up the strait
Yes — the strait is sheltered from the NE
No — a head wind on top of a foul current
Yes, keeping to mid-channel in the lane
questions.why: The Dardanelles current runs out to the SW; a NE Poyraz adds to it and raises a steep sea. You would make little over the ground.

questions.q: Your route tomorrow runs through the strait between two Cycladic islands. Where do you expect the “locally 8” of this forecast?

figure.title: Greek forecast, Cyclades
lines: Sea 2.5 to 4 m in the open
Your route: the strait between two islands

options: In the open sea, far from land
Only in the hours before dawn
In the lee of the high islands
In the straits and off the capes
questions.why: The Meltemi accelerates where the land squeezes it: “locally 8” falls in the straits between islands and round the capes.

questions.q: You anchor at A for the night, in the lee of this high island, with a Meltemi blowing outside. What do you prepare for?

figure.note: Meltemi N 7; anchored at A from dusk

options: Hard gusts down the slopes — dig in, ample scope
A calm night — the island blocks the wind
The wind backing to S as the land cools
A swell wrapping round from the south side
questions.why: In a strong Meltemi the wind spills over a high island and falls down its lee slopes in violent gusts, often worst at night.
questions.ref: Local effects — lee of a high island

questions.q: You are in a river marina in October and plan to leave down the river at 0700 tomorrow. What do you expect at dawn?
options: Clear air, as a high brings fine weather
Radiation fog lying in the river valley
Sea fog rolling in from the coast
Frontal fog in steady rain
questions.why: A clear, calm autumn night cools the land and the air over it to the dew point: radiation fog fills the valleys by dawn.

questions.q: On this spring evening you are heading towards colder water, with warm moist air blowing along your route. Where do you first expect fog?

figure.note: Sea temperature at each mark

options: At A — the sea is already cooler than the air
At B — within a degree of the dew point
At C — the sea there is below the dew point
At D — the sea must be 2°C below the dew point
questions.why: Air over the sea cools to the sea temperature: fog forms where the sea is at or below the 12°C dew point — first at C, 11.5°C.

questions.q: You plan to sail out of a Galician ría at 1400 for a short coastal hop. What happens to the visibility at the mouth by then?

figure.title: Galician ría, August, 1000
lines: Ría clear and hot, light air off the land
Fog bank lying 3 M off the mouth

options: The sun burns the bank off by noon
It clears as the sea breeze freshens
The air off the land holds it out
The sea breeze carries the fog bank in
questions.why: The fog lies over the cold sea; the afternoon sea breeze blows it in towards the hot land and fills the mouth of the ría.
questions.ref: Fog — sea fog and the sea breeze

questions.q: On a night passage across the western Channel in May you log the air temperature and the dew point each hour. What do you prepare for?
options: Fog soon — radar on, fix the position, horn ready
