A calm soon — the breeze dies at dawn
Rain soon — a front is close behind
Clearer air — the spread shows it drying
questions.why: The air temperature has closed to within 1°C of the dew point: the air is near saturation and fog is close. Fix and prepare now.

questions.q: You are on passage in the Channel, and a low will pass north of you tonight, fronts and all. In which order do you expect your log entries?

figure.title: Forecast for your area, 1800
lines: Low 988 moving E, centre 150 M N of you
Warm front, then cold front tonight

options: Rain, back SE; back E; back NE, showers
Rain, veer SW; drizzle; veer NW, showers
Showers, veer NW; drizzle; back SW, rain
Fog, back SE; rain; veer SW, drizzle
questions.why: North of you, the warm front veers the wind S to SW with rain, the warm sector brings drizzle, the cold front a veer to NW and showers.

questions.q: You and a friend sailed through the same night, 60 miles apart on a north–south line. Comparing logs in the morning, where did the low centre pass?

figure.title: Same night, two boats
lines: Friend, 60 M N: SE 6 → E 6 → NE 7

options: South of both boats, moving E
North of both boats, moving E
Between the two boats, moving E
Over your boat, then turning N
questions.why: A veering wind puts the centre to your north, a backing one to your south: you veered, your friend backed — it passed between you.
questions.ref: Depressions — the track of the centre

questions.q: You are where the boat is drawn, and this low tracks east over the next 12 hours. How does your wind change?

figure.note: Low moving E, north of you

options: It veers to N, then backs through W to S
It stays about SSW and eases as it passes
It backs from about SSW through SE to E
It veers from about SSW through W to WNW
questions.why: South of a low moving E the centre goes by to your north: the wind veers, from about SSW now to W and WNW behind it.

questions.q: Your position on this morning's chart is west of the low centre. From which direction do you expect the wind?

figure.note: You: west of the centre

options: From about NNW
From about ENE
From about WSW
From about SSE
questions.why: Air turns anticlockwise round a northern low, angled in: on its west side it flows south, so the wind is about NNW.
questions.ref: Pressure systems — wind round a low

questions.q: You are planning the next two days from this chart. Which way do you expect the low centre to move?
options: SSE — across the warm-sector isobars
ENE — along the warm-sector isobars
WSW — into the warm-sector wind
N — towards the cold air
questions.why: A frontal low tends to move along the isobars of its warm sector, the way the warm-sector wind blows: here to the ENE.
questions.ref: Reading a synoptic chart — movement of a low

questions.q: You are on an overnight coastal passage, and an occluded front will cross you around midnight. What do you expect as it passes?

figure.title: Forecast, 1800
lines: Ahead of it: SE 5, barometer falling

options: Steady rain, with the wind backing all night
Clear skies at once, and no rain at all
Rain for some hours, then a veer to W and showers
A sudden calm and fog for the rest of the night
questions.why: An occlusion acts like a warm front and a cold front together: a band of rain, then a veer and brighter, showery air.

questions.q: You are on a night passage, and the log shows this since midnight. What weather do you plan for the rest of the night?

figure.title: Night log
lines: 0400 rain stopped, stars to the W

options: Steady rain, with the SW wind returning
A calm, then a slow back to the SE
Fog, as the clear air cools over the sea
Gusty NW with showers and good visibility
questions.why: A squall, a sharp veer and a jump in pressure: the cold front has passed. Behind it comes cold, gusty NW air with showers.

questions.q: You must make a 45-mile leg to the south-east some time in the next three days. Which day do you sail?

figure.title: Forecast for the next 3 days
lines: Day 1: warm sector, SW 6, poor vis
Night 1: cold front, squalls, veer NW

options: Day 2 — a fair NW 4–5 and good visibility
Day 1 — sail before the front arrives
Day 3 — once the next low has settled
Night 1 — ride the front through fast
questions.why: Behind the cold front a NW wind is on your quarter for a SE leg, in clear air; day 1 runs into the front, day 3 into the next low.
questions.ref: Reading a synoptic chart — a 48 h plan

questions.q: You are anchored off the coast and read this at midnight. Between which times could the low centre reach you?

figure.title: Synoptic chart, 0000 UTC
lines: Low 980 hPa, 400 M to the W of you
You: anchored, open to the S and W

options: Not before about 0300 UTC tomorrow
From about 1130 to 1600 UTC
From about 1600 to 0240 UTC
From about 0900 to 1130 UTC
questions.why: “Rather quickly” is 25–35 kn: 400 M takes 11.4 to 16 h, so about 1130 to 1600 UTC. 15–25 kn would be “steadily”.

questions.q: You are reading the forecast for your area before a coastal passage. What does the word “cyclonic” warn you of?
options: A steady wind from one direction all day
Light winds circling a high over you
Big, quick shifts of wind near a passing centre
A tropical storm on its way to you
questions.why: “Cyclonic” means the centre of a low passes over or close to the area: the wind changes direction a lot, and quickly.

questions.q: You hear this gale warning just before leaving on a 7-hour coastal leg. Could the gale catch you at sea?
options: No — “soon” means 12 to 24 hours ahead
No — not before 1800 UTC at the earliest
Yes — at any moment in the next hour
Yes — it could arrive from about 1200 UTC
questions.why: “Soon” is 6 to 12 hours from issue: from 1200 to 1800 UTC — well inside your time at sea.

questions.q: You measure the isobar spacing over your area on the synoptic chart. What surface wind do you plan for at sea?

figure.title: Synoptic chart, isobars every 4 hPa
lines: Surface wind at sea: about ⅔ of that
Over your area: isobars 50 M apart

options: About 32 kn — F7
About 16 kn — F4
About 48 kn — F10
About 8 kn — F3
questions.why: Half the spacing doubles the wind: 24 × 100/50 = 48 kn geostrophic; × ⅔ at the surface = 32 kn, force 7.

questions.q: Your chart's geostrophic scale is drawn for 50°N, but you are sailing at 40°N in the Mediterranean. What does the same isobar spacing give you?
options: Less — about 17 kn
More — about 24 kn
Less — about 13 kn
The same — 20 kn
questions.why: The same gradient blows harder nearer the equator: 20 × 0.77 / 0.64 = 24 kn at 40°N.

questions.q: You are writing up the log at midnight and must describe the barometer in forecast terms. Which word fits the tendency?
options: Falling very rapidly
Falling slowly
Falling quickly
Falling
questions.why: 4.5 hPa in 3 h: “slowly” is under 1.6, “falling” 1.6–3.5, “quickly” 3.6–6.0, “very rapidly” over 6.0.

questions.q: Your crew says the boat's barometer reads wrong, so its fall tonight means nothing. What do you tell them?
options: It reads 3 high, so the fall is only 2 hPa
Wait for the coastguard's next report
An aneroid that reads high is no use at all
The 5 hPa fall in 3 h is real — prepare now
questions.why: A constant error does not change the tendency: 1011 to 1006 is 5 hPa in 3 h, well past 3 — strong wind is on its way.

questions.q: You are on a night passage with 20 miles to go at about 5 knots, and you read back the barometer log at 0500. What does it tell you?
options: A slow fall — carry on, in by 0900, keep logging
A fast fall — run for shelter now
A rise — the low has already passed
No change — stop logging it until dawn
questions.why: 1.5 hPa every 3 h is “falling slowly”: the change is many hours off. 20 M at 5 kn = 4 h, in by 0900 — but keep watching.

questions.q: You are anchored at A at dusk, lying to a light breeze off the beach, as a thunderstorm comes in from the west over the sea. What do you do?

figure.note: Dusk: E 2 off the beach

options: Take everyone ashore until it has passed
Re-anchor further out before the gust arrives
Stay — the anchor is well set for the E breeze
Shorten the chain so that you swing less
questions.why: The gust front will swing you 180° towards the beach: 30 m of chain from 40 m off leaves no room. Move out now.

questions.q: You are anchored for the night and time the thunder after each flash. How far off is the storm now, and is it closing?

figure.title: Storm to the W, you at anchor

options: About 5 km, closing at about 16 kn
About 3 km, and moving away from you
About 3 km, closing at about 16 kn
About 9 km, closing at about 48 kn
questions.why: 9 s ÷ 3 = 3 km now, 15 s ÷ 3 = 5 km before: 2 km in 4 min is 30 km/h, about 16 kn towards you.

questions.q: You are anchored in a bay under high mountains on a still August day. When, and from where, do you expect trouble?
options: At noon — as the sea breeze peaks
Not today — the sky clears by 1600
At dawn — squalls from the open sea
Late afternoon — squalls off the mountains
questions.why: Daytime heating builds cumulonimbus over high ground; the storms break late in the day and their gusts pour down off the hills.

questions.q: You are alone on watch at 0200 under full sail and notice these signs to windward. What is your first move?
options: Call the skipper and reef now
Wait until lightning shows you the cloud
Hold on — the wind drops under the cloud
Bear away to outrun the cloud
questions.why: A black, starless sky to windward with cold air and lightning is a squall on its way: reef before it, not in it.

questions.q: Before a 30-mile leg along a coast of headlands, the GRIB on your tablet and the official coastal forecast disagree. Which do you plan on?
options: The GRIB — it shows the wind hour by hour
The official forecast — reef for F6–7
The average of the two — about F5
The GRIB — its numbers are more precise
questions.why: The official forecast is a forecaster's reading of several models and local effects; a raw GRIB is one model's mean wind.
questions.ref: GRIB files vs the official forecast

questions.q: You plan to leave at 0800 tomorrow on a 60-mile leg, and two weather models disagree about the cold front. How do you plan?

figure.title: Two models, the same cold front
lines: Model A: front through at 1800 tomorrow
Model B: front through at 0600 next day
Squalls and a veer to NW 7 with it
Your leg: 60 M at 6 kn from 0800

options: Go — model B gives you the whole day
Go — split them, the front comes at midnight
Wait — on model A the front meets your arrival
Go — the model with the finer grid is right
questions.why: 60 M at 6 kn = 10 h: in at 1800, just as model A brings the front. When models disagree, plan on the earlier one.

questions.q: Your crew shows you the GRIB they downloaded in port three days ago. Which forecast do you plan today's leg on?

figure.title: Chart table, 0700
lines: GRIB from 3 days ago: NW 10 kn today

options: Neither — the sky and the barometer
The GRIB — it gives one exact number
The GRIB — it was made for today
The NAVTEX — it is the newest forecast
questions.why: A forecast loses accuracy with age: a three-day-old model run is out of date. Plan on the latest official forecast.
questions.ref: GRIB files — age of the forecast

questions.q: You zoom in on the GRIB at your next waypoint and read this wind barb. What wind does it show?

figure.title: GRIB wind barb at the waypoint
lines: Shaft runs from the dot towards the SW
Two long feathers, one short feather
Feathers at the far end of the shaft

options: SW 25 kn
NE 25 kn
SW 30 kn
SW 15 kn
questions.why: A barb points into the wind, here from the SW; each long feather is 10 kn and a short one 5: 10 + 10 + 5 = 25 kn.

questions.q: You are planning an open-water leg of six hours under this forecast. What are the biggest waves you should be ready for?
options: About 9 m, now and then
About 6 m, now and then
About 4 m, now and then
About 3 m, as forecast
questions.why: The forecast height is the significant wave height; over a few hours single waves of nearly twice that will come through.

questions.q: You are working out the sea you will meet on the leg from the two parts of this forecast. About how high is the combined sea?
options: About 0.5 m
About 2.0 m
About 2.5 m
About 3.5 m
questions.why: √(2.0² + 1.5²) = √6.25 = 2.5 m. The two heights do not simply add, and the swell alone is not the whole sea.
questions.ref: Sea state — swell and wind sea

questions.q: You are running dead downwind in a 12 m catamaran, and the instrument shows the apparent wind. What does the reefing chart tell you to do?

figure.title: Catamaran, running dead downwind
lines: Boat speed 9 kn, apparent wind 14 kn
Reef chart: 1st reef at 18 kn true
A cat does not heel to warn you

options: No reef — 14 kn is under the first reef
No reef — the true wind is about 5 kn
Reef 2 now — the true wind is about 28 kn
Reef 1 now — the true wind is about 23 kn
questions.why: Dead downwind the true wind is the apparent plus boat speed: 14 + 9 = 23 kn, past the 18 kn first reef but short of 24.

questions.q: You are beating at night and must log the true wind force from the instruments. What do you write?

figure.title: Night, close-hauled
lines: Apparent wind 24 kn, 35° off the bow

options: About 19 kn — F5
About 14 kn — F4
About 24 kn — F6
About 30 kn — F7
questions.why: Take the boat's speed out of the apparent wind: along the bow 24 × 0.82 − 6 = 13.7, across 24 × 0.57 = 13.7; √ = 19 kn.
questions.ref: Beaufort — the true wind at night

questions.q: Your crew thinks a rise from 16 to 24 knots adds only half as much again to the load on the rig. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Wind rising on passage
lines: Force on the sails goes as wind²

options: About 3½ times — drop all sail
About 2¼ times — reef now
About 1½ times — no change yet
About the same — the boat heels it off
questions.why: Wind load goes with the square of the speed: (24 / 16)² = 2.25, not 1.5. Reef for it.

questions.q: Your track crosses this offshore bank, and the forecast has just been upgraded. What do you do?
options: Cross it — 6 m is plenty for a 2 m draft
Cross it fast, to be over it sooner
Route round the bank — the sea may break on it
Cross it near high water, for more depth
questions.why: Waves steepen and break where the depth falls to about their height: 3–4 m seas, and the bigger ones, will break on a 6 m bank.

questions.q: You are bound west round the Point today with a westerly force 6 blowing. At which of these times off the Point would the sea be worst?

figure.title: Off the Point, springs
lines: W-going stream: HW+1 to HW+7, max HW+4

questions.why: The W-going stream runs against a W wind, at its strongest at HW+4: 1040 + 4 h = 1440. At 0840 the stream runs with the wind.
questions.ref: Wind against tide — timing at a headland

questions.q: You will round this headland at A this afternoon, while the spring stream runs west. What sea do you expect there?

figure.note: Forecast: W 5, sea moderate

options: Short, steep and breaking — rough, not moderate
A long, low swell rolling in from the W
Flatter than forecast — the stream smooths it
Moderate, as forecast — the stream makes no odds
questions.why: A W wind over a W-going stream is wind against tide: the waves shorten and steepen, and off a headland they break.

questions.q: You plan to sail 8 miles out from this south-facing coast and back this afternoon. What wind do you expect out there?

figure.title: South-facing coast, July
lines: Gradient wind: N 3, off the land
Sea breeze expected from the S by 1300

options: A sea breeze from the N, off the land
A calm belt offshore, where the two winds meet
The N 3 all day — it stops the sea breeze
A strong S breeze — the N wind adds to it
questions.why: A light offshore gradient holds the sea breeze back; where the two meet, a few miles out, lies a belt of calm, fickle air.
questions.ref: Sea breeze — against an offshore wind

questions.q: You are coasting towards a harbour whose entrance faces south over a shallow bar. When do you plan to arrive?

figure.title: Approach, Turkish coast, August
lines: Entrance faces S, over a shallow bar
Mornings: calm or light N off the land
Sea breeze S 5 from about 1200 to 1800
Short steep sea builds on the bar

options: At dusk, while the sea is still running
Mid-afternoon, with the breeze behind you
In the morning, before the sea breeze sets in
At 1300, while the breeze is still young
questions.why: The sea breeze blows onshore through the afternoon and builds a short sea on the bar: arrive in the calm of the morning.

questions.q: You are cruising in Greek waters and want the NAVTEX weather in English. Which frequency do you select on the receiver?
options: 490 kHz
518 kHz
questions.why: 518 kHz is the international NAVTEX service, in English; 490 kHz carries the national-language broadcasts.

questions.q: You brief a crew of five at the pontoon before a night passage. Only you have used the VHF before. Who do you show how to send a DSC distress alert?

figure.title: Safety briefing
lines: Only the skipper has used the VHF

options: Every crew member — the skipper may be the casualty
Nobody — the skipper makes every distress call
Only those who hold a radio licence
Only the mate — one operator besides you is enough
questions.why: The skipper can be the one overboard or injured; everyone aboard must be able to raise the alarm.

questions.q: It is 0200, the wind is F5 and you come up to take your watch. The jackstays run from the bow to the cockpit. When do you clip on?
options: Only when you need to go forward of the mast
To a strong point by the hatch, before you leave the cabin
As soon as you can reach the jackstay on deck
Once you are seated in the cockpit at the helm
questions.why: Clip on before you go out — falls happen stepping into the cockpit; then move the hook to the jackstay.

questions.q: The day before a 50-mile passage you go through this check list. What does it tell you about the liferaft?

figure.title: Pre-passage check
lines: Service interval on the label: 3 years

options: Fine — a raft is rated for its crew plus two more
Fine — only the flares carry a date to watch
Too small for six and overdue — change it before sailing
Overdue, but a 4-person raft can still take six
questions.why: A raft must hold everyone aboard and be in date: serviced 2022 + 3 years = due 2025.

questions.q: You are dismasted at night 6 M off the coast. The lifeboat searching for you is now about a mile away. Which flare do you use?
options: An orange smoke canister, thrown downwind
A red parachute rocket, fired straight up
A white handheld flare, held up high
A red handheld flare, held out downwind
questions.why: A rocket is for when nobody knows where you are; close in, a red handheld pinpoints you. Smoke is for daylight.

questions.q: You have abandoned to the liferaft with the grab bag. What do you do with the EPIRB and the SART?

figure.title: In the liferaft
lines: Grab bag: handheld VHF, flares, water

options: Keep the EPIRB on; put the SART up high on its pole
Switch the EPIRB off now; switch on the SART later
Keep both off until you see a ship or an aircraft
Keep the EPIRB on; lay the SART flat on the raft floor
questions.why: The EPIRB stays on until the MRCC says otherwise; the SART answers X-band radar, so the higher it is, the further it shows.

questions.q: A crew member's lifejacket carries an AIS MOB beacon and he also wears a PLB. If he goes over at night, which one shows him on your own plotter?
options: Neither — only the rescue centre can see them
The AIS beacon — AIS sets nearby show it at once
The PLB — the satellite sends it to your plotter
Both — each one shows on any plotter within 4 M
questions.why: An AIS MOB beacon is received by AIS sets nearby; a PLB's 406 MHz signal goes via satellite to the rescue centre.

questions.q: You are about to cross a busy area in poor visibility with a passive octahedral radar reflector. How do you hoist it?

figure.title: Radar reflector
lines: Spare flag halyard to the spreader

options: On the pushpit, wherever it does not chafe
At the masthead, with one point straight up
As high as you can, in the 'catch-rain' position
Just above the guardrail, one point straight up
questions.why: Height adds radar range; in the catch-rain position (a corner cup facing up) an octahedral gives its strongest echo.

questions.q: At 2300, 8 M off, the wheel suddenly spins free: the steering cable has parted. What do you do?

figure.title: Steering failure
lines: Emergency tiller in the aft locker

options: Keep sailing and hope she holds her course
Call MAYDAY and wait by the radio for help
Motor on at full speed for the nearest port
Heave to or stop, then fit the emergency tiller
questions.why: Slow or stop the boat first, then ship the emergency tiller on the rudder stock — it is aboard for this.

questions.q: In tonight's MOB drill a fender with a light goes over without warning. What are the first actions?

figure.note: Night drill · a fender with a light

options: Shout, throw the danbuoy, press MOB, one crew points
Call the coastguard first, then turn back
Drop all sail, then sweep with the searchlight
Start the engine, tack, then look for the light
questions.why: Shout and throw flotation at once, mark the position, and keep one person pointing — a small light is soon lost.

questions.q: In the Solent at night a crew member falls in and you press MOB at once. When you get back to the MOB waypoint there is nothing there. Where is he likely to be?

figure.note: Night · no lights seen at the waypoint

options: About 2.0 M east (090°T) of the waypoint
About 0.5 M east (090°T) of the waypoint
At the waypoint — the stream carries you both
About 0.5 M west (270°T) of the waypoint
questions.why: The waypoint is fixed to the ground; he moves with the water: 2.0 kn × 15 min = 0.5 M down-tide.

questions.q: You are beating with a full crew when someone goes over the side. Using the quick-stop, what is your first move?

figure.note: Close-hauled, F4 — a crew has just gone over

options: Reach off for ten lengths, then tack and come back
Drop the jib, then start the engine and turn
Tack at once, leaving the jib sheeted, to stop near him
Bear away onto a run and gybe after ten lengths
questions.why: The quick-stop keeps you close: tack at once with the jib backed and the boat stops and lies near the casualty.

questions.q: You are on a beam reach and choose the reach-turn-reach method for a man overboard. On what point of sail do you make the final approach?

figure.note: Beam reach — reach-turn-reach

options: A broad reach, so the boat keeps up her speed
Close-hauled, so you can point straight at him
A run, so you come down on him from upwind
A close reach, so the sails can be let fly to stop
questions.why: On a close reach you can spill the sails to stop and sheet in to go — speed stays under control to the pick-up.

questions.q: You motor back to a man overboard, heading into the wind. He is now two boat lengths off the bow. What do you do with the engine?

figure.note: Under power, heading into the wind

options: Neutral, so the propeller is stopped as he comes by
Astern hard to stop the boat right beside him
Ahead with more revs to hold the bow to the wind
Ahead slow until he is level with the cockpit
questions.why: A turning propeller is the main danger to a swimmer; be in neutral as he comes alongside.

questions.q: Your man overboard is alongside, held by a line. How do you get him back aboard?

figure.title: Casualty alongside
lines: Freeboard 1.2 m; swim ladder at the stern

options: Haul him over the rail by his lifejacket
Lift him level, with two strops on a halyard and a winch
Lift him upright by one strop under his arms
Guide him to the stern ladder and let him climb up
questions.why: After long immersion a vertical lift risks collapse, so lift level; an exhausted swimmer can't climb, and the stern pitches.

questions.q: A crew member falls into the sea at 12°C. What is the greatest danger to him in the first minute?
options: Hypothermia setting in within that minute
The lifejacket slipping off as it inflates
Gasping and breathing in water from cold shock
Cramp in his legs that stops him swimming
questions.why: Cold-water shock brings a gasp and fast breathing for about a minute; a lifejacket with a sprayhood keeps the airway clear.

questions.q: You have recovered your man overboard and got him below. What do you do for him?

figure.title: Casualty below
lines: Recovered after 25 min in the water

options: Walk him round the cockpit to warm him up
A tot of brandy and a brisk rub of his limbs
A hot shower at once to warm him quickly
Dry clothes, wrap him up warmly, warm sweet drinks
questions.why: Warm gently: shelter, remove wet clothes, insulate; warm sweet drinks only if fully conscious. No alcohol, no rubbing.

questions.q: At 0300 your crew loses sight of the man overboard's light. When do you raise the alarm?

figure.title: 0300, man overboard
lines: Crew has lost sight of his light
Wind F5, seas 1.5 m, 10 M off

options: Now: a DSC distress alert, then MAYDAY on 16
After 30 minutes of searching on your own
At first light, when searchers can see him
Once your own search pattern is complete
questions.why: A person in the water at night is in grave and imminent danger: alert at once so ships and SAR can join the search.

questions.q: At anchor, a pan of oil catches fire on the stove. What do you do?

figure.title: Galley fire
lines: Pan of oil alight on the stove

options: Carry the pan up and throw it over the side
Smother the pan with the fire blanket and turn the gas off
Blast it with dry powder from close range
Throw a jug of water on it to cool the oil
questions.why: Starve it of air: lay the blanket over the pan, gas off, leave it covered; water makes burning oil erupt.

questions.q: Smoke pours from the engine box while you are motoring, and the panel shows this. What do you do?
options: Open the engine box to find the fire, then spray it
Pour buckets of seawater into the engine box
Stop the engine and fuel, then discharge through the fire port
Keep motoring for the harbour 2 M away
questions.why: Shut off fuel and air; opening the box feeds the fire — use the fire port or the fixed system, box closed.

questions.q: Acrid smoke is coming from behind the switch panel. What do you do first?

figure.title: Smoke at the panel
lines: Acrid smoke behind the switch panel
Aboard: CO2, dry powder, foam, blanket

options: Water from the galley tap onto the panel
Pull the wires out by hand to stop the short
Foam into the panel, then the batteries off
Battery switches off, then CO2 into the panel
questions.why: Kill the power at the battery isolators, then use CO2 or powder; never water or foam on live electrics.

questions.q: Your fire is now out of control. What do you do?

figure.title: Fire out of control
lines: Wind S F4; 6 M off the coast

options: DSC alert and MAYDAY, launch the raft to windward on its painter
Open up the cabin to clear the smoke, then fight on
Launch the raft to leeward and cut it free at once
DSC alert and MAYDAY, launch the raft to leeward on its painter
questions.why: Call while you can; launch upwind of the fire so smoke and flames blow away from the raft, and keep it on its painter.

questions.q: You go below in the morning and smell gas in the saloon. What do you do first?

figure.title: Below at 0700
lines: Smell of gas in the saloon

options: Start the engine so the blower clears the cabin
Shut it off at the cylinder; no switches, ventilate
Switch the cabin fan on to blow the gas out
Run the electric bilge pump to clear the bilge
questions.why: LPG sinks into the bilge and a spark ignites it: shut the cylinder, no electrics, open up, pump with the hand pump.

questions.q: The bilge alarm wakes you at 0400 and you find this. What do you do first?

figure.title: Water over the floorboards
lines: Water 10 cm over the cabin sole

options: Prepare the liferaft and grab bag on deck
Call MAYDAY at once, then look for the leak
Pump and find the source — taste, seacocks, hoses
Bail with buckets until the water is out
questions.why: Pump while you hunt: salt or fresh tells you a lot; check seacocks, hose clips, the stern gland and transducers.

questions.q: The heads' inlet seacock has sheared off and water is spurting in. What do you do?

figure.title: Leak in the heads
lines: Softwood bung tied to the fitting

options: Stuff a towel in the hole and hold it there
Close the seacock handle as tight as it goes
Tape over the hole from inside the hull
Hammer the bung tied to the fitting into the hole
questions.why: With the valve gone, only the tapered softwood bung will seal it — keep one tied beside every through-hull.

questions.q: You are taking water through a damaged fitting you cannot reach. Can your pumps keep up with it?

figure.title: Leak below
lines: Manual pump: 0.6 L a stroke, 45 a min

options: Yes — both pumps together gain 17 L/min
Yes — the electric pump alone gains 10 L/min
No — together they still lose 13 L/min
No — each pump alone loses, so abandon
questions.why: Manual: 0.6 × 45 = 27 L/min; with the electric 30 that is 57 L/min against 40 in — 17 L/min in hand.

questions.q: It is 1630 and this is the state of things. What do you do now?

figure.title: Flooding
lines: 8 M off, wind F5, dark in 2 h

options: Call PAN-PAN and ask for a pump to be dropped
DSC alert and MAYDAY, raft ready, keep pumping aboard
Abandon to the raft at once while it is still light
Keep looking for the leak before making any call
questions.why: Water you cannot stop is grave and imminent danger: call now, but stay with the yacht until you step up into the raft.

questions.q: You must abandon ship and the raft is in its valise on deck. How do you launch and board it?

figure.title: Abandon ship
lines: Raft in a valise on deck

options: Inflate it on the deck, then slide it over the rail
Raft over to windward first, then make the painter fast
Painter fast, raft over to leeward, pull to inflate, step in dry
Painter fast, raft over, then jump into the sea to board
questions.why: Tie the painter first or the raft is lost; launch to leeward, pull the painter to fire it, and step in from the deck.

questions.q: You have sent the DSC distress alert and now make the voice call. After your identity, what comes next, in order?
options: Persons aboard, position, help needed, nature of distress
Help needed, position, persons aboard, nature of distress
Nature of distress, persons aboard, position, help needed
Position, nature of distress, help needed, persons aboard
questions.why: Position first, so help can start even if the call breaks off; then what is wrong, what you need, how many aboard.

questions.q: Your yacht is flooding fast and you need to send a distress alert now. What do you do?
options: Send the alert, then the MAYDAY with your position on 16
Key in the position, then call MAYDAY on channel 13
Reconnect the GPS first, then send the DSC alert
Send the MAYDAY with your position by voice on 70
questions.why: Don't delay: the alert raises the alarm without a position; ch 70 is for DSC data only — voice and position go on 16.

questions.q: On watch you see this. There is no traffic about it on channel 16. What do you do?

figure.note: 0130 · bearing 040°M, about 5 M

options: Send a DSC distress alert with your own MMSI
Note the bearing and time, then MAYDAY RELAY on 16
Note it in the log and carry on your course
Call the vessel that fired it on 16 and wait
questions.why: You may be the only one who saw it: relay it with bearing and time; a DSC alert of your own would say you are in distress.

questions.q: Your yacht has only a fixed VHF DSC set. Where can you count on a coast station receiving your DSC alert?

figure.title: GMDSS sea areas
lines: A1: in range of a VHF DSC coast station
A2: in range of an MF DSC coast station
Your passage: up to 40 M offshore

options: Only within sight of the coast station's mast
In area A2 — out to about 150 M from the coast
In area A1 — about 20–30 M from a VHF coast station
Anywhere, as the alert is relayed by satellite
questions.why: VHF reaches a coast station only in sea area A1, typically 20–30 M; beyond it you rely on ships, MF or an EPIRB.

questions.q: The rescue helicopter lowers its hi-line to your deck. What do you do with it?

figure.title: Helicopter rescue
lines: Winchman will come down on a hi-line
Weighted line lowered to the deck
Crew of 4 on deck, clipped on

options: Grab it at once and make it fast to a cleat
Tie it to the guardrail and stand well clear
Take a turn round a winch to hold it steady
Let it earth in the sea; hold it by hand, never tie it
questions.why: Let it touch the water to discharge static; gather it in by hand — never make it fast, the aircraft may have to pull away.

questions.q: A helicopter is coming to lift off your injured crew. How do you prepare the yacht?

figure.title: Helicopter ETA 10 min
lines: Pilot will call you on VHF 16
Bimini up, dinghy on the foredeck

options: Stow the bimini and loose gear; keep listening on 16
Fire a red rocket as it makes its approach
Drop all sail and lie beam-on to the wind
Light an orange smoke now and keep it burning
questions.why: The downwash blows away anything loose; the pilot briefs you on 16 — course, speed and where the crew should be.

questions.q: A lifeboat is about to pass you a towline. How do you make it fast?

figure.title: Lifeboat tow
lines: Engine failure, 3 M off a lee shore
Bow cleats small; bow roller strong

options: To the stern cleats, so the bow stays free
To a bridle round strong points, led over the bow roller
To one bow cleat, with a turn for quick release
Round the forestay, held there by a crew member
questions.why: Share the load over strong points with a bridle, lead it fair through the bow roller and protect it from chafe.

questions.q: You have 25 M to go, close-reaching under full sail with a furling genoa, and this forecast comes in. What do you do now?

figure.note: Forecast: SW 6, gale 8 later

options: Roll the genoa to a scrap and leave it at that
Wait for the gale, then reef everything at once
Reef now and rig the storm jib while it is still easy
Keep full sail to get in before the gale arrives
questions.why: Reef and rig the storm jib early, in daylight and moderate wind; a deeply rolled genoa sets badly and can unroll.

questions.q: You tack without releasing the jib to heave to and rest the crew. Where do you put the tiller and the main?

figure.note: Hove to: the jib backed after the tack

options: Tiller amidships, main and jib both backed
Tiller lashed to leeward, main sheeted hard
Tiller lashed to windward, main sheeted hard
Tiller lashed to leeward, mainsheet eased
questions.why: The backed jib pushes the bow off and the rudder turns it up (tiller to leeward); ease the main so she lies quietly.

questions.q: You are running off before a gale, surfing on the crests, with this sea room to leeward. How do you make it last?

figure.note: Not to scale

options: Stream a drogue: the 21 M then last about 8 h 24 min
Lie beam-on to the seas, so you use no sea room
Stream a drogue: the 21 M then last about 4 h 40 min
Keep running: 21 M last 3 h, and that will do
questions.why: 21 M ÷ 7 kn = 3 h, short of the 6 h; with a drogue 21 ÷ 2.5 = 8.4 h = 8 h 24 min, stern kept to the seas.

questions.q: You are on a coastal passage with the coast to the east of you when this comes in. What do you do?

figure.title: Gale warning
lines: Only harbour: bar breaks in W 6 or more

options: Carry on along the coast as planned, 4 M off
Head out to sea now, to gain sea room before the gale
Run for the harbour and cross its bar before dark
Anchor close under the coast and wait it out
questions.why: A coast to leeward in a gale is the danger, and a bar breaks in an onshore blow — get sea room while you still can.

questions.q: One of your crew has been seasick since yesterday afternoon. What do you do?
options: Give her a big glass of water and a full meal
Leave her in her bunk below until she recovers
Small sips of rehydration fluid, and get medical advice
Put her on the helm to take her mind off it
questions.why: Long vomiting dehydrates: small, frequent sips of rehydration salts, keep her warm, and get radio medical advice.

questions.q: It is 2300 on passage in the Ionian and this is your situation. What is the safe decision?
options: Heave to offshore until all the crew recover
Press on, with the skipper on coffee at the helm
Press on: the port has fuel, shops and showers
Anchor in the sheltered bay, rest, and enter at daylight
questions.why: Fatigue and seasickness cut judgement and hands; an unlit rocky entrance at night is the risk to avoid.

questions.q: A fishing boat has just struck your port bow and backed off. What do you do first?

figure.note: Just hit on the port bow

options: Check the crew for injuries, then the hull for damage
Call MAYDAY at once, before anything else
Get the other boat's name and details first
Chase the fishing boat to keep it in sight
questions.why: People first, then the boat: a headcount and injuries, then look for water coming in — that decides which call to make.

questions.q: You have run onto a rock and this is what you find. What do you do?

figure.title: Aground on a rock
lines: Struck at 5 kn, 2 h before HW
Hole in the bow, water entering

options: Motor astern at once to get her off the rock
Stem the leak and call for help before she floats
Lay out the kedge and haul her off now
Wait for high water to lift her, then inspect
questions.why: On the rock the leak is limited; afloat she may flood faster than you can pump. Stem it and call before she lifts.

questions.q: Your engine dies halfway across the north-east-going lane of a traffic separation scheme, as the chart shows. What do you do?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme

options: Work on the engine and call only if the ship is close
Anchor in the lane until the engine is fixed
Call PAN-PAN and tell the VTS and the ship where you are
Call MAYDAY and launch the raft as a precaution
questions.why: Unable to keep clear in a shipping lane is urgency, not distress: a PAN-PAN tells ships and the VTS so they can act.

questions.q: Your engine stops off a rocky lee shore with the sails still in their covers. How long have you got, and what do you do first?

figure.note: Depths in metres

options: About 3 min: abandon to the raft at once
About 33 min: call PAN-PAN, then try the engine
About 20 min: work on the engine, then decide
About 20 min: anchor now, then call PAN-PAN
questions.why: 4 cables = 0.4 M; 0.4 ÷ 1.2 kn = 0.33 h = 20 min. In 12 m with 50 m of chain, anchor first to stop the drift.

questions.q: You have pulled a swimmer out after several minutes under water. What do you do?
options: Open the airway, give five rescue breaths, then CPR
Roll him on his front to drain out the water
Recovery position, then wait for help to come
Chest compressions only, with no breaths at all
questions.why: A drowned casualty is short of oxygen: five rescue breaths first, then 30 compressions to 2 breaths — and the MAYDAY.

questions.q: A crew member has been hit on the head by the boom in a gybe. What do you do?

figure.title: Hit by the boom
lines: Knocked out for about a minute

options: Give him painkillers and carry on the passage
Call PAN-PAN for medical advice and watch him closely
Let him sleep it off alone in his bunk
Wait until you are in port to have him seen
questions.why: Knocked out, then confused and vomiting: signs of a serious head injury — urgency call for radio medical advice.

questions.q: A crew member falls into the cockpit and hurts her forearm. You open the first-aid kit. What do you do?
options: Rub it well, then bandage it on tightly
Leave it free so that she can still work
Splint it as you find it, sling it, check her fingers
Pull the arm straight first, then splint it
questions.why: Support the limb as you find it — never straighten it; splint and sling, then check circulation beyond the injury.

questions.q: A pot of boiling water slides off the stove onto a crew member's forearm. What do you do?
options: Burst the blisters, then dry the skin
Hold ice on it for about a minute
Cover it with butter or a greasy cream
Cool it under cool clean water for 20 minutes
questions.why: Cool with clean cool water for 20 min, then cover loosely with cling film; no creams, no ice, leave blisters intact.

questions.q: Your mast has just been struck by lightning and the crew are all unhurt. What do you check next?
options: The hull and through-hulls for leaks
The compass deviation on each heading
The VHF and plotter for damage
The masthead lights and wind gear
questions.why: A strike can blow out a through-hull or the hull near the keel; check the bilge first — electronics and compass after.

questions.q: You pass this in the approach to a busy harbour. What call do you make?

figure.title: Hazard sighted
lines: 3 M south of the harbour entrance

options: MAYDAY, as it is a danger to all
SÉCURITÉ, to warn other vessels
PAN-PAN, as your own boat is at risk
No call — a note in the log will do
questions.why: A hazard to navigation is a safety message: SÉCURITÉ, giving what it is and where.

questions.q: A crew member has slipped off the stern at anchor in a calm bay, water 24°C. She is fit and swimming to the stern swim ladder. The engine is ticking over in neutral. What do you do?

figure.title: Calm anchorage, 1100
lines: Crew fell off the stern 2 min ago
Water 24°C, she is fit and swimming

options: Go slow ahead so the boat holds her head
Go slow astern to close the gap to her
Stop the engine before she reaches the ladder
Leave it in neutral, ready to manoeuvre
questions.why: The propeller turns a few feet under the swim ladder; neutral can be knocked into gear — engine off before a swimmer comes near.

questions.q: You skipper a 12 m catamaran and motor back to a man overboard on both engines. Where do you bring him to get him aboard?
options: To the bows, in the gap between the hulls
Between the hulls, under the bridgedeck
Amidships, over the side-deck guardrail
To the stern steps of one hull, that engine stopped
questions.why: The low transom steps are the easiest way up; between the hulls the bridgedeck can slam down on him — and stop the prop by him.

questions.q: In the debrief of tonight's MOB drill you read this. What do you change for the next one?

figure.title: Drill debrief, 2240
lines: Fender with a light thrown at 2210
Pointer helped to roll the genoa

options: The pointer only points, and does nothing else
The helm takes over pointing as well as steering
Nobody points; the plotter's MOB mark is enough
The pointer also helps to roll the genoa away
questions.why: A small light at night is lost in seconds: one crew keeps eyes and arm on the casualty and is given no other job.

questions.q: In the drill debrief you look at the times. How far along your track from where the fender went in did the MOB waypoint go?
options: About 1.8 M: press MOB the moment he goes
About 0.3 M: press MOB the moment he goes
None: the plotter marks the moment he fell
About 0.18 M: press MOB the moment he goes
questions.why: Three minutes at 6.0 kn: 6.0 × 3/60 = 0.3 M — the waypoint marks where you pressed, not where he fell.

questions.q: Under sail a crew has gone over and you are about to start the engine to go back. What do you check first?

figure.title: MOB under sail
lines: Genoa sheet washed over the side

options: That the plotter's MOB mark is on the screen
That the fuel tank has enough for an hour
That no sheets or lines are trailing in the water
That the engine's oil level is up to the mark
questions.why: A rope round the propeller leaves you without an engine just when you need it — look over the side before you engage gear.

questions.q: You are running under spinnaker in F4 when a crew member goes over the side. After shouting and the danbuoy, what is your plan?

figure.note: Running under spinnaker, F4 — a crew has gone over

options: Gybe at once with the spinnaker set, and head back
Keep running until the spinnaker is packed below
Round up hard with the spinnaker still drawing
Press MOB, get the spinnaker down, then turn back
questions.why: You cannot come back upwind under a spinnaker; drop it at once (a pointer on him all the time), then return under main or engine.

questions.q: Your man overboard is alongside on a line, exhausted and too heavy to lift by hand. You have no lifting strop. How do you get him aboard level?

figure.title: Casualty alongside
lines: 20 min in water at 14°C, very tired
Too heavy to lift by hand

options: Roll him up in a sail on a halyard: a parbuckle
Two crew haul him up the topsides by his arms
Wait until he recovers and climbs the ladder
A bowline round his chest, winched up upright
questions.why: A sail with its foot made fast on deck and a halyard on the other edge rolls him up horizontally — no vertical lift after immersion.

questions.q: At night you find your danbuoy with its light, but there is no sign of the man it was thrown to. Where do you search first?

figure.note: Night · thrown beside him 20 min ago · wind W F5

options: At B, downwind of the danbuoy
At A, upwind of the danbuoy
At C, across the wind to the north
At D, across the wind to the south
questions.why: Both drift with the stream, but the tall danbuoy blows downwind faster than a swimmer: he is likely to windward of it.

questions.q: Tidying the chart table, a crew member presses the DSC distress button and the alert goes out. Nothing is wrong. What do you do?

figure.title: False alert
lines: DSC distress alert sent by mistake

options: Wait for the MRCC to call you, then explain
Send a second alert marked 'test' on channel 70
Cancel it on the set, then tell all stations on 16
Switch the set off and make no further call
questions.why: Stop the alert, then a voice call on 16: ALL STATIONS, your name, call sign and MMSI, cancel my distress alert of (time UTC).

questions.q: You are about to call the marina on channel 16 when you hear this. What do you do?

figure.title: Channel 16, 1120
lines: A MAYDAY is being worked by the MRCC

options: Switch off the VHF until the coastguard is done
Make the marina call — a short one is allowed
Reply 'SEELONCE MAYDAY' to show you heard
Keep off 16 unless you can help with the distress
questions.why: SEELONCE MAYDAY imposes silence on the channel for the distress; keep listening in case you can help.

questions.q: An hour later, after the distress you heard, the MRCC sends this on 16. What does it mean?
options: The distress is over; 16 is back to normal use
Silence on 16 for one more hour from now
Restricted working: urgent calls only on 16
The casualty is still missing; keep silent
questions.why: SEELONCE FEENEE ends distress traffic; PRUDONCE would mean restricted working may resume while the distress continues.

questions.q: Your DSC set sounds this alarm. No coast station has answered on 16 after a few minutes. What do you do?
options: Acknowledge at once by DSC from your own set
Listen on 16; with no coast station, acknowledge by voice
Leave it — the coast station will deal with it
Relay it at once by DSC to all ships
questions.why: A yacht does not acknowledge a distress alert by DSC: listen on 16, and if no coast station answers, acknowledge by voice and tell the MRCC.

questions.q: You plan this crossing with a fixed VHF DSC set and a 406 MHz EPIRB. How much of it lies outside sea area A1, and what alerts the MRCC there?

figure.title: Crossing plan
lines: Each coast: VHF DSC station, A1 ≈ 25 M

options: The middle 20 M; nothing can raise the MRCC there
The middle 45 M; the EPIRB still raises the MRCC
The middle 20 M; the EPIRB still raises the MRCC
None of it; A1 covers 60 M off any coast
questions.why: 70 − 2 × 25 = 20 M out of reach of a coast station by VHF; the EPIRB works by satellite anywhere, and ships nearby still hear your DSC.

questions.q: You are dismasted and rig your spare VHF aerial. Can you still reach the coast station?

figure.title: Dismasted
lines: Spare aerial on the pushpit: 4 m

options: Yes — still about 29 M, as from the masthead
Yes — about 40 M now, with plenty in hand
No — about 4 M now: only for ships alongside
No — about 24 M now: call ships nearby
questions.why: 2.2 × (√4 + √81) = 2.2 × 11 = 24.2 M, short of 26 M; from the 16 m masthead it was 2.2 × 13 = 28.6 M.

questions.q: Your GPS has failed and you fix by this light. In the MAYDAY you give your position from it. What do you say?

figure.note: Hand-bearing compass, no deviation

options: 220°T from the light, 4.0 M
223°T from the light, 4.0 M
226°T from the light, 4.0 M
040°T from the light, 4.0 M
questions.why: 043°M − 3°W = 040°T to the light, so you lie on the reciprocal from it: 040 + 180 = 220°T, 4.0 M.

questions.q: Ten minutes ago you sent a PAN-PAN. Now this is your situation. What do you do?

figure.note: 0200 · at anchor · not to scale

options: Keep the PAN-PAN: about 2 h to the rocks
MAYDAY now: about 30 min to the rocks
Keep the PAN-PAN: about 50 min to the rocks
MAYDAY now: about 5 min to the rocks
questions.why: 0.3 M ÷ 0.6 kn = 0.5 h = 30 min; a crewed yacht about to go on rocks at night is grave and imminent danger.

questions.q: You are searching for a liferaft and your radar shows this. Where is the raft?

figure.title: Radar, 12 M range
lines: No other echo on that bearing

options: At the dot just beyond the nearest
In the middle of the line of dots
Near the dot nearest to you, on 300°
At the far end of the line of dots
questions.why: A SART answers your radar with 12 dots running outward; the one nearest to you marks it. Close in, the dots become arcs, then rings.

questions.q: Your crew has been in the water for a few minutes and has switched on his PLB. How should he hold it?
options: Flat on his chest under the lifejacket
Floating beside him on its lanyard
Inside his lifejacket, where it stays dry
Out of the water, aerial up, held as high as he can
questions.why: A PLB's 406 MHz and GNSS antennas need open sky: aerial vertical, clear of the water and of his body.

questions.q: Your yacht has the AIS fitted as on this card. Crossing a shipping lane at night, can the ships see you on their AIS?
options: No — a receiver sends nothing; only a transponder is seen
Yes — but only within about 2 M of the ship
Yes — any AIS set shows on the ships' screens
Only if the VHF is switched to channel 16
questions.why: A receive-only AIS shows you the ships; to appear on theirs you need a Class B (or A) transponder.

questions.q: At night a red parachute rocket is needed and the cloud is low. How do you fire it?
options: Straight up, as for a clear night sky
At about 45°, downwind, so it burns under the cloud
Two at once, straight up, to be sure
Into the wind, so it drifts back over you
questions.why: A rocket climbs about 300 m; in low cloud angle it 45° downwind (it turns into the wind) so the flare hangs below the cloud base.

questions.q: You are becalmed with no engine at night. This ship is closing and does not answer on 16. Which flare do you use?

figure.note: 0230 · bearing steady, about 1 M · no engine, no wind

options: A red handheld flare, held over the bow
An orange smoke, as her radar can see it
A white handheld flare, to show you are there
A red parachute rocket, to make her stop
questions.why: A white flare warns of collision; red flares mean distress and would start a rescue you do not need.

questions.q: At the pre-season check one crew's lifejacket shows this. What do you do?

figure.title: Lifejacket check
lines: Gas cylinder: loose in its thread

options: Blow it up by mouth before each watch instead
Nothing — a red indicator shows it is armed
Tighten the cylinder by hand and wear it
Re-arm it with a new cylinder and cap before use
questions.why: Red (or a missing clip) means fired or not armed; fit a new rearming kit and screw the cylinder home.

questions.q: Your liferaft sits in a deck cradle like this. If the yacht sinks before anyone can launch it, what happens?

figure.title: Liferaft stowage
lines: Painter tied to the HRU weak link

options: The release frees it, it floats up and inflates
It inflates in its cradle and stays there
Nothing — it can only be launched by hand
It goes down with her, held by the painter
questions.why: At a few metres' depth the hydrostatic release lets go; the painter pulls to fire the gas, then the weak link breaks.

questions.q: All four of you are in the raft beside your sinking yacht. What do you do now?

figure.title: In the raft
lines: Yacht low in the water, sinking
Wind W F5, coast 20 M east

options: Get clear, close up, and drift with no drogue
Cut the painter, get clear, stream the drogue
Stay tied on to her until she goes under
Cut free and paddle hard for the coast
questions.why: A sinking hull can pull the raft down or hole it; once clear, the drogue steadies the raft and keeps it near the alert position.

questions.q: Your liferaft has inflated upside down beside you in the water. How do you right it?

figure.title: Raft capsized
lines: Crew in the water, lifejackets on

options: Board it as it is and wait for it to flip
Swim under it and push the floor up from below
Climb onto the gas bottle side and pull the righting strap
Cut a hole in the floor to let the air out
questions.why: Stand on the cylinder, hold the righting strap and lean back; the raft comes over towards you — then swim clear from under it.

questions.q: You will step into the raft in two minutes. The grab bag is packed as listed. What else do you take?

figure.title: Grab bag
lines: EPIRB still in its bracket below

options: The plotter, unscrewed from the chart table
Tins of food from the galley lockers
The ship's papers, passports and cash
Extra water, warm clothes and the EPIRB
questions.why: Water and warmth keep you alive; the EPIRB brings the rescue. Papers can be replaced; food matters far less than water.

questions.q: Your crew want to take to the liferaft. This is the state of things. What do you decide?
options: Stay aboard — the yacht is a far safer raft
Take to the raft now, while it is light
Put two crew in the raft, tied on astern
Take to the raft once the MRCC agrees
questions.why: Step up into the raft only when the yacht is sinking or on fire; a sound, dry hull is bigger, warmer and easier to find.

questions.q: A cushion in the saloon is smouldering where a candle fell on it. Which extinguisher do you use?

figure.title: Smouldering cushion
lines: Candle fell on a saloon cushion
Aboard: dry powder, CO2, foam, bucket

options: Dry powder, then leave it to cool by itself
Foam or water — they cool it so it will not flare again
None — throw it into the cockpit as it is
CO2 — it leaves no mess on the upholstery
questions.why: A class A fire (solids) is put out by cooling: water or foam; powder and CO2 knock it down but it can reignite.

questions.q: You are fitting out a yacht for a season of coastal passages. Where do you mount the fire extinguishers?

figure.title: Fitting out
lines: Galley aft, engine under the steps

options: Over the stove, where most fires start
In a cockpit locker, away from the heat
By each exit, so the way out is behind you
All together in the engine bay, by the risk
questions.why: Fight a fire with your escape behind you: one by the companionway, one by the forehatch, the blanket by the galley.

questions.q: You are fitting a gas alarm in a yacht with an LPG cooker. Where do you put its sensor?

figure.title: Gas alarm
lines: Bottle in a deck locker, drained overboard

options: At head height by the companionway steps
In the gas locker on deck, by the bottle
High up over the cooker, at the deckhead
Low down near the cooker, just above the bilge
questions.why: LPG is heavier than air and collects low, so the sensor goes below the cooker, under floor level, clear of bilge water.

questions.q: You have fitted a new gas regulator and want to check the joints for leaks. How?

figure.title: New regulator
lines: Hose and joints to the cooker

options: Soapy water on each joint, with the bottle on
Sniff each joint with the bottle turned off
Light the cooker and watch the flame colour
A lit match held close to each joint
questions.why: Bubbles show a leak; never use a flame. Many systems also carry a bubble tester or gauge to check the whole line.

questions.q: It is a cold, wet evening at anchor and these are the symptoms below. What do you suspect and do?
options: Gas leak — run the hand bilge pump
Carbon monoxide — everyone into fresh air now
Seasickness — give them tablets and rest
Dehydration — water and an early night
questions.why: Headache, drowsiness and nausea in a closed cabin with an engine or heater running point to CO; ventilate, get out, stop the source.

questions.q: The bilge alarm goes off and you find this. Where do you look first?

figure.title: Water in the bilge
lines: Bilge water tastes fresh, not salt
Pressure pump runs on its own

options: Every seacock, closing them one by one
The stern gland, tightening it at once
The fresh-water tanks, pipes and pump
The deck fittings and mast step for rain
questions.why: Fresh water and a pump that runs by itself point to the domestic system: switch the pump off and look for the leaking pipe.

questions.q: Your two bilge pumps are losing to the leak. You close the engine's raw-water seacock and put its intake hose in the bilge, engine running. Where do you stand now?
options: Gaining about 97 L/min
Level: 70 in and 70 out
Losing about 13 L/min
Gaining about 27 L/min
questions.why: Out: 30 + 27 + 40 = 97 L/min against 70 in — 27 L/min in hand. Keep a strainer on the hose so debris does not stop the engine.

questions.q: A collision has holed your port bow just above the waterline, and water comes in on every wave. You must sail 12 M to port. How do you sail?

figure.title: Holed
lines: Hole in the port bow, just above the WL
Wind W F4; port 12 M to the north

options: On port tack, so she heels to starboard
Under engine, upright, at full speed
Dead downwind, so she sits upright
On starboard tack, so she heels to port
questions.why: Heel her so the damaged side lifts: wind on the port side heels her to starboard and lifts the port bow clear.

questions.q: You touch a sandbank and stop, with the tide falling. What do you do at once?

figure.title: Aground on sand
lines: Draught 1.9 m, depth at the bow 1.8 m

options: Wait — she will float off on the next tide
Go astern now, crew on the boom to heel her
Call MAYDAY first, then try to get off
Lay out the kedge, then wait a few hours
questions.why: On a falling tide every minute makes it worse: try at once, astern along your track, heeled to cut the draught.

questions.q: She would not come off and will dry out on this bank before the next flood. How do you let her lie?

figure.note: Bank slopes down to the east

options: Heeled to the deep side, kedge laid towards the shallows
Upright, and let her fall whichever way she goes
Heeled to the shallow side, padded, kedge out to deep water
Heeled to the deep side, so she slides off later
questions.why: Lying up the slope, her low side sits higher, so the flood lifts her before it reaches the coamings; the kedge stops her driving further on.

questions.q: The gale is at its height and the crew suggest this to get some rest. What do you say?

figure.title: Gale, 0400
lines: W gale 8–9, seas 5 m, crests breaking
Suggestion: drop all sail, lie a-hull

options: Yes — once all the crew are below, hatch shut
Yes — the keel keeps her stable beam-on
Yes — with no sail up she cannot be knocked down
No — beam-on, a breaking crest can roll her
questions.why: Lying a-hull leaves her beam-on to the seas; in breaking seas that is how yachts are rolled. Heave to or run off instead.

questions.q: You have to ride out this gale. Which tactic fits the sea room you have?

figure.title: Gale tactics
lines: Sea room to the SW: 30 M
Bare poles: 5 kn; hove to: 1.5 kn drift

options: Heave to: about 15 M of the 30 M used
Lie a-hull: she uses no sea room at all
Heave to: only about 1.5 M of drift in all
Run off: 30 M ÷ 5 kn = 6 h, so that fits
questions.why: Running: 10 h × 5 kn = 50 M, more than the 30 M; hove to: 10 h × 1.5 kn = 15 M, well inside it.

questions.q: A seasick crew member needs to be sick over the side during her night watch. Where and how?

figure.title: Night watch, 0130
lines: Lee rail low in the water

options: Alone on the foredeck, away from the others
Clipped on in the cockpit, a bucket, someone by her
Unclipped at the lee rail, so she can lean out
Down in the forepeak bunk with a bowl
questions.why: Seasick crew are weak and slow — a classic MOB at night; keep her clipped on, in the cockpit, and watched.

questions.q: A crew member who is often seasick joins you for tomorrow's 0600 start. When should he take his seasickness tablet?
options: Only after he has been sick once
Only if the forecast is F5 or more
Some hours before sailing, as the packet says
Once he first feels queasy at sea
questions.why: Tablets work to prevent seasickness, not to cure it — once vomiting starts they are not kept down.

questions.q: Your engine dies off this lee shore, but the sails are ready to hoist. How long have you got, and what do you do?

figure.note: Depth 40 m · not to scale

options: About 90 min: wait and see if she drifts clear
About 40 min: call MAYDAY and wait for help
About 67 min: work on the engine before sailing
About 40 min: set sail and claw off, then report
questions.why: 1.0 M ÷ 1.5 kn = 0.67 h = 40 min — time enough to hoist sail and beat off; tell the coastguard once you are clear.

questions.q: You take over a yacht the day before a night passage. When do you find out how her emergency tiller fits?
options: Now, by fitting it once alongside the pontoon
Only if the wheel starts to feel stiff
When the steering fails, from the manual
Never — the base fits it if it is needed
questions.why: In the dark with the boat rolling is no time to learn; fit it once in harbour and know where it lives.

questions.q: Your catamaran has capsized in a squall and floats upside down. The crew are all accounted for. What do you do?

figure.title: Capsized catamaran
lines: Inverted after a squall, floating high
Crew of 4 in the water by the hulls
Coast 3 M; EPIRB in the grab bag

options: Swim for the shore, 3 M away, together
Stay with the hull — get in through the escape hatch
Dive inside to fetch the VHF from the saloon
Launch the raft and leave her at once
questions.why: An unballasted catamaran floats when inverted: stay with it, shelter in the hull via the escape hatch, set off the EPIRB.

questions.q: This crew member is getting worse and you will call for radio medical advice. What do you have written down before you call?
options: Only your position — the doctor asks the rest
Her passport, insurance and next of kin
Pulse, breathing, temperature, history, kit list
The marina's phone number and your ETA there
questions.why: The doctor can only advise on what you report: the signs, what happened, medicines given, what is in your kit — and your position.

questions.q: You pulled this crew member out after a minute under water. Now he says he feels fine. What do you do?
options: Let him sleep it off alone in his bunk
Nothing more — he is breathing and talking
A hot drink and back to his watch
Get medical advice — trouble can follow hours later
questions.why: Water in the lungs can cause breathing problems hours afterwards: anyone who has inhaled water needs a doctor's view.

questions.q: You have recovered this man overboard. How do you handle him?
options: Keep him flat, move him gently, insulate him
Sit him up and give him a hot sweet drink
Put him in a hot shower to rewarm him fast
Rub his arms and legs to get the blood moving
questions.why: Severe hypothermia: rough handling or sitting up can stop the heart; no drinks when unconscious. Lie him flat, wrap him, get help.

questions.q: You have cooled this scald under water for 20 minutes. What next?

figure.title: Galley scald
lines: Boiling water over forearm and hand

options: A fluffy dressing taped down firmly over it
Cover it loosely with cling film; get medical advice
Burst the blisters and leave it open to the air
Burn cream on it, and carry on the passage
questions.why: A burn larger than the casualty's palm, or on the hand, needs a doctor: cling film laid on, not wrapped tight.

questions.q: The helicopter pilot tells you your mast and rigging make a deck lift unsafe. What may he ask you to do?

figure.title: Helicopter on scene
lines: Pilot: mast too close for a deck lift

options: Cut the backstay so the winchman can land
Lie beam-on and stop the engine for the lift
Put the casualty in the dinghy on a long line astern
Lower the mast before he makes his approach
questions.why: On a yacht the rig can foul the winch wire; the lift is often made from the dinghy or raft streamed well astern.

questions.q: A thunderstorm is coming towards you and you cannot avoid it. How do you prepare?
options: Hoist full sail to outrun it for the harbour
All on deck, holding the shrouds to earth themselves
Go up the mast and unplug the VHF aerial
Crew below, clear of the mast; spare handhelds in the oven
questions.why: Keep people off the rig and its chainplates; disconnect what you can, and keep a handheld VHF and GPS in the oven as a shielded spare.

questions.q: You are leaving a quay in a fresh crosswind. The stern line will be under load until the moment you let it go. Which knot do you tie to the ring?

figure.note: Leaving: you let go under load

options: Round turn and two half hitches
Clove hitch and a half hitch
Bowline through the ring
Figure of eight through the ring
questions.why: The round turn takes the load, so the half hitches can be cast off and the line eased even while it is loaded.

questions.q: You come alongside a fishing quay with bollards. Your crew steps ashore with the bow line and wants a fixed loop in its end to drop over a bollard. Which knot?
options: Reef knot
Bowline
Rolling hitch
Clove hitch
questions.why: A bowline makes a fixed loop that will not slip or jam, and unties easily once the load is off.

questions.q: Hours into a long starboard tack, the genoa sheet has a riding turn on the winch and will not ease. What do you do?

figure.note: Riding turn: the sheet is jammed on the drum

options: Lift the turns off the drum while it is still loaded
Winch in harder until the jammed turns jump free
Take the load off with a rolling hitch led to another winch
Take a clove hitch on the sheet to the nearest cleat
questions.why: A rolling hitch grips a loaded line along its length; with the strain on another winch the riding turn can be cleared.

questions.q: You are hanging fenders on the guardrail before entering a harbour where you will change their height at each berth. Which hitch do you use?

figure.note: Fender heights change at each berth

options: Reef knot, tied round the rail
Sheet bend, tied round the rail
Bowline, tied round the rail
Clove hitch, with a half hitch on top
questions.why: A clove hitch is quick to tie and to adjust on a rail; the half hitch stops it working loose.

questions.q: Your stern line is too short to reach the bollard, so you join a thinner spare line to it. Which knot?
options: A double sheet bend
A figure of eight
A clove hitch
A reef knot
questions.why: A sheet bend joins lines of different thickness; doubled, it holds better in slippery synthetic rope.

questions.q: Before a night passage your crew re-reeves the genoa sheets through the cars. What goes in the end of each sheet?
options: A half hitch round the track
A figure-of-eight stopper knot
A bowline loop
A clove hitch round the car
questions.why: A figure of eight stops the sheet running out through the car and is easy to undo.

questions.q: Your crew has made the loaded bow line fast: a turn round the base, a figure of eight, then three locking hitches piled on top. What do you tell them?

figure.note: Turn · figure of eight · 3 locking hitches

options: Take off the turn round the base first
Leave it — each extra hitch adds holding
Take off two hitches — one locking hitch is enough
Add a bowline over the horn as well
questions.why: Turn, figure of eight, one locking hitch: more hitches can jam under load and slow you when you need to let go.

questions.q: You are stowing the dinghy on deck for this passage. How do you lash it?

figure.title: Before a 40-mile passage
lines: Dinghy upside down on the coachroof

options: Shock cord to the handrails, so it can give in a sea
Loose on deck, so it can be launched in a hurry
One line over the middle, tied off to the guardrail
Several turns to strong points, frapped tight, finished with hitches
questions.why: A lashing takes several turns to strong points and frapping turns tighten it; guardrails and shock cord give way in a sea.

questions.q: After a swim your crew is exhausted in the water beside the boat and the ladder has broken. You will lift her with the main halyard. What do you tie in the middle of a spare line to make a sling?
options: A bowline on the bight
A running bowline under her arms
A reef knot round her waist
A clove hitch round her chest
questions.why: A bowline on the bight gives two fixed loops in the middle of a line that will not tighten: a seat and a chest loop.

questions.q: You are holding off the waiting pontoon and must get a line to the marinero. How do you throw it?

figure.note: Marinero on the pontoon, 10 m to port, upwind

options: Throw the whole coil in one bundle straight at him
Make the end fast, split the coil, throw past him into the wind
Make the end fast, throw short and let the wind carry it
Tie a fender to the end to give it weight, then throw
questions.why: Secure the standing end and throw the outer half of a split coil overarm; aim beyond him, as the wind will check it.

questions.q: You have bought a new length of three-strand nylon to make a mooring line with a permanent eye. How do you finish it?
options: A bowline at one end, a stopper knot on the other
An eye splice at one end, an overhand knot on the other
An eye splice at one end, a whipping on the other
A figure-of-eight loop at one end, nothing on the other
questions.why: A splice keeps most of the rope's strength and never shakes loose; a whipping stops the cut end unlaying.

questions.q: You are choosing rope for each item on this list. Which choice is right?
options: Low-stretch for the warp and mooring lines, nylon for the halyard
Polypropylene for all three — it floats and costs less
The same polyester braid for all three items
Nylon for the warp and mooring lines, low-stretch for the halyard
questions.why: Nylon stretches to absorb snatching at anchor and in a berth; a halyard must not stretch or the sail loses its shape.

questions.q: You arrive in this Breton anchorage two hours after high water to stay the night. Where do you anchor?

figure.note: Depths now · 3.0 m still to fall to LW · draft 1.9 m

options: B — sand, and enough water at LW
A — 4.2 m is plenty for a 1.9 m draft
C — the weed holds well among the moorings
A — sand, and the closest in to shelter
questions.why: Depth at LW = depth now − 3.0 m: A 1.2 m (aground), B 4.5 m; C is weed among moorings — poor holding, no room.

questions.q: You are anchored off the east coast of an island in an offshore westerly. What do you do about tonight's forecast?

figure.note: Forecast: W 4, veering N, then NE 5 after midnight

options: Stay — a NE wind blows along this coast, not onto it
Move before dark to a bay sheltered from the north-east
Move at midnight, when the wind starts to veer
Stay, and let out more chain as the wind veers
questions.why: Veering W → N → NE turns this east coast into a lee shore at night; move in daylight to shelter from the NE.

questions.q: You are motoring to your chosen spot to anchor. How do you make the approach?

figure.note: Final approach to the spot, 6 m of water

options: Downwind with way on, let go and let her swing round
Across the wind, let go and let all the chain run
Slowly into the wind, stop, let go as she starts to go astern
Slowly into the wind, let go while still going ahead
questions.why: Head to wind gives control; letting go as she moves astern lays the chain out in a line, not in a heap on the anchor.

questions.q: You anchor at low water in a Breton river to stay for 24 hours. What is the least chain you let out?
options: About 18 m
About 14 m
About 28 m
About 32 m
questions.why: Work from the HW depth at the bow: (3.6 + 3.4 + 1.0) × 4 = 32 m.

questions.q: You anchor at high water on this rode for a settled night. What is the least you let out?
options: About 54 m — 6:1 for a mostly rope rode
About 27 m — 3:1 is plenty in F3
About 36 m — 4:1, as for all chain
About 32 m — 4:1 of the water depth
questions.why: A rope rode needs more scope than chain, about 6:1 or more: (8 + 1) × 6 = 54 m.

questions.q: You have let out 30 m of chain. How do you check that the anchor is holding?

figure.note: Anchor down, 30 m out · chapel and rock in line abeam

options: Watch the depth: if it stays the same, she holds
Go astern to firm revs and watch the transit abeam
Wait for her to lie head to wind, then go below
Watch the chain: taut means the anchor is holding
questions.why: Back down under power to set it; a transit abeam that stays closed shows the boat is not moving over the ground.

questions.q: You set the plotter's anchor alarm for the night. Where do you centre it, and how big do you make it?

figure.title: Setting the anchor alarm
lines: Depth 5 m, bow roller 1 m above water
Anchor position marked on the plotter

options: On the boat now, radius about 42 m
On the anchor, radius about 15 m
On the anchor, radius about 42 m
On the boat now, radius about 100 m
questions.why: She swings round the anchor: √(30² − 6²) ≈ 29 m of chain + 12 m of boat ≈ 42 m; centred on the boat it alarms on a swing.

questions.q: Your anchor is down and holding. Will you swing clear of the rock tonight?

figure.title: Swinging room
lines: 35 m chain out, depth 5 m, roller 1 m
Rock awash 40 m east of your anchor

options: Yes — she stays within the chain's run, about 34 m
Yes — on all chain she barely swings, about 12 m
Yes — she cannot go more than 35 m from the anchor
No — her stern can reach about 46 m from the anchor
questions.why: Swing radius ≈ the chain's horizontal run plus the boat: √(35² − 6²) ≈ 34 m + 12 m ≈ 46 m — past the rock at 40 m.

questions.q: You decide to stay the night here. How do you run it?
options: Anchor watches in turns, engine ready, alarm on
You stay up alone all night so the crew can sleep
All turn in; the plotter's alarm will wake you
Let out all the chain, then everyone turns in
questions.why: In rising wind someone must be awake on deck: a rota of anchor watches, with the engine and a plan ready.

questions.q: You are on deck in seconds. What do you do?

figure.title: 0230 at anchor
lines: The transit has opened: you are moving

options: Wait — a dragging anchor usually resets itself
Start the engine, motor up to ease the load, re-anchor
Let all the remaining chain run out at once
Drop the kedge over the stern to stop her
questions.why: Engine first, to take the strain and keep control; then lift and re-anchor with more scope, or move.

questions.q: You must anchor overnight in this narrow tidal river with little swinging room. How?

figure.note: River 80 m wide · the stream turns every 6 h

options: Two anchors in tandem on one chain, both upstream
One anchor with extra scope to ride the turn of tide
A Bahamian moor: anchors up and downstream, the bow between
Bow and stern anchors, so she lies across the stream
questions.why: A Bahamian moor holds the bow between two anchors laid up and down the stream, so she turns in little more than her length.

questions.q: You have run onto a sandbank at the mouth of a river. How do you get off?
options: Let go the bower anchor at the bow and wait for the tide
Wait aboard: the rising tide will float her off as she is
Go full astern now until she slides off the sand
Lay the kedge astern into deep water by dinghy and haul on it
questions.why: A kedge laid in deep water holds her against the wind as the tide rises and lets you haul her off; hard astern sucks up sand.

questions.q: You decide to anchor here for the night. What do you rig?

figure.title: Pilot book: the anchorage
lines: Good shelter from N and W

options: A tripping line from the anchor's crown to a small buoy
A second anchor on the same chain
A rope rode, so it is cheaper to cut away
Extra scope, so the anchor digs in deeper
questions.why: A tripping line pulls the anchor out backwards by its crown if it hooks under old chain or rock.

questions.q: You are leaving this crowded bay. How do you weigh anchor?

figure.note: Y = you · 1–3 yachts at anchor, 30–40 m off

options: Lift it with the engine off, so the propeller is safe
Motor gently up the chain as the bow crew points; the windlass only lifts
Break it out at full ahead, then lift it on the move
Let the windlass haul the boat up to the anchor
questions.why: Motor up to the anchor so the windlass only lifts the chain; the crew's hand signals show where it lies and when it breaks out.

questions.q: You will go stern-to this quay on your own anchor, with the wind across the harbour. Where do you let go?

figure.note: Depth 7 m · roller 1 m · 4:1 · boat 12 m

options: About 45 m out, a little downwind of your slot
About 15 m out, straight off your slot
About 45 m out, a little upwind of your slot
About 30 m out, a little upwind of your slot
questions.why: (7 + 1) × 4 = 32 m of chain plus 12 m of boat ≈ 45 m; let go upwind, as the wind pushes you down while you reverse.

questions.q: You put the engine astern from rest on a calm day. What does the stern do first?

figure.note: Going astern from rest · right-handed propeller

options: Kicks to starboard
Goes straight back
Stays put; the bow swings to port
Kicks to port
questions.why: A right-handed propeller walks the stern to port going astern, most strongly before she gathers way.

questions.q: You can choose which side to put to this pontoon. Which, and why?

figure.title: Visitors' pontoon
lines: Space on either side of the hammerhead

options: Port side to — going astern to stop pulls the stern in
Either side — prop walk only acts at speed
Port side to — going astern swings the bow in
Starboard side to — going astern pulls the stern in
questions.why: Astern kicks the stern to port, so port side to, the brake also brings the stern in alongside.

questions.q: You must turn round in this marina fairway. Which way do you turn?

figure.note: Fairway two boat lengths wide · right-handed prop

options: To port: prop walk astern swings the bow to port
To starboard: ahead with full helm, then astern, and repeat
Either way: prop walk cancels out over a turn
To port: ahead and astern with the helm hard to port
questions.why: Astern kicks the stern to port and the bow to starboard: it helps a clockwise turn and fights an anticlockwise one.
questions.ref: Boat handling — turning in a tight space

questions.q: You motor ahead off this quay and put the helm hard to port to turn away. What does the stern do?

figure.note: Starboard side to, leaving ahead

options: Stays where it is while the bow turns
Follows the bow straight out
Swings to starboard, towards the quay
Swings to port, away from the quay
questions.why: Going ahead she pivots about a third of her length from the bow, so the stern swings opposite the turn — into the quay.

questions.q: You are coming alongside the waiting pontoon in this river. Which way do you head for the final approach?

figure.note: Mooring buoys in yellow

options: West, with the stream, to keep steerage way
West, into the wind — a yacht always lies to it
