North, straight in, so neither has a grip
East, into the stream, as the moored yachts lie
questions.why: Approach into whichever acts more on the boat — here the 2 kn stream, as the moored yachts show by lying head to it.

questions.q: You want to drop into this gap on the pontoon to starboard against a 2 kn stream. How?

figure.note: Gap: one boat length + 4 m

options: Stem the stream at its speed, angle the bow slightly in, crab across
Turn in at 90°, bow first, and let the stream swing her
Stem the stream at its speed, angle the bow slightly out
Run down with the stream and go hard astern at the gap
questions.why: Ferry gliding: stemming the stream at its speed holds you still; a small angle of the bow towards the berth moves you sideways.

questions.q: You are pinned starboard side to by the wind, with boats close ahead and astern. How do you get off?

figure.note: Wind F5 onto the pontoon · right-handed prop

options: Let go everything and go full astern with helm to port
Bow line led aft, fender the bow, slow ahead; stern out, then astern
Stern line led forward, slow astern; bow out, then ahead
Push the bow off hard, then motor ahead with helm to port
questions.why: Ahead on a bow spring swings the stern out into the wind; then astern, and prop walk to port carries the stern further off.

questions.q: The wind is blowing you off this pontoon. Your crew has made a midships line, led aft, fast to a pontoon cleat. What now?

figure.note: Wind F4 off the pontoon · midships spring on

options: Neutral, and the crew hauls her in by hand
Slow astern, wheel turned away from the pontoon
Slow ahead, wheel turned away from the pontoon
Slow ahead, wheel turned towards the pontoon
questions.why: Ahead against a midships spring pulls her in bodily; the wheel turned away from the pontoon stops the stern swinging out.

questions.q: You are picking up this mooring buoy under power. How do you make the final approach?
options: Heading north, across the stream, then stop
Heading east, then astern to stop beside it
Heading east, with the stream, slowly
Heading west, into the stream, slowly
questions.why: Stem the stream: you keep steerage at low speed and can stop over the ground with the buoy at the bow.

questions.q: The marinero hands the lazy line up to you at the stern. What do you do with it?

figure.title: Stern-to, Croatian marina
lines: Stern lines on, engine slow ahead
Marinero hands you the lazy line
Its sinker is well ahead of the bow

options: Walk it to the bow outside everything, haul it taut, cleat it
Let it drop: the two stern lines hold you in place
Walk it forward inside the shrouds, cleat it slack
Cleat it at the stern next to the stern line
questions.why: The lazy line holds the bow off the quay: take it forward clear of everything, haul taut, cleat at the bow; keep it out of the prop.

questions.q: The town quay is full and you are told to raft outside a larger yacht. How do you lie?
options: Lines to her and shore lines; masts level abeam
Lines to her and your own shore lines; masts staggered
Shore lines only, with fenders against her side
Lines to her only; she holds both boats on hers
questions.why: Your own shore lines take your weight off her; masts staggered so the spreaders cannot lock as you roll.

questions.q: You will sail onto this mooring buoy. With which sail do you make the final approach?

figure.note: Approaching the buoy under sail

options: Full sail — luff head to wind beside the buoy
Main only — luff head to wind to stop at the buoy
Jib only — furl it to slow down as you stem the tide
Main only — ease the sheet to stop as you stem the tide
questions.why: You stem the tide, so the wind is astern: a mainsail cannot be spilled downwind, a jib can be furled or let fly.

questions.q: You will sail off the anchor here. The main is up and the chain is up and down. How do you get her heading east, on port tack, as the anchor breaks out?

figure.note: Wind N 3 · open water to the east

options: Back the jib to starboard, so the bow pays off to port
Sheet the main hard in, so the bow pays off to starboard
Back the jib to starboard, so the bow pays off to starboard
Back the jib to port, so the bow pays off to starboard
questions.why: A jib held aback on the port side pushes the bow to starboard: port tack, heading east, away from the rocks.

questions.q: You want to heave to so the crew can reef in peace. How?

figure.note: Close-hauled, starboard tack · tiller steering

options: Tack, leave the jib sheet made fast, ease the main, tiller to leeward
Luff head to wind, drop the jib, lash the tiller amidships
Tack, leave the jib sheet made fast, sheet the main in, tiller to windward
Gybe, leave the jib sheet made fast, ease the main, tiller amidships
questions.why: Hove to, the backed jib pushes the bow off and the tiller lashed to leeward brings it up: she lies quietly, drifting slowly.

questions.q: You put in the first reef. In what order?

figure.title: Reefing at sea, F6
lines: Kicker and mainsheet still hard on

options: Fix the tack, pull the reef line, then ease the kicker and sheet
Ease kicker and sheet, lower the halyard, fix the tack, re-hoist, pull the reef line
Lower the halyard with the kicker still on, then fix the tack
Pull the reef line first, then lower the halyard and fix the tack
questions.why: Kicker and sheet off so the boom can rise; tack cringle on, halyard tight again, then the reef line pulls the clew down.

questions.q: You are fighting the helm on this beat; the rudder is well over all the time. What do you do first?

figure.note: Close-hauled F5 · heeled 30° · heavy weather helm

options: Sheet the main harder to flatten it
Reef the genoa and leave the main as it is
Ease the traveller down and reef the main
Move the crew to leeward to steady her
questions.why: Weather helm comes from too much main and heel: ease the traveller and reef the main, and the balance moves forward.

questions.q: You will run like this for three hours before you gybe. How do you rig a preventer?

figure.note: Running in F5 and a rolling sea

options: No preventer: ease the kicker right off instead
From the boom end straight down to the toe rail abeam
From the middle of the boom to the base of a shroud
From the boom end, forward to a bow block, back to the cockpit
questions.why: Led from the boom end to the bow and aft, it holds the boom against a gybe and can be eased from the cockpit; mid-boom it can break.

questions.q: Your boat slams and stops on every third wave on this beat. How do you steer?

figure.note: Beating into a short, steep sea · F5

options: Bear away a little for speed; luff up the face, bear off over the top
Bear away onto a beam reach and sail across the waves
Pinch as close to the wind as she will go
Hold a dead straight course and let her punch through
questions.why: Steering a little free keeps her moving; luff into the face, bear away over the crest so she does not fall off the top.

questions.q: You are entering your berth in this marina in a fresh crosswind. What is the plan?

figure.note: Fingers in grey · fairway to the east

options: Dead slow, aim at the middle; first line: leeward bow
With way on, aim at the windward finger; first line: windward midships
With way on, aim at the leeward yacht; first line: windward stern
Dead slow, aim at the windward finger; first line: leeward stern
questions.why: Some speed keeps steerage against the wind; aim upwind in the slot and get the windward midships line on first to stop her blowing down.

questions.q: You have lost your engine and this yacht will tow you into port. How do you make her towline fast on your boat?

figure.note: Engine failed · a yacht takes you in tow

options: To the windlass drum, which is built for the load
To the pulpit, so it is clear of the stem
A bridle to both bow cleats, led through the bow roller
To one bow cleat, with a hitch you can slip
questions.why: A bridle shares the load between strong points and keeps the line central; the windlass and pulpit are not built to tow.

questions.q: You are towing this yacht. How long a towline, and how fast?
options: About 10 m, at about her hull speed
About 30 m, well below her hull speed
About 40 m, at about her hull speed
About 40 m, well below her hull speed
questions.why: A multiple of the wave length (2 × 20 m) keeps both boats on the same part of a wave; near hull speed everything is overloaded.

questions.q: You must turn your catamaran to port on the spot in this fairway. How?

figure.note: Twin-engine catamaran · fairway 1.5 lengths wide

options: Port engine astern, starboard engine ahead
Both engines ahead, rudders hard to port
Port engine ahead, starboard engine astern
Port engine astern only, rudders hard to port
questions.why: The engines are far apart: one ahead and one astern spin her about her middle; port astern and starboard ahead turn her to port.

questions.q: Your crew want to go back to the boat in one trip. What do you do?

figure.title: Taverna, 2300
lines: Five crew, dinghy rated for four
400 m to the boat, wind offshore F4
Outboard with kill cord, one torch

options: One trip, with the strongest swimmer outside
Two trips, lifejackets on, kill cord on, torch showing
One trip, everyone sitting low and still
Two trips; lifejackets only for non-swimmers
questions.why: Never overload; lifejackets, the kill cord and a light — an offshore wind carries a swamped dinghy out to sea.

questions.q: You are anchored for the night on all chain and want a nylon snubber to take the load off the windlass. There is no chain hook aboard. How do you fix the snubber to the chain?
options: A reef knot round the chain
A sheet bend through a chain link
A rolling hitch round the chain
A clove hitch round the chain
questions.why: A rolling hitch grips along a loaded chain or line and will not slide; the snubber's stretch then takes the snatch off the windlass.

questions.q: You are looking over this winch before a long passage. What do you do about it?

figure.title: Port genoa winch
lines: Four turns on the drum, self-tailer fine
New lead block: sheet runs down onto the drum

options: Take a turn off the drum so the sheet runs freer
Put one more turn on the drum before it is loaded
Tighten the self-tailer jaws so the turns stay down
Re-lead the sheet so it meets the drum slightly from below
questions.why: A sheet must reach the drum a few degrees from below, so each turn is pushed up and clear; led down onto the drum, the turns ride over each other.

questions.q: Your crew is about to open the clutch on the loaded main halyard to lower the sail for a reef. What do you tell her first?

figure.note: Halyard held in a clutch, the sail fully loaded

options: Three turns on the winch, take the load, then open the clutch
Put the handle in the winch, then open the clutch
Open the clutch slowly, holding the tail in both hands
Open the clutch, then quickly take turns on the winch
questions.why: A loaded clutch opened with no turns on the winch lets the halyard run and burns hands; take the load on the winch, then ease it out.

questions.q: Your crew must ease the loaded genoa sheet a few centimetres on a winch with no self-tailer. She has wrapped the tail twice round her hand for grip. What do you tell her?

figure.note: No self-tailer · easing a few centimetres

options: Flick all the turns off the drum, then re-wrap
Unwrap it; palm flat on the turns, ease a little at a time
Turn the winch handle backwards to ease it out
Fine — the wraps give her the grip she needs
questions.why: A loaded sheet can run without warning and drag a wrapped hand into the winch; ease with the palm on the turns and the tail free.

questions.q: You are buying a new painter for the dinghy you tow astern between anchorages. Which rope do you choose?
options: Low-stretch polyester braid, so it stays short
Nylon, so it stretches when the dinghy snatches
Floating polypropylene, so it stays clear of the propeller
Dyneema, so it is thin and very strong
questions.why: A painter that sinks can wrap round the propeller when you go astern; floating polypropylene stays on the surface.

questions.q: You are staying two nights on this quay. What do you do about your lines?

figure.title: Harbour wall, swell running in
lines: Boat surging on her lines all night
Lines run over a rough concrete edge
Single nylon bow, stern and springs

options: Change to low-stretch lines, which wear less
Leave them; nylon is strong enough on its own
Haul every line bar-tight so she cannot move
Chafe guards at the edge, double the lines, add snubbers
questions.why: In a surge keep the stretch and stop the chafe: guards where the lines touch, doubled lines, and snubbers to soften each snatch.

questions.q: You are coiling the long braided tail of the main halyard after hoisting, and every round turn twists it into kinks. How do you coil it?
options: In figure-of-eights, which add no twist
In tight turns round your hand and elbow
In anticlockwise turns, twisting each one out
In clockwise turns, twisting each one in
questions.why: Braid has no lay, so round turns twist it; figure-of-eight loops cancel the twist and the line runs out clean.

questions.q: You decide to lay the kedge in tandem with the bower. How is it rigged?

figure.title: Gale tonight, open bay
lines: Weed over sand, holding only fair
Bower 20 kg; kedge 12 kg with 5 m chain

options: Kedge slid halfway down the bower's chain as a weight
Kedge ahead of the bower, its chain shackled to the bower's crown
Kedge on its own rode, dropped 30 m off to one side
Kedge shackled to the bower's ring, the two side by side
questions.why: In tandem the kedge lies ahead on a short chain from the bower's crown, both in one line: for a strong wind from one steady direction.

questions.q: Your anchor is just below the surface, with the other chain hooked over it. How do you free it?

figure.title: Leaving the town quay, Hydra
lines: You lay stern-to on your own anchor
It comes up with a chain across it
The neighbour's chain, laid over yours

options: Motor hard ahead to drag your anchor out from under it
Lift both higher on the windlass, then drop them with a jerk
Pass a line under his chain, make it fast aboard, lower yours clear
Lower yours to the bottom again and motor away fast
questions.why: Take his chain's weight on a line from your deck, lower your anchor clear of it, then slip the line from aboard.

questions.q: You are leaving at dawn and the anchor will not break out. What do you do next?
options: Keep the windlass hauling until the anchor breaks out
Cut the chain at once and buoy the end to come back
Cleat the chain short and go full ahead into the wind
Cleat the chain short, motor slowly the opposite way to the set
questions.why: Take the strain off the windlass, then pull from the other side: an anchor hooked under something often comes out the way it went in.

questions.q: The anchor has started to drag again. What do you do?

figure.title: 0300 at anchor
lines: Rocks 150 m astern, open sea 1 M out
Engine fine, crew of four awake

options: Weigh and motor out to open water until daylight
Re-anchor and hold her up on the engine all night
Let out all the chain and set the alarm again
Re-anchor closer in, where the water is shallower
questions.why: Holding has failed twice, the onshore wind is rising and rocks are close astern: sea room is the safe place until daylight.

questions.q: You will anchor in this Greek bay before a blow. Which spot do you choose?

figure.note: No tide · 40 m chain, roller 1 m · 5:1 for F6

options: C — 9 m of sand: 40 m is over 4:1 of the depth
B — 7 m of sand: 40 m is 5:1 with the roller
A — 6 m of weed: it leaves the most chain spare
C — 9 m of sand: the bower holds best when deep
questions.why: Scope counts from the bow roller: (7 + 1) × 5 = 40 m. At C you would need 50 m, and A's weed holds badly.

questions.q: You are on all chain and arrive in this crowded bay for the night. Where do you anchor?

figure.note: Light winds, shifting overnight

options: B — the boats on rope lie quietly, well apart
B — just upwind of them, where the bottom is clear
A — among the boats lying to chain, as you do
C — boats on buoys barely swing, so room is easy
questions.why: Boats on similar rodes swing alike; rope rodes range widely and buoys hardly at all, so a chain boat among them touches when the wind shifts.

questions.q: You are writing the orders for tonight's anchor watch. Which do you write?
options: If she drags, let out more chain, then call me
Call me at the end of each watch with a report
Call me only if the plotter's anchor alarm goes off
Call me if a bearing shifts, the wind tops F5, or a boat drags near
questions.why: The watch must know exactly when to wake you: the bearings that show dragging, a wind limit, another boat moving — before it is urgent.

questions.q: The wind wakes you and you come up to find this. What do you do first?

figure.title: 0100 at anchor
lines: A yacht 50 m upwind is dragging onto you
No one moving on her deck
Wind F6; your anchor holding well

options: Engine on, fenders out, horn and a torch to wake her crew
Call the coastguard on channel 16 and wait for them
Weigh anchor at once and leave the bay in the dark
Go to the bow to fend her off by hand as she comes
questions.why: Be ready to move or take the blow, and wake her crew with sound and light; hands between two hulls in F6 get crushed.

questions.q: You are rigging a tripping line before you let go. How long do you make it?
options: About 13 m
About 8 m
About 4 m
About 6.5 m
questions.why: Depth at HW 4.0 + 2.5 = 6.5 m; a little more keeps the buoy afloat at HW without a long loop on the surface at LW.

questions.q: Your stern lines are on, but the bow is sagging downwind towards your neighbour. What do you do?

figure.note: Stern lines on · your anchor 45 m out to the south

options: Run a line from your bow to the neighbour's bow
Ease the anchor chain so the bow can settle by itself
Tighten the anchor chain on the windlass, then trim the stern lines
Haul both stern lines bar-tight to pull her straight
questions.why: The anchor holds the bow up to windward: take up the chain until she lies straight, then adjust the stern lines to keep clear of the quay.

questions.q: You anchor your catamaran for the night. How do you take the load off the windlass?
options: Leave the chain on the windlass brake all night
Make the chain fast round the foot of the mast
A single snubber from one bow cleat to the chain
A bridle from both bows to a hook on the chain
questions.why: A bridle from both hulls holds the cat straight to the wind, takes the snatch off the windlass and stops her sheering about.

questions.q: You anchor two hours after low water and will stay through high water. Using the rule of twelfths, what is the least chain you let out?
options: About 30 m
About 16 m
About 35 m
About 21 m

questions.q: You engage astern from rest to back into your slot. What does the stern do first, and how do you allow for it?

figure.title: Stern-to, calm harbour
lines: Your slot dead astern, 3 lengths off

options: Kicks to starboard: go astern dead slow all the way in
Kicks to starboard: start with the stern a little to port of the line
Kicks to port: start with the stern a little to starboard of the line
Goes straight back: prop walk only matters at speed
questions.why: A left-handed propeller walks the stern to starboard going astern; aim off to port and get sternway on so the rudder takes over.

questions.q: Which way will her stern kick when you go astern from rest?

figure.title: Taking over a charter boat
lines: Nobody knows which way she walks
Lines on, you go astern at 1500 rpm
The wash boils up along her port side

options: To port — she behaves like a right-handed prop
To port — the stern follows the side of the wash
To starboard — she behaves like a left-handed prop
Neither way — a fixed propeller has no prop walk
questions.why: The wash comes out on the side opposite the kick: wash to port means the stern walks to starboard, as with a left-handed propeller.

questions.q: You reverse out of this pen into the fairway, turning the wheel to bring the stern round to port. Which part of the boat do you watch most closely?

figure.note: Bow-in pen · a yacht 1 m off each side

options: The stern — going astern she pivots near the bow
The keel — she pivots on it whichever way she goes
The stern — the pivot point stays amidships
The bow — going astern she pivots near the stern
questions.why: Going astern the pivot point moves aft, so the bow sweeps a wide arc and can hit the boat beside you as you turn.

questions.q: You are leaving this pontoon with the stream from ahead and boats close ahead and astern. How do you get the bow out?

figure.note: Starboard side to · wind light

options: Single up to a stern spring, let go forward; the stream pushes the bow out
Single up to a bow spring, let go aft; the stream pushes the stern out
Let go everything and motor out with the helm hard over
Single up to a stern line led aft and go slow astern
questions.why: The stream from ahead holds her back on the stern spring and gets between bow and pontoon; once the bow is out, go ahead and slip.
questions.ref: Leaving a berth — using the stream

questions.q: You are leaving this bow-in berth astern, with the wind on the beam. How do you do it?

figure.note: Wind E 4, on the starboard beam · finger to starboard

options: Slip the windward lines first, then go astern dead slow
Slip the leeward lines, the windward ones last; go astern firmly
Slip every line at once and let her drift out astern
Slip the leeward lines first, then go astern dead slow
questions.why: The windward lines hold her off the yacht to leeward until the last moment; firm sternway gives the rudder grip before the bow blows off.
questions.ref: Leaving a berth in a crosswind

questions.q: You are coming alongside this pontoon with the wind blowing you onto it. How do you make the approach?

figure.note: Berth: starboard side to

options: Come in bow first and get the bow line on before the stern
Come in parallel with way on and stop right alongside
Stop parallel, about a beam's width off, and let her blow in
Come in at 45° and turn parallel at the last moment
questions.why: With the wind onto the berth, stop level with it a little way off: she drifts in square, with fenders low and lines ready fore and aft.

questions.q: Your berth is on the leeward side of this pontoon, so she will blow off it as soon as she stops. What approach do you plan?

figure.note: Berth: port side to · wind off the pontoon

options: A shallow angle, dead slow; the stern line on first
Stop parallel a beam's width off and let her drift in
A steeper angle, dead slow; the bow line on first
A steeper angle with more way; the midships line on first
questions.why: Blown off, she must be got in before she stops: a steeper angle with enough way, then the midships line holds her while you motor in on it.

questions.q: You are picking up a mooring here under power, with the wind against the tide. Which way do you head for the final approach?

figure.note: Wind against tide

options: West, into the wind, as the moored yachts lie
East, with the wind astern, to keep good steerage
North, across both, and stop beside the buoy
East, into the stream — a buoy is always taken uptide
questions.why: Approach the way the moored boats lie: here the F5 wind beats the weak stream, so she stops best heading west, into it.

questions.q: Your bow crew has the buoy's pick-up line on the boat hook, but the bow is falling away fast and the hook is being dragged from her hands. What should she do?

figure.note: Pick-up hooked · the bow is falling away

options: Jam the handle against the pulpit and hold on
Let go of the hook; you will come round again
Hold on and lean back to stop the boat
Kneel down and hold on with both hands
questions.why: A boat hook cannot hold a yacht: let it go, keep the crew aboard, and make another approach slower and closer.
questions.ref: Picking up a mooring — the boat hook

questions.q: You stop for lunch on this buoy and will sail off it later. How do you make fast?

figure.note: Lunch stop, then you sail off

options: A round turn and two half hitches on the ring
A bowline through the ring, its tail cleated aboard
A slip line through the ring, both ends cleated aboard
A clove hitch round the ring, its tail cleated aboard
questions.why: A slip line is let go from the deck in seconds — one end freed and pulled back through — with no one reaching down to the buoy.

questions.q: You are going stern-to in this lazy-line marina with the wind across the berth. Which line goes on first?

figure.note: Lazy-line marina · wind W 4 across the berth

options: The leeward stern line, then the lazy line to the bow
The lazy line first, then both stern lines together
Both stern lines first, then the lazy line at leisure
The windward stern line, then the lazy line to the bow
questions.why: The windward stern line stops her blowing down onto the next boat; then the lazy line, taken forward quickly, holds the bow up.

questions.q: You are ready to leave this berth. In what order do you let go?

figure.title: Leaving a lazy-line berth
lines: Stern lines and lazy line on
Engine running, crew at bow and stern

options: Drop the lazy line, let it sink, slip the stern lines, go
Slip every line at once and motor straight out
Slip the stern lines, go ahead, then drop the lazy line
Drop the lazy line and go ahead hard as it sinks
questions.why: The lazy line must be on the bottom before the propeller turns ahead; the stern lines hold her while it sinks.

questions.q: You are the inside boat of this raft and must leave first. How do you get out?

figure.note: You: inside, port side to the quay

options: Out ahead, up-tide; she swings in on a stern line to the quay
Out astern, down-tide; she swings in on a bow line to the quay
Out astern, down-tide; she swings in on a stern line to the quay
Out ahead, up-tide, once she has let go and motored clear
questions.why: Leave down-tide: the outer boat keeps her up-tide bow line, now led to the quay, and the stream swings her in behind you.

questions.q: You are towing the dinghy and are about to reverse into a Med berth. What do you do with it first?
options: Leave it astern on its long painter as it is
Lengthen the painter so it trails well clear
Pull it alongside on a short painter, clear of the prop
Pull it right up under the stern, against the transom
questions.why: Going astern you run over your own painter; tie the dinghy short alongside, forward of the propeller, before you reverse.

questions.q: You will sail onto anchor at X, among the other yachts. How do you make the final approach?

figure.note: Wind N 3 · no stream · • yachts at anchor

options: Under main alone, let go while she still has way on
Under full sail, let go at speed so the anchor bites
Under jib alone, run in downwind and let go at speed
Under main alone, luff to stop, let go as she falls back
questions.why: The main alone lets her luff head to wind and stop; let go as she gathers sternway, so the chain lays out and the anchor sets.

questions.q: You are lying to the stream on this mooring, with the wind from astern. How do you sail off?

figure.note: Lying head to the stream · moorings all round

options: Unroll the jib, slip, and sail clear; hoist the main later
Hoist the main, slip, and let the stream carry you back
Hoist main and jib, slip, and sail off close-hauled
Hoist the main, slip, and bear away clear
questions.why: With the wind from astern the main cannot go up cleanly — it fills against the shrouds; the jib alone is set and furled at will.

questions.q: The watch leader calls you below. When and how do you reef?

figure.title: 0200, watch of two
lines: Wind SW 5 and rising, F6 forecast
Slab reefing, lines led to the cockpit

options: At F6, when the reef is really needed
Now, from the cockpit, everyone clipped on, the main eased
Now, bearing away to a run to take the load off
At dawn, when everyone can see what they are doing
questions.why: Reef early at night: the work is slower in the dark, so do it before it is urgent — clipped on, main eased, lines led aft.

questions.q: You need to roll away half the genoa. How do you do it?

figure.note: F6 · furling genoa · the main already reefed

options: Winch in the furling line with the sheet still hard on
Let the sheet fly, then winch in the furling line
Ease the sheet under control while you pull in the furling line
Luff head to wind and let it flog while you furl
questions.why: Some tension on the sheet rolls the sail tight and even; a flogging genoa rolls loose and chafes, and a sheet left hard on overloads the furler.

questions.q: You have been running with a preventer for hours and must now gybe. What do you do first?

figure.note: Running for hours, preventer on · time to gybe

options: Free the preventer as the boom swings across
Ease the main right out, then put the helm over
Gybe with the preventer on; it controls the boom
Free the preventer and sheet the main in to the centre
questions.why: A preventer left on stops the gybe and lays her over; free it, centre the boom, gybe, ease out, then re-rig it on the new side.

questions.q: You are running with the boom out to starboard, and the wind has crept round to where the figure shows it. What do you do?

figure.note: Wind over the starboard quarter · boom to starboard

options: Turn a few degrees to port, to bring the wind to port
Turn a few degrees to starboard, to run deeper
Ease the main right out against the shroud
Hold on; the kicker will keep the boom out
questions.why: Wind on the same side as the boom means you are by the lee and close to a gybe; turn away from the boom side until the wind is on the other quarter.

questions.q: You plan to heave to here until it is light. Is there room?

figure.title: Waiting for daylight
lines: The lee shore is 4 M downwind

options: Yes — about 1.2 M of drift leaves 2.8 M spare
No — about 4.8 M of drift; heave to further out
Yes — hove to, she lies almost stopped
Yes — about 3.6 M of drift leaves a margin
questions.why: Hove to she still drifts: 4 h × 1.2 kn = 4.8 M, more than the 4 M to the shore. Heave to with room to spare.

questions.q: Your catamaran keeps stopping head to wind when you tack in this chop. What do you change?

figure.note: Catamaran · F4, short chop · she stalls tacking

options: Let the jib sheet fly as soon as the helm goes over
Sheet the main hard in as you come through the wind
Hold the jib aback until the bows are well through
Put the helm over slowly so she loses less speed
questions.why: Light and with little keel, a cat loses way fast head to wind; the backed jib pushes the bows round onto the new tack.

questions.q: She won't point, and you hold the tiller to leeward to stop her bearing away in the gusts. What do you do?

figure.note: Two reefs in the main, full genoa · F5

options: Sheet the genoa in harder to make her point
Ease the mainsheet to take power out of the main
Move the crew forward to lift the stern
Roll away some genoa to bring the balance aft
questions.why: Lee helm means too much sail forward: with two reefs in the main, reduce the genoa until the helm is near neutral or a little weather.

questions.q: A yacht with a failed engine asks you for a tow into harbour, 6 miles away. Which of your lines do you use as the towline?
options: The nylon anchor warp, for its stretch
The floating dinghy painter, for safety
The polyester genoa sheets, joined together
The Dyneema spare halyard, for its strength
questions.why: Nylon stretches and absorbs the snatch of a tow; low-stretch line shock-loads the cleats, and a thin painter can part.

questions.q: The tow has two hours still to run. What do you do about the towline?

figure.title: Towing, hour three of five
lines: 40 m of nylon out, moderate swell
Line jerks bar-tight every few waves

options: Shorten it so the line never goes slack
Lengthen it, hang a weight in the middle, pad the fairlead
Swap to a low-stretch line that won't snatch
Speed up so the line stays tight all the time
questions.why: A longer line with a weight in the middle sags and cushions each snatch; a chafe guard at the fairlead stops it wearing through.

questions.q: You will tow this yacht to harbour. What speed and ETA do you plan?

figure.title: A long tow
lines: Her hull speed is about 7 kn
You can tow at 5 or at 7 kn

options: 5 kn, ETA 1540
7 kn, ETA 1414
5 kn, ETA 1524
7 kn, ETA 1409
questions.why: Tow well below her hull speed: 22 ÷ 5 = 4.4 h = 4 h 24 min, so 1100 + 4 h 24 min = 1524.

questions.q: You will tow this yacht with your boat. Where do you make the towline fast?

figure.note: You are towing · one towline

options: One stern cleat, on the side the wind comes from
The backstay chainplate, in the middle of the stern
The pushpit rail, high enough to clear the rudder
A bridle from both quarters, so the pull is central
questions.why: A bridle across both quarters spreads the load and keeps the pull central, so you can still steer; a pushpit or backstay fitting is not built for it.

questions.q: You have towed this yacht to the marina entrance. How do you take her the last 400 m?

figure.title: Into the marina
lines: Last 400 m through a tight marina
Calm; you are an 11 m yacht

options: Alongside, your stern aft of hers, lines and springs tight
Alongside, bows level, with bow and stern lines only
Alongside, your bow ahead of hers, with one spring
Astern on a short towline, at dead slow speed
questions.why: An alongside tow steers like one boat: your rudder and prop aft of her stern, and tight springs to take the load ahead and astern.

questions.q: You are holding your catamaran beam-on to the wind while you wait for a berth, and her bows keep blowing off. How do you bring them back up without moving ahead?

figure.note: Twin-engine catamaran · bows blowing off

options: Leeward engine astern, windward one in neutral
Leeward engine ahead, windward engine astern
Windward engine ahead, leeward engine astern
Both engines ahead, the rudders to windward
questions.why: The bows have less grip and blow off first; leeward ahead with windward astern turns her on the spot, bows towards the wind.

questions.q: Your catamaran is pinned to this pontoon, with boats close ahead and astern. How do you swing the stern out to leave astern?

figure.note: Catamaran · wind W 5 · bow spring on

options: Both engines ahead, the rudders hard to port
Port engine astern, starboard engine in neutral
Port engine ahead, starboard engine in neutral
Starboard engine ahead, port engine in neutral
questions.why: On the bow spring the outboard engine's thrust, far from the spring, swings the stern out; then both astern to back away.

questions.q: How do you tow the dinghy on this passage?

figure.title: Before a 12-mile passage
lines: Forecast: following wind F4, short sea

options: Outboard aboard, one painter, right up to the transom
Outboard left on, one painter, close under the stern
Outboard left on, one painter, as long as it will go
Outboard aboard, two painters, on the back of a wave
questions.why: Lift the outboard aboard, add a second painter in case one parts, and set the length so she rides on the back of a following wave.
